# H.264 decoding

Status: Accepted. Code: [`crates/coreav-h264`](../../crates/coreav-h264)
(parsing, entropy decoding, control code) and
[`crates/coreav-kernels-h264`](../../crates/coreav-kernels-h264) (pixel
kernels). The decoder reaches users only through an opt-in backend of the
decode boundary (`docs/design/decode.md`), never in a default build.

## What this is

Track N of the roadmap asks whether CoreAV
can decode H.264 itself, in memory-safe Rust, correctly and fast enough to
be worth shipping. Two spikes answered the first halves of the question:

- N1 (`docs/spikes/h264-n1/`, passed): a clean-room decoder is bit-exact
  on all 97 in-scope JVT conformance bitstreams and agrees with FFmpeg frame
  for frame on the real-file corpus.
- N2 (`docs/spikes/h264-n2/`): with Rust control code and Rust-intrinsics
  kernels it decodes at a median 1.476 (x86-64) and 1.499 (arm64) times
  FFmpeg's single-threaded time — above the 1.15 pass bar. There is no kill
  threshold: the bar to meet is 1.15, on the path to parity that the FFmpeg speed
  bars set out.

The stage-gate verdict was to **graduate the decoder now and
continue the performance work in the production crate**. This note is the
design of that production decoder, and it pre-registers the bars it is
measured against. Spike code is never moved here as it is: the
production decoder is written fresh under the hardened gates, with the
spikes as the record of what works.

## Scope

In scope, as in N1: the streams a High profile decoder must decode (clause
A.2.4: `profile_idc` 77 or 100, or `constraint_set1_flag` = 1), with
`chroma_format_idc` = 1 (4:2:0), 8-bit luma and chroma, and
`frame_mbs_only_flag` = 1 (progressive frames). Both entropy coders (CAVLC
and CABAC), I, P and B slices, multiple slices per picture, long-term
references, memory management control operations, all three picture order
count types, and the 8x8 transform and scaling lists of High profile.

Out of scope, each rejected with [`Error::Unsupported`]: field pictures and
MBAFF, 4:2:2 and 4:4:4, bit depths above 8, lossless transform bypass, data
partitioning, SP and SI slices, slice groups (FMO and ASO), and the
extensions of Annexes G, H and I (SVC, MVC, 3D-AVC). A stream outside the
scope is an error, never a wrong picture.

## Packaging: opt-in, separately packaged, with a disclaimer

Decoding H.264 can need a patent licence depending on the jurisdiction and
the use. The roadmap therefore allows
shipping it only as an opt-in, separately packaged backend before the patents
expire, and the maintainer owns that decision.

What follows from that, and what the code enforces:

1. No default build contains the decoder. The CLI, the Python module, the
   WebAssembly module and the npm packages reach it only through a
   non-default Cargo feature. A default build that is asked for the native
   H.264 backend fails with `unsupported_feature`, as the FFmpeg fallback
   does.
2. Backend selection does not change: NVDEC where it is available, then the
   sandboxed FFmpeg fallback. The native decoder is chosen only when the
   operator names it.
3. `crates/coreav-h264/README.md` and the crate's documentation state the
   patent position and that the crate is not enabled by default. The same
   disclaimer goes in the backend's documentation.
4. Publishing anything that contains it (crates.io, PyPI, npm, a public
   release) is on the maintainer's list, as is any change to the default
   selection.

The crates are workspace members, so CI builds, lints, tests and fuzzes them
like everything else. Being a workspace member is not being in a default
build: nothing in a shipped artifact depends on them unless the feature is
on.

## Architecture

```
coreav-h264                         safe Rust, forbid(unsafe_code) but src/fast/
  nal      NAL headers, Annex B and length-prefixed framing, RBSP
  bits     the RBSP bit reader (u(n), ue(v), se(v), te(v))
  params   sequence and picture parameter sets, scaling lists
  slice    slice headers, reference list construction, marking
  cabac    the arithmetic decoding engine and the binarizations
  cavlc    the variable-length codes
  mb       the macroblock layer: modes, residuals, reconstruction
  inter    motion vector prediction, reference fetching, weighting
  deblock  boundary strengths and the filter's driver
  dpb      the decoded picture buffer, output order
  picture  decoded pictures and their cropping

coreav-kernels-h264                 deny(unsafe_code) from the SIMD step on
  views    Block, BlockMut, IntraMut, EdgeMut: validated windows of samples
  intra    intra prediction's reference, safe Rust
  scalar   the reference kernels, safe Rust
  simd     AVX2 and NEON behind the same trait (SIMD step)

coreav-backend-h264                 safe Rust, forbid(unsafe_code)
  lib      the `native` backend of the decode boundary: avcC, packets
           in, frames out, the boundary's limits as the decoder's
```

### Sans-IO, and limits everywhere

The decoder reads no files, and starts no threads unless the caller asks
for them (`Decoder::with_threads`, "Threading (step 7): our design"). The
caller hands it NAL units; it hands back pictures. `AnnexB` turns a byte stream arriving in
chunks into NAL units without I/O, and `length_prefixed` does the same for
MP4 and Matroska samples. This is what lets the same code run in a
WebAssembly build and inside the decode boundary on a server.

Every entry point takes [`Limits`]. The decode
defaults the limits policy left "TBD from Stage 1 measurements"
are set here for H.264:

| Limit | Default | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `max_mbs` | 139,264 | MaxFS of level 6.2 (Table A-1); 8192x4320 is 138,240 |
| `max_dpb_frames` | 16 | the specification's own maximum (clause A.3.1) |
| `max_slices_per_picture` | 139,264 | one slice per macroblock is legal |
| `max_nal_bytes` | 64 MiB | bounds what the byte-stream splitter holds |

A caller that knows what it is willing to decode lowers them:
`Limits::for_size(1920, 1080)` bounds the picture size to that. The decode
boundary sets them from its own policy, so an upload cannot make a worker
allocate an 8K picture.

### The kernel boundary

Pixel work happens in `coreav-kernels-h264` behind one trait. The decoder
hands each kernel a `Block`, `BlockMut` or `EdgeMut`: a view built once from
a plane, an offset and a geometry, whose constructor checks every length,
stride and range with checked arithmetic. A kernel reads and writes only
inside its view, so a SIMD implementation's `unsafe` rests on the view's
invariant instead of on the decoder's control code being right.

Decisions:

1. **Views instead of raw slices, strides and offsets.** The N2 spike passed
   `(slice, offset, stride, w, h)` and validated them in a `checked` wrapper
   module. Its post-run review found three defects at exactly that boundary
   (an intermediate pointer formed past the end of a plane, edge geometries
   whose lines overlap, and length checks that could overflow). A view makes
   those states unrepresentable: the overlap rule is part of `EdgeMut::new`,
   and every range is computed once, with `checked_*`, before any sample is
   touched. Rejected: keeping the wrapper functions (the same defect class
   stays reachable); returning `Result` from the kernels themselves (the
   check then runs per call, in the hot path, and a kernel cannot fail for
   any other reason).
2. **The scalar kernels are the reference and are shipped.** They are what
   the WebAssembly build runs and what `--kernels scalar` selects, and every
   other implementation is compared against them bit for bit. They are
   therefore written for clarity first, but without allocation and without
   per-sample bounds checks: the views hand out exact row slices and the
   kernels iterate over them.
3. **One trait, monomorphised.** The decoder is generic over `Kernels`
   (`Decoder<K>`), and `Auto::detect()` picks the implementation at run
   time. Rejected: `dyn Kernels` (a virtual call per 4x4 block), and
   compiling the whole decoder for `x86-64-v3` (the control code would get
   AVX2 and BMI2 too, which is not comparable with FFmpeg's baseline C).
4. **`Simd` is the implementation; `Auto` decides when it is worth
   calling.** A `#[target_feature]` function cannot be inlined, so a
   kernel over a 4x4 block, or over four chroma samples a row, is as fast
   in the reference, which the compiler inlines and vectorizes itself.
   A kernel that uses only the target's baseline (SSE2 on x86-64) needs no
   `#[target_feature]` and is inlined like the reference; chroma
   interpolation is one ("Kernel round: chroma interpolation inlined").
   Where small blocks come in groups, the trait takes the group in one
   call instead: the 4x4 inverse transform goes four blocks a call
   (`idct4x4_add_quad`, round 9).
   `Simd` takes the vector path wherever it has one, so that a test, a
   benchmark or a fuzz target reaches every kernel; `Auto`, which the
   decoder uses, holds the measured rule about which is faster, per
   architecture (`examples/bench.rs` is the measurement, recorded in
   `docs/measurements/h264-kernels.md`). Rejected: putting the rule in
   `Simd` (a differential test then compares two paths to the same
   reference); rejected: using the vector path everywhere (slower on the
   small shapes); rejected: dropping the small shapes from the trait (the
   decoder needs them, and the reference defines what they give).
5. **No `unsafe` outside the kernel crate, except the hot-path module's sites.**
   Parsing of untrusted bytes, CABAC, CAVLC and all control code stay in
   safe Rust, except at the named sites of
   `src/fast/` that the hot-path exception allows, each with a
   bit-identical safe twin.
   The CABAC engine is treated separately below.

### Pictures that need no other picture

`Mode::KeyframesOnly` decodes the pictures that need no other picture and
skips the rest, which is most of the work of a stream and all a thumbnail
at a keyframe needs.

**What it guarantees.** For each access unit whose picture is one, the
mode returns the picture full decoding *decodes* for that access unit,
sample for sample, and returns them in decode order. It is bar C5, and
`crates/coreav-h264/tests/conformance.rs` checks it both ways: nothing the
mode returns is a picture full decoding does not return for the same
access unit, and no IDR access unit fails to produce one. The access unit
of a picture is carried through the reordering by the caller's mark
(`Decoder::set_mark`, `Picture::mark`), so the two runs are compared
picture by picture rather than by position.

What it does not promise is the *output* process: a later access unit may
tell a full decoder to drop pictures it has decoded but not yet output
(`no_output_of_prior_pics_flag`, clause C.4.4), and a keyframe-only
decoder has returned them already. A caller that asked for the frame at
that access unit wants it, and no decoder can know the future.

**A keyframe is decoded as if the stream started at it.** When a picture
is skipped, nothing of it is kept: not its samples, not its place in the
decoded picture buffer, and not the state the next picture would predict
from. The decoder is therefore restarted at each keyframe (the picture
order count origin, `frame_num`, the random access state and the buffer),
which is exactly what "needs no other picture" means. Rejected: carrying
the skipped pictures' state forward by parsing their slice headers. It
costs the bookkeeping of a full decode in the mode whose point is to skip
it, and it is what broke the first version: the keyframes of an open group
of pictures came out with a picture order count derived from skipped
pictures and were dropped as preceding the random access point, and the
`frame_num` of a keyframe after skipped pictures looked like a gap —
which, where the stream allows gaps, had the decoder *decode* an inferred
picture for each skipped one.

**A picture is a keyframe only if every one of its slices is intra.** Two
conformance streams (`CABAST3_Sony_E`, `CABASTBR3_Sony_B`) mix intra and
predicted slices in one picture; such a picture is decoded in part and not
returned. Rejected: deciding per slice, which returns the intra slices of
a mixed picture as a picture of their own, which full decoding never
returns.

**Picture boundaries come from the last slice seen**, not from whether a
picture is being decoded: clause 7.4.1.2.4 compares consecutive slices,
and in this mode the slices between two keyframes are not decoded. Where
the stream itself says an access unit ended — an SEI, an access unit
delimiter, an end of sequence or stream, `Decoder::flush`, or
`Decoder::end_access_unit` from a caller whose packets are access units —
the comparison is dropped and the next slice starts a picture, whatever
its header holds.

### Reusing a picture without clearing it

The decoder keeps a pool of pictures and hands out whichever one nothing
else holds. It does not clear the one it hands out. Clearing a 1080p
frame costs about 3 MB of stores, and a conforming stream writes every
sample of every picture anyway, so the clear is wasted work on every
picture of every stream.

What makes that safe is an invariant: **a macroblock whose `MbInfo.slice`
is not 0 has had all 384 of its samples written.** Every macroblock path
writes its whole area before `finish_mb` records it — I\_PCM copies 384
samples or fails first, intra predicts every block before any residual is
added, and the four inter paths tile the macroblock completely, including
the case where neither list is used. A macroblock whose decode fails part
way never reaches `finish_mb`, so it keeps `slice == 0`, which is the safe
direction.

The uncovered macroblocks are filled with grey as `Picture::black` leaves
them, and their motion cleared, by the deblocking loop as it passes them
(`BandData::clear_macroblock`): it visits every macroblock anyway, so a
conforming stream pays one test per macroblock and nothing else.
Deblocking never sees an uncovered macroblock: it skips `slice == 0` and
does not take one as a neighbour, which is why filling it when its row is
filtered is as good as filling it before decoding starts. Filling at the
end of the picture would be too late for a band published before the
picture ends ("Threading (step 7): our design").

The same reasoning does not reach the pictures invented for a frame\_num
gap (clause 8.2.5.2), which no slice covers at all. Those are concealed
from the previous reference picture where there is one of the same size,
and filled with grey where there is not — without that they would keep
the pool's previous contents, and they are stored as references a later
picture may predict from.

The motion field is a separate matter and *is* cleared per picture:
intra macroblocks never write motion, but the deblocking filter reads the
motion of every macroblock through `strengths()`, so a stale entry there
would change the output of a conforming stream. That difference —
samples are only read where they were written, motion is read
everywhere — is why one may be left dirty and the other may not.

A conforming stream is unaffected by any of this. A stream that stops
mid-macroblock sees a changed concealment: the partly written macroblock
used to keep its partial samples and is now grey. Both are deterministic;
neither is more correct than the other under clause 8.2.5.2.

### The decode-boundary backend

`coreav-backend-h264` is the `native` backend of `coreav-decode`
(`docs/design/decode.md`): `NativeH264` says which streams it takes and
opens a decoder for them; `NativeDecoder` takes one access unit per packet
and returns frames in display order. It is a separate crate because it is
separately packaged (above) and because the decoder itself stays sans-IO
and free of the boundary's types.

- **One packet is one access unit**, length-prefixed as the `avcC` in
  `StreamConfig.config` says, or an Annex B byte stream where there is no
  record. The backend reads the record for the length size and feeds its
  parameter sets to the decoder when it opens.
- **The scope is decided before a decoder is opened.** A profile code
  point says nothing about interlaced coding, slice groups or lossless
  transform bypass; the parameter sets do, and `supports` reads them
  (`Decoder::parameter_sets_in_scope`). Selection then falls through to
  the next backend, which is the whole point of an opt-in backend: if
  the first packet were the first refusal, `coreav_decode::open` would
  have returned this decoder already and the operation would fail where
  the fallback would have decoded it. A stream that declares it may code
  field pictures (`frame_mbs_only_flag` 0) is refused here as well,
  before a field picture appears far into it. What only the slices
  decide — data partitioning, SP and SI slices — is still refused when
  they arrive.
- **Timestamps come back with their pictures.** The decoder returns
  pictures in display order, which is not decode order, so each packet is
  marked (`Decoder::set_mark`) and the mark read back from the picture
  gives `Frame.pts`. The marks of packets that produced no picture are
  dropped once they are older than a decoded picture can wait for output
  (a full buffer, 16 frames).
- **`Packet.discard` means decode it and keep its frame to yourself**: the
  frame is not built at all, which saves the copy out of the decoder.
- **The limits are the boundary's.** `max_pixels`, `max_width` and
  `max_height` become the decoder's `max_mbs`, `max_reference_frames` its
  `max_dpb_frames` and `max_packet_bytes` its `max_nal_bytes`, each no
  wider than the decoder's own default; `check_frame`, `max_decoded_bytes`
  and `max_pending_bytes` are checked per frame, and the deadline on every
  call. An in-process backend has no address space of its own to run into,
  so `max_memory_bytes` becomes the decoder's own budget, which it checks
  before the first picture of each coded size: it decodes with fewer
  threads, or refuses the stream with `Limit`, rather than decode it into
  the host's memory ("Limits").
- **The container may trim the picture.** An MP4 whose sample entry is
  854 wide for a stream whose parameter set crops to 864 says that the
  last ten columns are padding; FFmpeg honours that, so the sandboxed
  fallback's frames are the smaller size. The native backend honours
  `StreamConfig.width` and `StreamConfig.height` too, but only where they
  are inside the coded picture and within one macroblock of it: that is
  the padding a container trims, and anything else is metadata this
  decoder does not trust against the bitstream. Two files of the
  measurement's held-out set differ between the backends without this
  (`docs/spikes/h264-native-thumbnail/`), and the decoded samples agree with
  FFmpeg frame for frame in both.
- **No new hook in the `Decoder` trait.** The caller skipping the
  non-reference access units before the frame it wants needs nothing from
  the backend but that it keep no state such an access unit would have
  left; `crates/coreav-backend-h264/tests/decode.rs` decodes a stream with
  those access units removed and requires the later frames to be identical.
  The keyframe-only mode is a property of the decoder a caller constructs
  (`NativeOptions`), not of a packet, so it needs no trait change either.
- **The caller orders the backends by the work it will ask for.** The
  `Decoder` trait is one picture at a time and says nothing about how
  many will be asked for, so the choice belongs to the policy:
  `coreav thumbnail` puts the native backend first for a thumbnail at a
  keyframe and the sandboxed fallback first for `--exact`
  (`docs/design/decode.md`, "Selection"), because the native decoder was
  single-threaded when that order was set. It now decodes on the host's
  cores ("Threading (step 7)" below); the order for `--exact` changes
  when bar P3 says the threaded decoder is the faster of the two.
- **Threads.** The backend decodes with as many threads as the host has
  cores (`std::thread::available_parallelism`), or as `NativeOptions`
  asks, at most `Limits::max_threads`, and one on WebAssembly, within its
  memory budget ("Threading (step 7): our design", "Limits"). Frames come
  out up to one picture per thread later than a packet's own picture, so
  the backend keeps the marks of that many more packets. A slice's error
  can be reported by a later call than the one that sent it, so the
  backend decodes every NAL unit of a packet and ends its access unit
  even after one fails, and returns the first error: a caller that
  carries on after errors gets the same frames whatever the thread count,
  and one that stops at the first gets a prefix of what one thread gives.
- **The backend has a fuzz target of its own**: an `avcC`
  record and the packets after it are untrusted bytes, and the backend
  reads the record, splits the packets and sizes its frames from what
  the container declares. `crates/coreav-backend-h264/fuzz` drives it as
  the boundary does — selection, `open`, packets, `send_eof` — and
  checks that every frame is inside the limits the decoder was opened
  with and that a failure is one of the boundary's error kinds.
- **WebAssembly.** The crate builds for `wasm32-unknown-unknown`, whose
  standard library has no clock: `Instant::now` is not implemented there
  and would abort the module. The deadline is therefore not read on that
  target, and the host that runs the module keeps the time as it keeps the
  memory; every other limit is enforced as usual.

## The plan, in steps

Each step is one pull request, reviewed independently; the kernel and
`unsafe` steps get a second, independent review.

1. **Crate skeleton and this note.** The two crates, the error and limits
   types, NAL framing, the bit reader, the picture model, the kernel trait
   and the scalar kernels. (Done.)
2. **The decoder.** Parameter sets, slice headers, CAVLC, CABAC, prediction,
   transforms, deblocking, the decoded picture buffer; the conformance
   harness and bar C1. (Done: 97 of 97 conformance streams bit-exact,
   `docs/measurements/h264-decoder.md`.)
3. **SIMD kernels.** AVX2 and NEON behind the same trait, with the
   equivalence property tests and fuzz targets of bar C3, the
   `docs/unsafe-sites.md` rows, and the policy-conforming lint table.
   (Done: bit-identical to the reference, 97 of 97 conformance streams
   with them on, and the per-kernel measurement that decides which call
   goes where — `docs/measurements/h264-kernels.md`.)
4. **The backend and the WebAssembly build.** A selectable H.264 backend of
   the decode boundary behind a non-default feature, and a
   `wasm32-unknown-unknown` build. (Done: `coreav-backend-h264` and the
   `native-h264` feature of the CLI, "The decode-boundary backend" above.
   On the held-out H.264 files of corpus v1, a thumbnail at a keyframe is
   **0.437** of the `ffmpeg` command line and level with the sandboxed
   fallback, every image byte-identical to the fallback's;
   `coreav thumbnail --exact` is 4.6 times FFmpeg, which is the
   single-thread gap and the reason for step 7 —
   `docs/spikes/h264-native-thumbnail/`.)
5. **Fuzzing.** Decoder and kernel fuzz targets in CI, and bar
   C4's campaign. The kernel targets are the differential ones bar C3 asks
   for: each compares a vector kernel with the reference. The backend's
   target joins them: step 4 added a crate that reads untrusted bytes, so
   C4's set names it. (Targets and CI: done. **The campaign is deferred to
   the one before release**: a campaign measures the code it ran on, and
   the performance work of steps 6 and 7 rewrites the hot paths it would
   have covered, so running it now would buy a result that the next
   optimisation invalidates. The per-pull-request fuzz targets
   still run on every change that can affect them, which is what guards
   each optimisation. The corpus of the first, discarded run is kept as
   seeds for it: `fuzz/h264-corpus-272dbe2ebd0e/corpus.tar.gz` in the
   private corpus bucket, SHA-256
   `272dbe2ebd0ea22e0604e64ac80da151e91c15f3f0c7f868cb5653ae2b9138e8`.)
6. **Performance rounds.** Safe-Rust optimisation with a profile after each
   step, then the measured run of bars P1 and P2 on a fresh held-out draw.
   (Measured: bar P1 is not met. On the fresh held-out draw the
   decoder at the round-4 tip is **3.36** times FFmpeg 7.0.2 on one
   thread (discard; write 3.10), median over 64 streams, and slower on every one —
   `docs/measurements/h264-n2-heldout/README.md`, "Result (P1)" below.
   `docs/measurements/h264-decoder-speed.md` has the rounds and the
   erratum on what N2 measured. The stage-gate verdict: optimisation
   continues, and P1 is measured again on a fresh draw; "Result (P1)".)
7. **Frame threading.** Pictures in bands with aprons, one worker thread
   per picture in flight, the caller's thread keeping everything that is
   sequential in the stream, and the backend choosing the thread count
   within its memory budget ("Threading (step 7): our design"). (Done:
   bars G1 to G3 passed on the tuning streams, at 2.30 of FFmpeg with 8
   threads on both sides against 2.94 with one; P3 and P4 are measured in
   the held-out run.)

## Bars

Pre-registered: every threshold here is committed before the run that
measures it.

### Correctness

| Bar | Set | Threshold |
|---|---|---|
| C1 conformance | the 97 in-scope JVT conformance bitstreams of N1 (`docs/spikes/h264-n1/conformance/streams.json`) | 97 of 97 bit-exact against the reference decoded files, with the scalar kernels and with the SIMD kernels, on x86-64 and on arm64 |
| C2 corpus | N1's C2 set (corpus v1 `real` H.264 streams in scope) | per stream, the same outcome as N1's measured run: every stream that agreed with FFmpeg still agrees, and each of the 13 known divergences still diverges with the same frame count and the same first differing frame |
| C3 kernels | every kernel implementation against the scalar reference | bit-identical output in property tests over all block sizes, fractional positions and boundary strengths (including edge and extreme values), and in a fuzz target per kernel family run for at least 10 minutes per target per architecture without a difference |
| C4 robustness | every fuzz target of the three H.264 crates: the decoder's (`coreav-h264`), the kernels' (`coreav-kernels-h264`) and the decode-boundary backend's of step 4 (`coreav-backend-h264`), as the campaign's plan lists them when it runs | no crash, hang or out-of-memory report in at least 24 cumulative CPU-hours; any finding resets the count. A CPU-hour is one fuzzer with a core to itself for an hour (`docs/design/fuzz-campaign.md`), counted by the CPU time the kernel charged it. No `unwrap`, `panic!` or slice indexing in the crates (the workspace lints) |
| C5 keyframe-only mode | the conformance set and the corpus | the picture the keyframe-only mode returns for an IDR access unit is identical to the one full decoding returns for it, and the mode returns one for every IDR access unit |

C1 and C2 keep what N1 and N2 measured: graduation may not lose correctness.

**C5's wording changed after its first run, and this is the record of
it.** The threshold read "identical to the one full decoding *returns*
for it"; it reads "*decodes*" since commit `8757819`, with the
completeness half ("and the mode returns one for every IDR access unit")
added in the same edit. The reason is `no_output_of_prior_pics_flag`: an
access unit may tell a full decoder to drop pictures it has decoded but
not yet output, and a keyframe-only decoder has returned them already,
which no decoder can avoid without knowing the future. That flag is the
only way a picture leaves the decoded picture buffer without being
output, so the carve-out is complete rather than open-ended.

Under the original wording the measured result is the same: of the 1,309
keyframes of the 97 conformance streams, **none** is a picture full
decoding does not also return — the suite holds no stream that sets the
flag, and the case is covered by
`the_keyframe_mode_returns_a_picture_a_later_access_unit_discards` in
`crates/coreav-h264/tests/decode.rs`, where full decoding returns one
picture of three and the mode returns three.

C2's corpus run belongs to the step that finishes the kernels, so that it
measures the build users get rather than an intermediate one; the decoder
step checks the same method against FFmpeg on the streams already at hand
(`docs/measurements/h264-decoder.md`).

### Speed (step 6)

The speed-bar rule applies. The bars:

| Bar | Set | Threshold |
|---|---|---|
| P1 x86-64 | a fresh held-out draw, SIMD kernels | median per-stream wall-clock ratio to FFmpeg at most **1.10**, overall and per resolution class |
| P2 arm64 | the same streams, SIMD kernels | the same |

**Erratum on what N2 measured.** N2's P1 and P2 timed `--framemd5` on
both sides, where the spike hashes on a second thread
and `ffmpeg -threads 1 -f
framemd5` hashes on its only one: two of our threads against one of
FFmpeg's. On a 1080p tuning stream, 300 frames, hashing costs FFmpeg
0.486 s on a 0.538 s decode and the spike 0.097 s on 1.362 s. The same
spike binary measures **1.424** by that method — consistent with the
1.476 it reports — and **2.53** when both sides only decode. N2's
recorded bars and verdict stand as recorded; what changes is the reading
of them, and the rounds of step 6 are measured against a decode-only
comparison instead (`docs/measurements/h264-decoder-speed.md`).

Method: single-threaded (`ffmpeg -threads 1`), the two symmetric pairings
of `scripts/h264_parity.py` (ours `--discard` against `-f null`, ours
writing frames against `-f rawvideo`) rather than N2's `-f framemd5` (the
erratum above), interleaved rounds per stream on a pinned core, the per-
stream ratio of medians, the median over streams with a 95% bootstrap
confidence interval over 2,000 resamples. A measured run states its round
count and frames per class in its own README, which governs
(`docs/measurements/h264-n2-heldout/README.md` used 5 rounds). A claim
that CoreAV is faster than FFmpeg needs the upper bound of that interval
below 1.00. The scalar build is timed as an information row, not a bar.
**Erratum, from "Snapshot outliers":** until then FFmpeg ran with its default frame-rate
conversion, which duplicated or dropped frames of four training streams in the `-f rawvideo`
pairing (ratios to FFmpeg on the write pairing before it are overstated for them, the 4k
class's median by about 4%); the scripts now pass `-fps_mode passthrough`.

**How the write pairing writes.** Ours writes through the `decode`
example, which until this was corrected passed its frames through
`std::io::Stdout`. That handle is line-buffered even into a pipe and scans
every write for its last newline byte, and decoded samples almost never
hold one, so each 1 MiB flush was scanned to its start. On eight training
streams that scan was 2 to 15% of the write pairing's instructions
(callgrind); FFmpeg's `-f rawvideo -` does nothing like it. The example
now writes to a handle on the same file descriptor, with the same 1 MiB
buffer and the same bytes: instructions 0.854 to 0.982 of before on four
streams (`docs/measurements/h264-rounds/example-stdout/`). The decoder is
unchanged. Write ratios measured before this change carry the scan on our
side, the same in both arms of an A/B, so within-run ratios stand; ratios
to FFmpeg on the write pairing from before it are higher than the decoder
alone would give. An A/B pairs two builds from the same side of this
change on the write pairing, never one from each.

An A/B between two builds of this decoder builds both the same way: the
same profile (`dist`, fat LTO with one codegen unit), the same toolchain
and the same flags and features, apart from the change measured. Builds
made differently can differ by more than most changes do: the first CABAC
fast-mode prototype measured 0.987 against a build of `main` made another
way, where the same three sites, in builds of one tree made alike, measure
0.997 to 0.9995 (`docs/measurements/h264-rounds/cabac-fast-local.md`).

**Rounds at eight threads.** An eight-thread call (`--threads 8`, unpinned, FFmpeg at eight
threads too) was measured twice between the same two builds, once at five rounds and once at ten
(`docs/measurements/h264-rounds/build-alignment/`). At five rounds the per-stream ratios spread
over 0.865 to 1.184 (both pairings) and the 95% interval of the 32-stream median was 1.4% to
1.7% wide, where the one-thread calls' at five rounds were 0.6% to 0.8% wide. At ten rounds the
spread was 0.985 to 1.025 and the interval 0.55% to 0.65% wide. The two runs differ in more than
the round count (a different hour of the same host, with outliers in the first such as one stream
at 1.129 against 1.007), so the round count is not shown to be the cause. Eight-thread bars of a
half percent use ten rounds, which cost little, until a run that varies only the count says
whether five would do.

**Where the allocator puts the planes.** Builds made alike can still
place their picture planes differently, and that can move time. glibc maps
a large allocation on its own pages, but raises that threshold to the
size of each mapped block it frees. Every picture frees a record array
larger than a chroma plane, so the chroma planes come from the heap, at
offsets set by whatever was allocated before them; round 11's part M,
which frees no such array, has them mapped page-aligned. Measured on that
build under three placements (`MALLOC_MMAP_THRESHOLD_` at 128 KB,
every plane mapped; 600 KB, chroma on the heap; 32 MB, every plane on the
heap; six training streams, five rounds, the 2.50 GHz class): per stream
the placements differ by 1.2% to 7.8%, the heap placements against the
mapped one by a median 1.014 and 1.026; two runs of one placement differ
by up to 4.3%, a median 1.015 (the build's default against the 128 KB
setting, which should place alike since the build frees no large block;
`docs/measurements/h264-rounds/round11/placement.txt`). The simulated
cache counts the other way: `chroma_mc`'s simulated D1 misses double
when the planes are mapped. So placement moves a stream by a few percent,
about as much as the noise of one stream's ratio at five rounds; a
32-stream median absorbs it where both arms place alike, and not where
an arm changes the size or order of allocations made before the
pictures are pooled.

Which earlier results that touches: the arms of the rounds so far all
freed the record array each picture and placed chroma on the heap, but
for round 11's part M; rounds that changed what is allocated before the
pictures (round 8's edge buffer and round 9's buffers in `Scratch` and
`MbData`) may have measured a placement change with their code, by up
to the spread above per stream. Their medians cleared their bars by more
than that (round 9: 0.940 against 0.98), and round 10, closest to its
bars, changed no allocation. None is re-measured.

The guard, from round 12 on: an A/B whose arms differ in what they
allocate, in size or order, is also timed with
`MALLOC_MMAP_THRESHOLD_=131072` set for the whole run, which every
decoder (and FFmpeg) inherits: every buffer above 128 KB is then mapped
page-aligned in both arms whatever else they allocate. Its result is
reported beside the gating one, and a verdict that differs between the
two is reported as placement-sensitive.

**The held-out draw.** N2's 139-stream set is spent: it has been measured
against. The next measured run draws fresh streams that have never been used
for tuning or measurement, from corpus v1's in-scope H.264 streams minus
every stream in `docs/spikes/h264-n1/`'s and `docs/spikes/h264-n2/`'s tuning and held-out
sets. The draw is `HMAC-SHA256(salt, stream id)` ordered, taking the streams
with the smallest digest per resolution class; the salt and the resulting
list are committed before the run, with their SHA-256 in the step's
measurement note. Streams FFmpeg decodes in under 0.5 s are left out, as in
N2, so process start-up does not dominate a ratio.

**The bar machine.** A ratio to FFmpeg depends on the machine, not only
on the code and the streams (`docs/measurements/h264-training/README.md`,
"Machine calibration"), so the speed bars name one: the cloud VM class the
rounds of step 6 and step 7 ran on, which `/proc/cpuinfo` names `Intel(R)
Xeon(R) Processor @ 2.90GHz` (8 vCPU, 4 cores with 2 threads each,
AVX-512). It is the class every profile, A/B run and training-set
measurement has used, so a held-out number on it is comparable with all of
them. Every timing run records the CPU model, the clock it reports and the
logical CPU count (`scripts/h264_parity.py`, `machine` in the report), and
a gating run passes `--require-cpu "@ 2.90GHz"`, which stops before timing
anything on another model, or without a report if the model changes during
the run. A held-out run also measures the same binary on the 2.50 GHz class
that an earlier change ran on (its report recorded the clock, not the model string),
reported beside the bar as a secondary number that gates nothing: the
spread between the two classes is what users on other machines should
expect, and it is larger for this decoder than for FFmpeg (a likely reason,
untested: it spends more of its time on stores into the picture, round 5).
The class was chosen after the calibration showed it measures this decoder
about 10% better against FFmpeg than the 2.50 GHz class; the reason for it
predates that result: every profile, A/B run and training measurement of
the decoder ran on it. The model string alone may name different parts
under a hypervisor, so reports also record the CPU family, model and
stepping (on the bar machine: 6, 106, 6), and a gating run stops if any of
them changes during the run. (For rounds whose bars are committed later, the
bar machine is the Compute Engine class of the next paragraph; the 2.90 GHz class is secondary.)

**The one-thread class of rounds whose bars are committed from here on.**
The bar machine above is a shared cloud VM class, and its helper VMs were noisy
for hours at a time, so that one-thread arms waited on host gates. From the
merge of this paragraph, the one-thread arms of a new round (A/B bars and
held-out verdicts) run on a Compute Engine VM of its own: `c4-standard-8` with
`threadsPerCore=1` (4 vCPUs on 4 physical cores, no SMT), STANDARD
provisioning, `us-central1-a`, Intel Xeon Platinum 8581C @ 2.30 GHz (family 6,
model 207, AVX-512), the CPU of the eight-thread runs ("Where the eight-thread
arms run"). The 2.90 GHz class stays as a secondary class: information, and the
host of rounds whose bars were committed before (their hosts are as their bars
say). Evidence for the choice (`docs/measurements/h264-rounds/gcp-1t-class/` on
branch `measured/h264-gcp-1t-class`; plan and bars committed before the run, at
`1e0c8d52`; result at `7f17caca`): the three gate references five minutes apart
agreed within 0.41%; all 8 gate checks around the four calls and all 8 in-call
gate samples passed; two copies of one binary over the 32 training streams,
`--pin 2 --rounds 5`, read 1.0003 [0.9976, 1.0018] for discard and 1.0008
[0.9996, 1.0019] for write (95% bootstrap over streams; half-widths 0.21% and
0.12%), per class within 0.997 to 1.004, the largest stream deviation 1.7%, the
largest round spread 1.10, and no stream timed again: every bar of the plan was
met. It is one VM for 37 minutes. The same binary against FFmpeg 9.0.2 read 0.978
for discard overall there (faster on 21 of 32 streams; sd 0.940, 720p 1.013,
1080p 1.022, 4k 0.880) and 0.981 on the 2.90 GHz class (18 of 32; sd 0.930, 720p
1.037, 1080p 1.029, 4k 0.874): within 2.5% overall and per class. A smoke run of
the wrapper's mode below (two streams a class, three rounds; `wrapper-smoke/`,
branch `measured/h264-gcp-1t-class` at `a2f1d4a3`) passed all its checks; its
spend bound was 0.19 USD.

How a new round's one-thread arms run (the documented default):
`scripts/h264_parity_gcp.py --one-thread-class` (over `scripts/gcp_vm_job.py`)
uploads the decoders, FFmpeg 9.0.2, the harness, the streams and two reference
streams to one new VM and runs there, one call per class, `--pin 2` with the
round's `--rounds`, `--shuffle-seed` and `--null-arm`, no repeat, `--require-cpu
8581C` (the run stops if the CPU is not that part; the report records family,
model and stepping, and `host.txt` the SMT state and the sha256 of every file).
The host-health gate is that of `docs/measurements/h264-rounds/host-gate/` with
this class's own references, which each run measures itself: the median of three
FFmpeg measurements five minutes apart (they must agree within 5%), and a check
within 5% of them before and after each call; a call whose after-check fails is
run again, at most three attempts, and the voided files are kept. A run is void
when the references disagree, when a call never passed its checks, when a call
has no report, fewer streams than it was given or more than 2 unresolved, or
when the VM does not have 4 vCPUs with SMT off; a void run is run again on a new
VM into a new directory. The harness bars on this class are the one-thread ones
(null deviation 4%, round spread 1.50). Cost: from the calls of the calibration (30 command-runs a stream, 25.5 minutes
for the 32 training streams), a run of the 32 training streams with two arms and
a null copy at 20 rounds takes about 2.6 hours with its references and gates
(`--max-hours 3.5`, at most 2.1 USD by the 0.60 USD an hour bound of
`gcp_vm_job.py`), and a run of the 64 held-out streams at 5 rounds about 1.5
hours (`--max-hours 2`, at most 1.2 USD). The VM is deleted when the job ends
(in a `finally`, and by `maxRunDuration` if the runner dies), and `--cap-usd`
(at most 10) refuses a request that does not fit. A run that runs out of its
hours is void. The runs can go on separate VMs at once within the project's
CPU quota. Not established by the calibration: stability over several hours or
several VMs, which a round's own references and checks bound for that round.

ISA tiers: this CPU has the AVX-512 subsets the kernel tiers use, but it is
another microarchitecture than the 2.90 GHz class. A round whose gain depends on
a kernel tier (a vector kernel, an assembly site) also reports the 2.90 GHz
class's number, as information, and a round that adds a tier names in its bars
which class decides. Ratios to FFmpeg are of the class they were measured on and
are not compared across classes; the official snapshot reports both classes.

**Round A/B runs on more than one class.** A round's A/B run (the
branch against its base, and any per-part arms) may run on the one-thread
class of Compute Engine above (the default for rounds whose bars are
committed after it), the 2.90 GHz class (family 6, model 106) or the 2.50 GHz
class (family 6, model 85); the bars of an earlier round name their host.
A round that does not depend on an ISA tier may also run in a dedicated
container whose CPU class is recorded, with its own gate references;
rounds that depend on an ISA tier, and held-out verdicts, are excluded.
Its bars are ratios within one run, so they hold on any of these. The
conditions:
- every arm is timed in the same run on the same host;
- before and after each call, a host-health gate times FFmpeg 9.0.2 on
  two reference streams, and the call counts only if both times are
  within 5% of the host class's reference times
  (`docs/measurements/h264-rounds/host-gate/`: `hostgate.py`, the
  references per class, and `HOST-GATE.md`). A container takes its
  references from three gate measurements five minutes apart, which
  must agree within 5%, before the first call;
- on a VM class, `--require-cpu` names the class, and the run stops if
  the family, model or stepping changes; in a container, which may not
  report a stepping, the class is the vendor, family and model it
  reports, recorded with the run, and the gate around each call stands
  in for the stepping check.

Earlier rounds measured on both classes agreed in direction (the chroma
interpolation round: 0.962 on one, 0.954 on the other;
`docs/measurements/h264-rounds/chroma-mc/` and the branch
`measured/h264-chroma-mc-info-2p50`). A ratio to FFmpeg
from such a run is information about that class only. Held-out verdicts
(P1, P3) and the FFmpeg-ratio snapshots stay on a fixed class: the 2.90 GHz one
for those whose bars were committed before "The one-thread class of rounds whose
bars are committed from here on", the Compute Engine class for later ones, and a
snapshot after it reports both.

**Result (P1).** The draw and its bars were committed before the run
(`docs/measurements/h264-n2-heldout/README.md`: 64 streams, 16 per
resolution class, FFmpeg 7.0.2 and, as information, 9.0.2). The decoder
measured is `main` at `ca5e4bc8`, the round-4 tip. P1 is **not met, in
any cell**:

| Class | discard: median [95% interval] | write: median [95% interval] |
|---|---|---|
| overall | 3.359 [3.125, 3.506] | 3.095 [2.870, 3.284] |
| sd | 3.266 [3.155, 3.479] | 3.262 [3.057, 3.408] |
| 720p | 3.481 [2.976, 3.703] | 3.247 [2.861, 3.530] |
| 1080p | 3.537 [3.114, 3.760] | 3.246 [2.818, 3.451] |
| 4k | 2.704 [2.254, 3.567] | 2.370 [2.168, 2.870] |

No stream is faster than FFmpeg; per stream the ratio runs from 1.38 to
4.48. All 64 decode to FFmpeg's frames, MD5 for MD5. FFmpeg 9.0.2 is
indistinguishable from 7.0.2 here. P2 (arm64) was not measured. The
draw's floor was an estimated FFmpeg time of 0.4 s; measured, 14 of the
64 streams took FFmpeg under 0.5 s. They favour this decoder (median 2.63
against 3.46 for the other 50), so P1 is not met with or without them.

Two facts for what follows:

- **The rounds' ratio to FFmpeg understates the gap.** On the same kind
  of machine the round-4 tip measures 2.50 (discard) against FFmpeg on
  the eight tuning streams of the rounds, and 3.36 on this draw. Part of
  that is run length, not only which streams: at 300 frames FFmpeg
  decodes five of the eight tuning streams in under 0.5 s, and short runs
  favour this decoder here too (above). Ratios of one version of this
  decoder to another, which is what the rounds report, are not affected;
  a ratio to FFmpeg from short tuning runs is not a forecast of a
  held-out one.
- **Round 5 is not in this measurement.** It merged after the run, at
  0.964 [0.956, 0.981] of the round-4 tip on the tuning streams, which
  does not bring P1 within reach (3.36 × 0.964 is about 3.2). The draw is spent, and the next held-out
  measurement draws again.
- **The machine moved too.** The held-out run's VM reported a 2.50 GHz
  Xeon; the rounds ran on a 2.90 GHz one. The same binary on 16 of the
  held-out streams measures a ratio 0.903 [0.889, 0.936] as large on the
  2.90 GHz machine as an earlier change did, per stream
  (`docs/measurements/h264-training/README.md`, "Machine calibration"),
  so about 10% of a ratio to FFmpeg is the machine: this decoder gains
  more than FFmpeg from the faster one. On a 32-stream training set drawn
  like the held-out set and run with its frame counts, `main` measures
  2.82 on the 2.90 GHz machine, against about 2.94 expected there for the
  held-out level. Profiles and A/B runs use that set from here on, and
  ratios are compared only between runs on one machine class (the bar
  machine, above).

The stage-gate verdict: P1 is not met, and the optimisation work
continues. The bar is now **1.10** (P1 to P4, set at that stage
gate), against the default FFmpeg 9.0.2 build with its assembly, and
it is measured again on a fresh
held-out draw when the code is judged ready for one; the implementer
commits the level on the training set that sends the code to that draw
before spending it. From here on, speed runs and frame-MD5 identity are
against the pinned FFmpeg 9.0.2 build of an earlier change (BtbN
`n9.0.2-17-g2a571b6068`, archive SHA-256
`68ee646831adaae2495618346f3bba94ff207ff83bbd34d643e7004730d66269`), and
every result names the FFmpeg build it was measured against; results
against 7.0.2 stand as recorded. Bar C2 is the exception: it was fixed
against N1's measured outcome, whose oracle was FFmpeg 7.0.2, so it runs
against 7.0.2 as registered, with 9.0.2 beside it as information (a
divergence that moves only because FFmpeg changed is reported, not
counted against the bar).

**Regression guard.** Every user-facing operation needs a CI guard. The backend step adds the decode speed bar to
`bench/guard` so that a later change cannot quietly lose what step 6 wins.

### Threading (step 7)

P1 and P2 stay single-threaded, so that per-core efficiency stays
visible. They are not what a user measures: FFmpeg decodes on every core,
and the thumbnail measurement shows what that costs us where more than
one picture must be decoded — `coreav thumbnail --exact` through the
native backend is 4.6 times the `ffmpeg` command line and 5.6 times the
sandboxed fallback, while the same thumbnail at a keyframe is 0.437 of
FFmpeg (`docs/spikes/h264-native-thumbnail/`).

Frame-level and slice-level threading is therefore the next performance
item after step 6, and the larger lever of the two. The design is in
"Threading (step 7): our design" below. Its bars:

| Bar | Set | Threshold |
|---|---|---|
| P3 x86-64 | P1's held-out draw, SIMD kernels, both sides on the host's cores (`ffmpeg -threads N`, `--threads N`, N the host's core count) | median per-stream wall-clock ratio to FFmpeg at most **1.10**, overall and per resolution class |
| P4 arm64 | the same streams | the same |

The threshold is P1's, for P1's written reason: it is the milestone on the
path to parity, not parity. P3 and P4 are measured in the same held-out
run as P1 and P2, so that the threaded and the single-threaded ratio of
each stream come from one session. The user-visible comparison — the
backend's default thread count against `ffmpeg` with no `-threads`
option — is reported beside them as an information row.

## Measurement method: host faults inside a call

Rounds 19 to 23 and the kernel rounds timed their arms in a fixed order in
every round, and judged a disturbed host only between calls, with the
host-health gate (`docs/measurements/h264-rounds/host-gate/HOST-GATE.md`).
Round 23's 1080p swing (the same binary moved 14 to 21% on short streams in
one arm, inside a call whose gates passed) showed what that cannot see: a
disturbance shorter than a stream, or one that lands on one arm's slot in the
round. `scripts/h264_parity.py` gets five changes, each off unless its option
is given, so that a call without them times the same commands in the same
order and writes the same report keys plus additive ones. They apply to the
rounds whose bars are committed after this change; earlier rounds keep the
method their bars were written for.

### Thresholds

- **Null arm deviation: 4% with one thread, 8% with several.** A null arm
  times a second copy of one decoder (the same binary) in the same rounds. For
  each stream and each output mode the null arm's median over the rounds is
  compared with the arm it copies. A deviation above the bar either way,
  `|null / arm - 1|`, marks the stream as a host fault. The first version of
  this method set 3% and 10% from the same-binary cross-run variation of a
  stream's median in earlier rounds (0.5 to 2.3%); the calibration below
  replaced them.
- **Round spread: 1.50.** For each command of a stream, the slowest round over
  the fastest, `max / min`. Above 1.50 for any command marks the stream as a
  host fault: a single round half as slow as the fastest is what a gross
  disturbance looks like from inside the median, and the median hides it.
- **Retries: at most 2 per stream.** A stream marked as a host fault is timed
  again from its warm-up. Every attempt is stored in full (its per-round
  times and orders, its deviation and its spread), the last attempt is the one
  summarised, and a stream that is still marked after two retries is kept and
  flagged `unresolved` in the report, never dropped. The report counts them
  in `method.unresolved`. The spread and the deviation are recorded in every
  call; only a call with `--null-arm` acts on them.
- **In-call gate drift: 5%.** See below; the same 5% as the host-health gate.
- **Call length: at least 3 s.** Every timed call of a command is set to last
  at least 3 s: the repeat count is chosen from the stream's warm-up, so a call
  can come out a few percent under. `--min-seconds 3` is for eight-thread
  calls, which last 0.17 to 0.7 s without it, where a probe under the first
  version of this method ended with every stream unresolved. At 3 s,
  start-up jitter of a few milliseconds is well under 1% of the call. The
  harness does not check the length; a stream's call lasts `rounds[i] *
  repeat` of its row.

#### Calibration of the thresholds

Two idle-host calibrations on the 8-vCPU helper VM (Intel Xeon @ 2.90 GHz),
each a call of two copies of one binary beside FFmpeg 9.0.2, ten rounds, random
order; the reports and `calibration.py` are in
`docs/measurements/h264-rounds/parity-calibration/` on branch
`measured/h264-parity-calibration` (`dbbef55a`).

- **Eight threads, unpinned, `--min-seconds 3`: 32 training streams** (eight a
  class). Round spread over 192 commands: median 1.17, 95th percentile 1.37,
  maximum 1.47 (FFmpeg alone, 64 commands: median 1.13, maximum 1.30);
  deviation between the two copies' medians over 64 comparisons: median 1.4%,
  95th percentile 5.9%, maximum 7.4%. At the one-thread bars of the first
  version (10% and 3%) a quiet host marked most streams.
- **One thread pinned to core 2, no repeat: 12 training streams** (three a
  class). Round spread over 72 commands: median 1.07, 95th percentile 1.38,
  maximum 1.42 (FFmpeg alone, 24 commands: median 1.09, maximum 1.42);
  deviation between the two copies' medians over 24 comparisons: median 0.4%,
  95th percentile 2.9%, maximum 3.0%. The bars are above the observed
  maxima: 1.50 and 4% at one thread, 1.50 and 8% at eight.

**The noise of the statistic bars are set on.** A bar is on the median over
all 32 streams of a per-stream ratio. Of the same binary against itself
(`main2 / main`, per stream, then the median over the 32 streams) at eight
threads: discard 0.9977 and write 0.9984, and the 95% range of that median,
from a bootstrap over rounds within each stream and over streams together
(2,000 resamples), is [0.9818, 1.0119] for discard and [0.9838, 1.0119] for
write: about 1.5% either side of 1.000 (a bootstrap over streams alone gives
about 0.9% for discard and 1.1% for write). At one thread (12 streams) the same range is about 0.6 to 0.7%
either side. An eight-thread bar on that median has to be set with at least
this much room, and a measured effect smaller than it is not distinguished
from the host; the null arm's own ratio is reported beside every eight-thread
result.

The bars sit just above the observed maxima, so a call of 32 streams will
sometimes mark a stream by chance; it is timed again, which costs time and
does not change a result. The thresholds are chosen by thread count alone: an
eight-thread call without `--min-seconds`, a call with two or four threads and
an unpinned one-thread call are judged by bars calibrated for a neighbouring
case, in the looser direction. These bars replace the first version's (3%
and 10%) for every call with `--null-arm`; a round whose bars were written for
the first version is run with the script revision it was written for.

The cost of bars set above the noise is that a smaller disturbance than the
bar is not seen by a call; the in-call gate (one thread, pinned) and the
host-health gate between calls still see it.

### Where the eight-thread arms run

Eight-thread arms of a round whose bars are committed after this section
merges run on a Compute Engine VM, and the host is named beside every
eight-thread number. One-thread arms of rounds whose bars were committed before "The
one-thread class of rounds whose bars are committed from here on" stay on the
helper VM (Intel Xeon @ 2.90 GHz, family 6 model 106) of the host-health gate. The reason is the
calibration above and its twin on the Compute Engine host
(`gcp-c4-nosmt/` on branch `measured/h264-gcp-calibration-c4`, `af1a8599`): the same 32 training
streams, the same calls, two copies of one binary, ten rounds, at eight
threads.

| | helper VM (8 vCPUs, SMT on) | `c4-standard-16`, one thread a core (8 vCPUs) |
|---|---|---|
| null median of 32 streams, discard | 0.9977, 95% range [0.9818, 1.0119] | 1.0005, [0.9997, 1.0013] |
| write | 0.9984, [0.9838, 1.0119] | 1.0007, [0.9989, 1.0013] |
| round spread, median (maximum) | 1.17 (1.47) | 1.02 (1.06; FFmpeg alone one stream at 1.13) |
| null deviation of a stream, maximum | 7.4% | 0.9% |

The host: `c4-standard-16` with `advancedMachineFeatures.threadsPerCore=1`
(8 vCPUs on 8 physical cores, no SMT), STANDARD (on-demand) provisioning so
that a preemption does not void a run, `us-central1-a`, a
`hyperdisk-balanced` boot disk, Debian 13, Intel Xeon Platinum 8581C @
2.30 GHz (family 6 model 207). Ratios to FFmpeg and between arms are of that
host and are not compared with the helper VM's. The null median's noise there
is about 0.1% either side, so an eight-thread bar can be set that close.

- **Bars of the harness on that host: null deviation 2%, round spread 1.25.**
  Above the calibration's maxima (0.9% and 1.06; 1.13 for one FFmpeg
  command) and well under the helper VM's, which would not see a disturbance
  of a few percent on a host that quiet. `--null-bar` and `--spread-bar` give
  them to the harness.
- **How a run goes** (`scripts/h264_parity_gcp.py`, over
  `scripts/gcp_vm_job.py`): the decoders, FFmpeg, the harness and the
  streams of the calls are uploaded to one new VM; the calls run there one at
  a time, a class each, with `--threads 8 --min-seconds 3 --shuffle-seed N
  --null-arm A --gate-stream S --gate-threads 8` (the in-call gate is FFmpeg with
  eight threads like the arms, repeated like the arms' calls, so that it sees
  what they see) and `--require-cpu` for the CPU model; the
  reports come back with `host.txt` (the CPU, SMT state, sha256 of every file)
  and the run's cost; the VM is deleted in a `finally` and by
  `maxRunDuration`.
- **Host check, and when a run is void.** The gate stream's FFmpeg time, eight
  threads like the arms' calls, median of 3 calls, is taken before the first call
  and after the last. A run is void when the two differ by more than 5%, when
  a call ends with more than 2 unresolved streams, produces no report or has
  fewer streams in it than it was given (a decoder failed on one), or when
  the VM does not have 8 vCPUs with SMT off; a void run is run again on a new
  VM into a new directory, and the void directory is kept.
  Three smoke runs on that host (`gcp-gate-smoke/` on branch
  `measured/h264-gcp-gate-smoke`) chose the gate: a one-thread gate pinned to
  core 2 slowed by up to 9% in one 720p call while the eight-thread arms of the
  same streams did not move (a false void), and an unpinned one-thread gate
  drifted by up to 4.7% by itself; with the gate at eight threads like the arms,
  its samples stayed within 0.8% of the first in both calls, with no retry and
  a null deviation of at most 0.8% (five rounds). The rate of a false void by
  the gate is not measured beyond those calls.
  There is no host-health gate between calls on that host: the VM is new and
  dedicated, and the in-call gate and the null arm judge each call.
- **Spend.** `--cap-usd` (default 5) bounds a run: `scripts/gcp_vm_job.py`
  refuses to start unless `--max-hours` times 1.20 USD an hour (an upper bound
  of `c4-standard-16`'s on-demand price and its disk) is within it; the
  bound actually used, from the hours the VM existed, is printed
  with the run's other numbers. The calibration's 2.2 hours cost 2.66 USD by that
  bound. A request that does
  not fit is refused, and the caller splits it into runs by class
  (`--classes`) or by streams, each with its own host check; a run is not
  checked against its time estimate, and one that runs out of hours ends
  without its reference after and is void.

### Choices

- **Per-round arm order is random, with the seed recorded.** A fixed order
  puts the same arm first in every round, so a disturbance that follows a
  process start, or a slow period of a few seconds, always lands on the same
  arm. `--shuffle-seed N` draws the order of the commands anew in each round
  from a generator seeded with N, the stream's name and the attempt number (a
  retry does not replay the order that was faulty); the seed is written
  to `method.shuffle_seed`, and the order of every round is stored in the
  stream's row, so a run can be replayed. Not given, the order is the old
  fixed one. Rejected: raising the rounds from 5 to 9 for more resolution;
  deferred, the null arm and the spread rule measure the noise first.
- **Per-round times are stored**, as `rounds` in each stream's row, next to
  the medians. The medians alone cannot show the spread rule's cause, and an
  analysis could not re-judge a stream with another threshold.
- **The null arm is not a pairing.** It adds commands `NAME~null_discard` and
  `NAME~null_write` (`--null-arm NAME`) that time the binary of decoder NAME a
  second time; it creates no pairing and no summary entry, so analyzers that
  read the report's `ratio` and `summary` keep working unchanged. Its result
  is stored per stream as `null`. Rejected: a second named decoder; every
  analyzer would list it as an arm.
- **A reference stream gate runs inside the call.** `--gate-stream PATH
  --gate-every N` (`--gate-frames F`, default 300) times FFmpeg (the
  harness's own FFmpeg, one thread, pinned like the other commands, 3 runs,
  median) on one stream before the first stream, after every N streams and
  after the last, the first of them after one sample that is thrown away (a
  first run is cold, and a baseline taken from it reads every later sample as
  a drift: in an eight-thread call it marked every stream so, the gate's first
  sample 24% above the rest; its repeat count is taken from the warm probe of
  the baseline, not from the cold one). The baseline is the median of the last
  three samples once they agree within 5% (three samples, up to six; `method.gate_base`
  and `method.gate_baseline_stable` are written): in a Compute Engine call of 16
  streams (`gating-gcp-ip6-void1/` of branch `measured/h264-inter-place-gating`)
  one first sample 6% below all later ones was the baseline of every later one,
  and 12 streams ended unresolved. A sample more than 5% from the baseline is
  taken again at once,
  and only if the second is also beyond it is it a drift; it then marks the
  streams timed since the last good sample; they are timed again, within each
  stream's attempts (at most 3 timings of a stream in all, retries after a
  host fault and after a drift together), and the gate is sampled again. If
  that sample has drifted too, those streams are flagged `unresolved` and not
  trusted; a stream that was timed again after a drift carries `gate_drift`.
  Every sample is stored as `gates` with the number of streams it followed and its
  `kind` (`baseline`, at 0, `check` or `confirm`); the confirmation makes the gate less
  sensitive to a disturbance shorter than a sample, by design.
  This is the host-health gate's check moved inside the call, so a drift that
  starts and ends between two streams is seen, not only one that spans the
  call's start and end. The host-health gate between calls stays.
- **A call is a command run K times back to back (`--min-seconds S`).** The
  warm-up times each command once; K is the smallest count for which the
  fastest of those single runs, repeated K times, lasts at least S seconds
  (`K = ceil(S / fastest)`, 1 when a single run already lasts S). K is the same
  for every command of the stream, FFmpeg's and every arm's, the null arm's
  included, and is kept for the stream's retries; it is written to the stream's
  row as `repeat`. A timed value is the call's total divided by K, so
  `seconds`, `rounds` and the ratios keep their meaning of one decode and
  stay comparable with calls that do not repeat; the spread rule then judges
  what the repeats average. Each repeat is a new process, for every command
  alike, so the start-up cost is in each side as it is in a call without the
  option. Not given, K is 1 and nothing changes. Rejected: a fixed K per
  class (it would not reach 3 s on the fastest stream of a class, and would
  overshoot on the slowest); looping inside the decoder or `-stream_loop` in
  FFmpeg (a different code path on each side, which the symmetric pairings
  exist to avoid); a longer `--frames` (it changes what is measured, and a
  stream has a fixed length); more rounds (it averages the noise but leaves
  each call short, which is what the spread rule reads). The cost is time: a
  stream's commands times its rounds times 3 s, at least: at six commands and
  ten rounds, about 3 minutes a stream. K follows the fastest command, so a
  call may list one thread count only (`--min-seconds` refuses a list): the
  slower counts would last much longer. If a warm-up fails, the stream
  is timed once per call, with a message. The repeats average a
  disturbance shorter than about 3% of a call away from each round's time; the
  in-call gate and the null arm carry the judgment for those.
- **The harness decides nothing about a run's validity.** It records and
  retries; whether a call is void stays with the runner and the bars'
  author. Rejected: voiding inside the harness; the policy for a repeated
  fault is the runner's (REBASE and VOID in HOST-GATE.md). The one thing it
  does say is that a call is incomplete: a stream it could not time at all
  is named in the report and the call exits with status 3 (below).

### A round's bars: one analyzer, complete reports

A stream one of whose commands failed used to be printed as `FAILED,
skipped` and left out of the report: its rows, its `summary` and its
`method` gave no sign of it, so the summary medians were of the streams
that survived. Each round's analyzer was a copy of an earlier round's
`analyze.py` and kept the rows it could read, so a round's bars could pass
on fewer streams than the set: round 17's analyzer, given round 17's own
reports with one sd stream removed from the eight-thread call, still
passes B-1 to B-3 on 31 of the 32 training streams. A fix to one copy
reached no later round, which copied another. For the rounds whose bars are
committed after this change:

- **The harness names what it was asked and what failed.** The report gains
  `requested` (every stream the call was given, in order) and `failed`
  (each stream that has no row, with its class and the command and round
  that failed, as in `after_discard exited with an error in round 2 of
  attempt 1`). The other keys keep their meaning: `summary` is still of
  the rows, with `n` 0 and a null `median` where no stream has a row,
  instead of the call ending without a report. A call with a failure writes
  its report, prints `INCOMPLETE` with the streams, and exits with status
  3, so a caller that checks the status stops there;
  `scripts/h264_parity_gcp.py` names the failed streams among a void run's
  reasons. Rejected: leaving `summary` out when a stream failed (a reader
  of that key would crash instead of saying why); retrying a failed stream
  (a decoder that errors on a stream errors again: a defect, not a host
  fault).
- **One analyzer.** `scripts/h264_parity_bars.py BARS.json DIR` computes
  what the copies computed: per call (`g`, `t8`, `h`, `h8`), pairing
  and group (overall, each class, named subsets), the median per-stream
  ratio new/old with its 95% bootstrap interval and the streams faster, each
  build's ratio to FFmpeg, and the host-fault records. A round writes its
  bars as data, each check a call, a pairing, groups, `median_max` and
  `ci_high_below`, and commits that `bars.json` before the run, as it
  commits the bars, instead of an `analyze.py`. On round 17's committed
  reports it reproduces round 17's analyzer exactly, every median, interval
  and verdict (`scripts/tests/test_h264_parity_bars.py`).
- **Complete, or refused.** Each call's stream set is the manifest the
  round names, the set's `es.json` (`docs/measurements/h264-training/`,
  `docs/measurements/h264-n2-heldout/`), not the rows that came back. Per
  class, the report must exist, list no `failed` stream, have been asked
  for exactly the class's streams, and hold one row with both builds' times
  for each of them; otherwise no bar is evaluated, the refusal names every
  missing, failed or unexpected stream, and the exit status is 2. A call
  none of whose reports exists is pending, and so are the bars that read
  it. The manifest is the reference rather than `requested`: a runner that
  passed the harness seven streams gets a complete report of seven, and
  reports written before `requested` existed are checked too. A key the
  bars file does not define is an error, because a misspelt `median_max`
  would be a check that holds whatever is measured; so are an empty
  `groups` (a check that compares nothing) and two bars of one name (the
  later verdict would hide the earlier). A subset that has no stream in a
  call's set is not a group of that call, and a check that asks for it
  there is an error. Unresolved streams are
  reported, not refused: whether they void a call stays the runner's rule.
- **No new copies.** The `analyze*.py` files already under
  `docs/measurements` are the evidence of their rounds and stay as they
  are, listed in `scripts/tests/analyzers-grandfathered.txt`.
  `scripts/tests/test_measurement_analyzers.py` fails on any other
  `analyze*.py` under `docs/measurements` and names the shared analyzer;
  it runs in `deny.yml`, because `ci.yml`'s filter skips a change to
  `docs/measurements` alone. What a round needs and the analyzer lacks is
  added to the analyzer, once, for every later round. Rejected: rewriting
  the copies onto the shared analyzer (they would no longer be what
  produced their rounds' results); a check on every new Python file under
  `docs/measurements` (the rounds' extraction and profiling tools live
  there and are not analyzers). A copy under another name is not caught by
  the check; this note and review are what stop it.

## The CABAC restructure: our design

"Round 3" below is the work in — the deblocking shortcuts, the
full-sample chroma copy and the per-macroblock motion clear — measured
in `docs/measurements/h264-decoder-speed.md` and
`docs/measurements/h264-rejected.md`.

### What the measurement says

CABAC is 21.1% of wall time (`cabac::residual` 14.5%, `decode_cabac`
6.6%) and 1,182 instructions per macroblock, which is **20.2%** of the
decoder's 5,849 at the time of measuring and more than half of FFmpeg's
entire per-macroblock budget of 2,099. With the intra work of an earlier change in,
the decoder is 5,494 and CABAC's share is 21.6%: it is the one stage
round 3 did not touch, so its share rises as the others fall. Counted on the measured stream: **29.2 million
bins for 1.75 million macroblocks**, 16.7 a macroblock, of which 15.4%
are bypass. The stage costs about **71 instructions a bin**.

The arithmetic engine is not where that goes. It is already branchless —
the MPS and LPS paths are selected by a mask, not a branch — the context
array is 1024 bytes behind a 1023 mask so its bounds checks are
eliminable by construction, and `refill` runs about once every fifty
bins, which is 0.2% of the decoder. At roughly fifteen instructions a
bin the engine is about a fifth of the stage. **The other four fifths is
context derivation and syntax dispatch**, and that is what this design
addresses.

### Context derivation

Today a context index is computed from scratch for each bin: a base, a
table lookup for the increment, an addition and a mask. The design keeps
the arithmetic but moves what is invariant out of the bin loop.

- A residual block's `sig_base`, `last_base` and `abs_base` are constant
  for the block. They are resolved once per block into a small struct
  the loop reads, rather than being passed and re-added per bin.
- The significance and last-position increment tables are selected per
  block by category. The selection is a match per block today and stays
  so; what changes is that the chosen tables become a pair of slices of
  known length, so the per-bin read is an index into a bounded slice
  rather than a `get().copied().unwrap_or(0)`.
- The neighbour-dependent derivations — `coded_block_flag`'s increment
  from the left and upper blocks, and `mvd`'s from the sum of the
  neighbours' absolute differences — are the expensive ones, because
  they read `MbInfo` of two other macroblocks. They are computed once
  per macroblock into a per-macroblock cache, not once per block or per
  component, and the cache is built from the neighbour pointers
  `start_mb` already derives.

### Syntax dispatch

`decode_cabac` is 6.6% of wall time on its own. It decodes a macroblock
by walking syntax elements in order, each a small function reached
through a `Syntax` trait. The design flattens the common paths:

- The P and B skip runs, which dominate low-motion content, decode a
  skip flag and nothing else. That path is specialised so it does not
  enter the general macroblock walk at all.
- Macroblock type decoding is a short decision tree per slice type. It
  becomes a per-slice-type function chosen once when the slice starts,
  rather than a match on slice type inside each element.
- The `Syntax` trait exists so that CABAC and CAVLC share the macroblock
  layer. That sharing is worth keeping, but the CABAC implementation is
  the one on the hot path, and its methods are marked for inlining so
  the trait dispatch disappears where it is monomorphised.

### What this does not attempt

The bins of one block are serial: each decision reads the range and
value the previous one left. No arrangement of the context layer changes
that, and SIMD does not apply to it. The design therefore targets the
work *around* each bin, and the engine's arithmetic stays as it was. (As
built, the engine's refill, tables and placement in registers did
change; "What was built" says how and why.)

### The target

**35 instructions a bin, from 71**, which would take CABAC from 1,182 to
about 580 instructions per macroblock and the decoder from 5,849 to
about 5,250. Acceptance is by wall clock on a pinned core, as for every
other change in round 3: an instruction count that does not move the
clock is a rejection, which happened four times in that round.

Pre-registered before the work: **the bar is a pinned paired median at
or below 0.97 against the round-3 tip, over at least eight streams**,
with instructions reported beside it. If the instruction target is met
and the clock does not move, the restructure is rejected and recorded in
`docs/measurements/h264-rejected.md` like the others.

**Result.** Against the round-3 tip, pinned, seven interleaved rounds,
eight streams: **0.968 [0.952, 0.999]** on the discard pairing and
**0.957 [0.937, 0.990]** on the write pairing, both at or under the bar
of 0.97; the tip as shipped, timed directly against the round-3 tip in
another session, reads 0.966 [0.960, 0.968] and 0.969 [0.962, 0.975]
(`docs/measurements/h264-rounds/round4-cabac-ab.json`). The
instruction target is **not** met: CABAC went from 1,189 to 1,058
instructions per macroblock on the measured stream, 71 to 63 a bin on
the 29.2 million bins above. Time fell further than
instructions: the decoder's total went from 5,494 to 5,306 per
macroblock, 3.4%, against 3% to 4% of time. That fits what the steps
removed, which was mostly stores and reloads of the engine on the chain
from one bin to the next rather than instructions; the steps were not
timed one by one, so how the gain divides between them is not measured.

### What was built

Five steps, each measured against the one before it, then all of them
against the round-3 tip in one session
([`docs/measurements/h264-decoder-speed.md`](../measurements/h264-decoder-speed.md),
"Round 4: CABAC"). Output is byte-identical to the round-3 tip on all 32
tuning streams, and conformance stays 97 of 97.

- **A residual block is written where it belongs.** The CABAC residual
  decoder writes each level straight into the macroblock's coefficient
  array through the block's scan table, instead of into a list of
  (position, value) pairs that the macroblock layer then scattered. The
  `Syntax` trait's `block` takes the destination array and the scan, and
  its `block_context` is asked first, so the destination can be borrowed
  while the coder runs. Rejected: keeping the list and scattering faster,
  which keeps a second pass over every level.
- **coded_block_flag reads two words.** At the start of a macroblock's
  residual, the `cbf` words of macroblocks A and B are taken once
  (`SliceDecoder::neighbour_cbf`), an unavailable one standing in as all
  ones or all zeros by clause 9.3.3.1.1.9's rule for the current
  macroblock's prediction mode. Every other condition the clause asks
  about a neighbour (I_PCM, skipped, no coefficients in that quadrant or
  in chroma) is already answered by which bits a decoded macroblock set,
  so the increment is two bit tests. Rejected: a bordered grid of every
  4x4 block's flag, which costs a fill per macroblock to answer the same
  two questions.
- **The engine stays in registers in the residual loops.** The
  significance map and the levels are two out-of-line functions, each
  taking the engine as a local and writing it back once. In one function
  the compiler spilled codIOffset, the value every bin reads and writes,
  and kept it in memory; split, neither loop touches the stack per bin
  (checked in the generated code). Two things made that possible: the
  engine holds the unread data as one slice rather than the data and a
  position, a register fewer, and the rare paths (the bytes past the end,
  the Exp-Golomb suffix of a large level) take the engine by value, so
  its address never escapes the loop. (The entropy round, "Entropy round: the CABAC
  engine in three registers", later took the data out of the engine's
  registers altogether.)
- **The significance map is a mask, and the level contexts one state.**
  The map is a bit per scanning position; the levels walk its set bits
  from the top. The two counters that choose coeff_abs_level_minus1's
  contexts collapse to eight states, because until a level above 1 only
  the number of 1s up to three matters and after it only the number
  above 1 up to four. A 4x4 block's significance increment is its
  position, so it needs no table, and last_significant_coeff_flag's
  contexts are found at a fixed distance from significant_coeff_flag's.
  The sign is applied without a branch.
- **The engine refills after it consumes.** No operation consumes more
  than seven bits, so the engine keeps at least eight loaded and checks
  after consuming rather than before; a refill loads four bytes at once.
  The rangeTabLPS and transition tables are widened so that a state byte
  and `codIRange >> 6` index them without masks, and the transition is
  indexed by the decoded bin so the bin is computed once. Bypass is
  branchless.
- **mb_type and sub_mb_type** read their bin strings through a lookup
  built at compile time from the generated tables, one load per bin,
  instead of searching the list after every bin. Rejected: hand-written
  decision trees per slice type, which the committed design proposed;
  they cost the same bins and would have left the generated tables
  unchecked by the code that uses them.
- **The macroblock layer's per-macroblock work.** Clearing the previous
