## Round 9: macroblock-level work, decided once rather than per block

The first round chosen from the stage-by-stage gap to FFmpeg 9.0.2
(`docs/measurements/h264-gap-2/README.md`). Macroblock-level work
(entropy, macroblock control, intra prediction and the transforms
together) is the largest gap there, +2.99 s on eight streams, and most of
it remains against FFmpeg's C build: 2.0 times its instructions, with
compares and conditional branches 16.4 G of the 23.4 G difference. So the
round cuts decisions per macroblock and per block rather than vectorising,
in two parts: the derivation and storage of motion (part A), and
reconstruction, the inverse transforms and intra prediction (part B). The
one vector kernel it adds is the 4x4 transform, which lost before only to
its call.

### What the measurement says

Part A, motion:

- **Macroblock control is the largest part** (31.3 G instructions of the
  55.4 G, against FFmpeg's 11.8 G). Its functions are inter prediction's
  control: `predict_list` 7.8 G, `direct_8x8` 4.8 G, `store_motion` 4.4 G
  (36 M mispredicts, the most of any macroblock-level function),
  `inter_pred` 3.3 G, `motion_compensate` 2.2 G, `start_mb` 1.9 G,
  `neighbour_motion` 1.7 G, `mv_predictor` 1.3 G.
- **Per macroblock it is glue, not work.** On `b71b6b31e54f` (1080p,
  100 frames, mostly skipped B macroblocks), those functions execute
  about 2,240 instructions a macroblock of their own, kernels excluded, and
  are 49% of the decode's instructions. A B_Skip macroblock derived its
  direct motion four times (once an 8x8 quadrant), stored it four times
  (each a reference-identity lookup, a comparison with the first motion
  and a fill of a width known only at run time), then read the sixteen
  stored motions back to find that they agree. Each neighbour of motion
  vector prediction went through the generic neighbour derivation of
  clause 6.4.12: a branch per macroblock edge, a test of whether the
  block is derived yet, a test for intra.
- **Per slice, decided per block.** Temporal direct prediction searched
  list 0 for the co-located reference and divided for DistScaleFactor at
  every block; implicit weights divided at every bi-predicted block, up to
  four times (once to decide the averaging shortcut, once a plane in the
  weighting).

Part B, reconstruction:

- **The transforms:** the idct/dequant/add stage executes 6.5 G
  instructions on the eight streams against FFmpeg SIMD's 1.2 G, 4.24 G of
  ours the 4x4 inverse transform alone (the reference kernel, inlined into
  the decoder, about 330 instructions a block).
- **Intra prediction:** 5.6 G against FFmpeg C's 0.7 G, 4.6 times its
  sampled time, the largest ratio to C of any stage but picture output.
- **A vector 4x4 transform lost before, to the call.** The per-kernel
  benchmark measures a vector kernel for one 4x4 block at about the
  reference's time (`docs/measurements/h264-kernels.md`): a
  `#[target_feature]` function cannot be inlined, and one block does not
  pay for the call. So the 4x4 transform stayed in the reference.
- **The decoder transforms 4x4 blocks in groups of four.** The luma
  blocks of an inter or Intra_16x16 macroblock go one 8x8 quadrant at a
  time (luma4x4BlkIdx runs over the quadrants), and each chroma component
  has four AC blocks; only an Intra_4x4 macroblock needs each block
  before predicting the next.

- **Intra prediction decides per sample.** An Intra_4x4 or Intra_8x8 block
  computed each sample through a nine-way `match` on its mode and an
  accessor that branches on whether the sample is above, left or at the
  corner; reading a block's left column checked each sample's address on
  its own (about 230 instructions a call on `9db41aa16b5a`); and each
  block's availability went through the generic neighbour derivation of
  clause 6.4.12 four times.

### Design

Part A, motion:

1. **A motion context per macroblock** (`MotionCtx`, `inter.rs`). A grid
   of 4x4 blocks, six wide and five high: the row above (D, B, C), the
   column to the left (A), the macroblock, and the never-available column
   to its right. Filled once when the macroblock's prediction starts, from
   the motion its neighbours left in the picture: an intra neighbour left
   `NO_MOTION` there, which reads as available with reference index -1,
   as clause 8.4.1.3.2 wants. Unavailable blocks hold a reference index of
   -2, so the clauses that tell "not available" from "intra" or "list not
   used" (the C-to-D substitution, the B-and-C-to-A rule of 8.4.1.3.1,
   P_Skip's conditions) test one value; every other comparison is with an
   index of at least 0 and treats -2 as -1. The macroblock's own blocks
   start unavailable and are written as each partition is derived, which
   is exactly the availability of a partition decoded later. Motion vector
   prediction and spatial direct prediction then read neighbours by one
   load at a position known from the partition's shape. The reference
   indices of a list are one 32-byte array, so making a macroblock's
   blocks unavailable is one store; vectors are read only where the index
   is at least 0 and are never cleared. A P slice fills and writes list 0
   alone.
2. **One store for a one-motion macroblock** (`store_mb`). P_Skip, a
   16x16 partition, and B_Skip or B_Direct_16x16 with
   direct_8x8_inference_flag whose four quadrants agree store their motion
   once into the picture's sixteen blocks, and write nothing into the
   context, which no later partition of the macroblock reads. A direct
   macroblock (`predict_direct`) derives its four quadrants from the
   co-located corners first, with spatial direct prediction's neighbours
   derived once, and predicts quadrants of equal motion together as before
   (`predict_quadrants`). Partitions of other shapes store a row at a time
   with stores of fixed width.
3. **P_Skip reads A and B before anything else.** Its vector is zero
   where either is unavailable or holds a zero vector to reference 0
   (clause 8.4.1.1), which on still content is most macroblocks; the
   context is filled only when the predictor is needed.
4. **Per-slice tables** (`InterTables`): the picture identity of every
   list entry, whether list 1's first entry is short-term (colZeroFlag),
   DistScaleFactor for every refIdxL0 (Equations 8-193 to 8-196) and the
   weighting mode. Implicit weights are derived once a block and handed to
   the weighting.
5. **Motion goes to motion compensation as a value.** `motion_compensate`
   takes the block's motion instead of reading it back from the picture.

Part B, reconstruction:

6. **`Kernels::idct4x4_add_quad`**: the 4x4 transforms of an 8x8 block's
   four 4x4 blocks in one call, each where its bit of a mask is set; block
   `k` at column `(k % 2) * 4` and row `(k / 2) * 4`, which is
   luma4x4BlkIdx's order inside a quadrant and the chroma AC blocks'
   order. The trait's default is the reference one block at a time
   (`idct4x4_add_quad_by_blocks`), which is what scalar `Auto` and the
   arm64 and portable builds use for now.
7. **The AVX2 kernel works a horizontal pair at a time**: the pair's
   rows share 256-bit vectors, one block a 128-bit lane, and are
   transposed, passed horizontally, transposed back and passed vertically
   in 32-bit lanes (the reference's widths, so every input the trait
   allows gives the reference's samples); each row of the pair is then a
   row of eight of the 8x8 block, added as the 8x8 transform's rows are
   ("Kernel round: the transforms, a row to a vector"). A pair whose
   bits are clear is skipped; a clear block in a set pair is masked to
   zero coefficients.
8. **The decoder calls it per quadrant and per chroma component.** The
   DC of an Intra_16x16 block or of a chroma block is written into the
   block's coefficients, where an AC block leaves position 0 at zero, and
   the block's bit is set where the DC is not zero; the masks `MbData`
   clears by (`luma_nz`, `chroma_ac_nz`) record those blocks, so the next
   macroblock finds them cleared. Before, each such block was copied to
   set its DC.

9. **Directional intra modes by tables.** Every sample of the six
   directional modes of a 4x4 or 8x8 block (clauses 8.3.1.2.4 to 8.3.1.2.9
   and 8.3.2.2.5 to 8.3.2.2.10) is one of three things about the block's
   edge line, its neighbouring samples in order from p[-1, n-1] up the
   left column to the corner and along the row above: a sample of the
   line, the rounded average of two adjacent samples, or the (1, 2, 1)
   filter centred on a sample. The two equations that weight an end sample
   by 3 are that filter with the line's end repeated. So each sample is an
   index fixed by mode and position, which a `const fn` works out from the
   equations when the crate is compiled (`intra::source`). At run time a
   block builds the line, its averages and its filter once (38 values for
   4x4, 74 for 8x8) and reads each sample from them, with no branch.
   Vertical, horizontal and DC are filled directly.
10. **The left column in one range check**, read by stepping through one
   slice; the per-sample path remains for a block at the plane's end.
11. **Availability by rule.** Whether macroblocks A, B, C and D may be
   predicted from is decided once a macroblock; inside it, a block's left,
   upper and upper-left neighbours are always decoded before it, and the
   upper-right one is decided by decoding order as before.

Bit-exact by construction: each value is the clause's, derived from the
same inputs, in an order that does not change it. The transform kernel is
checked against the reference on every mask and on coefficients across
the range clauses 8.5.10 to 8.5.13 allow (`tests/equivalence.rs`, and the
`transform` fuzz target); the intra predictions against the frozen oracle
`intra_reference.rs`, every mode, every combination of available
neighbours and blocks at every position of a plane, its edges included
(`every_prediction_matches_the_code_it_replaced`); and the decoder's
output against `main`'s below.

Rejected:
- **Neighbour lookups through the grid alone, with storage unchanged.**
  Built first: the grid replaced `neighbour_motion` but the per-partition
  stores stayed, and instructions fell 0.8% on `b71b6b31e54f` before the
  stores were made fixed-width, and 2.2% after. The stores, not the
  lookups, were the cost.
- **The grid as one record per block** (both lists' vectors and indices,
  10 bytes): making the macroblock's twenty blocks unavailable is twenty
  stores of a record rather than one store a list, and a P slice writes a
  list it never reads; 1.5% more instructions on `b71b6b31e54f` than
  per-list arrays.
- **A smaller `Motion`** (a 16-bit picture identity, so that a block is 16
  bytes and stores vectorise): identities would repeat after 65,536
  pictures, and a long-term reference can outlive that, which would
  compare two different pictures as equal in the deblocking filter. Not
  worth a correctness argument for one store per macroblock.
- **Filling the context in every macroblock** (an intra one too): intra
  macroblocks read none of it.
- **A whole-macroblock call** (sixteen blocks and a 16-bit mask): one call
  instead of up to four for luma, but a second entry point for the same
  arithmetic, and a call per quadrant already amortises the call over
  four blocks.
- **16-bit lanes** (twice the blocks per vector): the reference computes
  in 32 bits, and a coefficient at the edge of its range would differ.
- **A DC-only path inside the kernel**: a test per block for what the full
  transform does in about forty vector instructions.
- **Per-mode code for the directional modes** (straight-line code per
  mode, rows as slices of the filtered line where a mode allows it): only
  diagonal down-left and down-right have rows that are slices; the other
  four alternate between averages and filters by position, which a table
  says in one load.

### Bars

Fixed before the A/B run, as rounds 6 to 8 and on the training set,
against FFmpeg 9.0.2 from here on: `scripts/h264_parity.py --pin 2
--rounds 5 --require-cpu "@ 2.90GHz"`, one call per class with the
class's frame count, the branch tip against `main` at `5dcea04` in the
same rounds, both built alike (`dist`, one toolchain), FFmpeg 9.0.2 (BtbN
`n9.0.2-17-g2a571b6068`) as the third command:

| Bar | Quantity | Threshold |
|---|---|---|
| R9-1 | median per-stream ratio, branch over base, discard | at most **0.98**, upper end of the 95% interval below 1.00 |
| R9-2 | the same, write | at most **0.985** |
| R9-3 | the same per class (sd, 720p, 1080p, 4k), discard | at most **1.005** in each |
| R9-4 | output | the 32 training streams byte-identical to the base at 1 and 8 threads; conformance 97 of 97 at 1, 2 and 8 threads and with scalar kernels |

The ratio to FFmpeg 9.0.2 is reported beside them as information.

Direction only, not a bar: part A alone, measured on the 2.50 GHz class
with the same script and three rounds, gave 0.980 [0.962, 0.990] on
discard (faster on 26 of 32 streams) and 0.982 [0.959, 0.992] on write.

Each part has to earn its place, as round 5's candidates did, so the same
run times three builds in the same rounds: `main` at `5dcea04`, part B
alone (branch `perf/h264-idct`, the same reconstruction code on `main`),
and A and B together (this branch). R9-1 to R9-4 are read as A and B
together against `main`, and:

| Bar | Quantity | Threshold |
|---|---|---|
| R9-5 | A and B together against B alone, discard and write | upper end of the 95% interval below 1.00 on both pairings (round 5's rule for a part on top of the others) |

If R9-5 fails, part A leaves the round for `docs/measurements/h264-rejected.md`,
and R9-1 to R9-4 are read for B alone against `main` from the same run.
The summary of the three builds is `docs/measurements/h264-rounds/round9/analyze.py`.

### Result: passed, both parts kept

`docs/measurements/h264-rounds/round9/` (one run on the 2.90 GHz class,
Xeon family 6 model 106, no failures, no reruns; the three builds'
outputs checked identical before timing, 128 of 128; `run-notes.txt`
records that the request changed twice before the run started: from two
builds to three, and the A and B build from `f23a9e8` to `325784d`, a
review fix that leaves valid streams' output unchanged):

| Bar | Result | Threshold |
|---|---|---|
| R9-1 | **0.940 [0.916, 0.948]**, faster on 30 of 32 streams | at most 0.98, upper end below 1.00 |
| R9-2 | **0.929 [0.920, 0.940]**, faster on 30 of 32 | at most 0.985 |
| R9-3 | sd 0.942, 720p 0.929, 1080p 0.924, 4k 0.938 | at most 1.005 in each |
| R9-4 | identical on 128 of 128 (both builds, 32 streams at 1 and 8 threads); conformance 97 of 97 at 1, 2 and 8 threads (291 decodes) and with scalar kernels | |
| R9-5 | A and B over B alone: discard **0.979 [0.952, 0.993]**, faster on 24 of 32; write **0.976 [0.948, 0.991]**, 26 of 32 | upper end below 1.00 on both |

B alone over `main`: 0.964 [0.955, 0.970] on discard, 0.963 on write.
Against FFmpeg 9.0.2 (median per-stream ratio, one thread, information):
discard 2.033 for `main`, 1.929 with B, **1.917** with A and B; write
2.016, 1.911 and **1.851**.

**Two streams lose to part A.** `ed75c044e944` (A and B over B 1.173 on
discard, 1.055 on write) and `81ed4778ece2` (1.054 and 1.078) are 4k
streams of P pictures that are nearly all P_Skip. They execute fewer
instructions with part A, and locally the loss reproduces (1.06 and
1.05, 41 rounds) with `store_mb` taking 5.8% of the samples: a motion
held in registers is stored as three narrow stores a block, two of them
8-byte stores across 20-byte records, 48 a macroblock into a motion array
that is not in cache at 4k, where `main` copied each record from memory in
two. Storing the first row and copying it to the other three removes the
loss locally (1.006 and 1.005). That change is measured as its own round
rather than added here after the run.

## Round 10: a macroblock's motion stored by copying rows

A follow-up to round 9, whose run found two streams slower with its part
A (`ed75c044e944` 1.173 and `81ed4778ece2` 1.054 on discard, A and B
over B): 4k streams of P pictures that are nearly all P_Skip.

### What the measurement says

Both execute fewer instructions with part A; the time is in `store_mb`,
5.8% of the samples on `ed75c044e944` locally. A motion held in
registers is stored as three narrow stores a 20-byte record (4 bytes,
then two 8-byte stores across the record), 48 a macroblock, into a motion
array that is not in cache at 4k. `main` before round 9 copied each
record from memory in two stores, a 16-byte and a 4-byte one.

### Design

`store_mb` stores the first row of four records and copies it to the
other three rows (`copy_within`, which moves the 80 bytes of a row in a
few wide moves). The records stored are the same.

Rejected: `fill` over the sixteen records (the same three narrow stores
a record, measured no better); a 16-byte `Motion` (round 9's reason).

## Kernel round: luma interpolation by position

### What the measurement says

The stage-by-stage comparison with FFmpeg 9.0.2
(`docs/measurements/h264-gap-2/`) puts luma interpolation at +1.15 s on
its eight streams: 0.83 of FFmpeg C's sampled time, but 3.9 times FFmpeg
SIMD's instructions with the same D1 misses. So it is instruction volume.
Two counts say where the instructions go (`docs/measurements/h264-rounds/luma-mc/`):

- **Which blocks.** A count of the decoder's calls on the 32 training
  streams at their class frame counts: 64.6 million luma blocks, 82% of
  them 16x16. Full-sample positions are 60% of the calls (16 wide: 50.1%
  predicted, 7.4% averaged into the other list's), fractional 16-wide
  ones 31%, 8-wide ones 11%, and 4-wide ones 0.4%.
- **What each costs.** Callgrind on a harness that calls `Auto` with one
  shape and position at a time (about 135 instructions a call are the
  harness's own): a 16x16 block at the half-sample b costs 2,555
  instructions, at j 3,686, at the quarter positions next to j 5,000 to
  5,700, and a full-sample block averaged into the picture 973. Weighted
  by the call counts that is 100 G instructions on the training set,
  66% of it in fractional 16-wide blocks and 18% in fractional 8-wide
  ones.

The kernel did the arithmetic in vectors, but around it:
- every 16 or 8 bytes were read through a helper that checks the slice's
  length;
- the sample at each position was produced by `tap_rows`, which the
  compiler kept out of line, with a `match` on the tap per call (about
  290,000 simulated indirect mispredicts in 60 pictures of
  `6da34958296c`), and
  `horizontal`, out of line too: an `#[inline]` function with
  `#[target_feature]` is inlined at the compiler's discretion, and at
  this size it declined;
- the one or two taps of a position were staged through 16-entry arrays
  on the stack before they were averaged and stored;
- the averaging form of a full-sample block went through the views' row
  iterators, about 50 instructions a row.

### Design

1. **One function per width and position.** `interpolate::<R, XF, YF>`
   is generic over the row type `R` (`Row16`, sixteen 16-bit lanes in a
   256-bit vector; `Row8`, eight in a 128-bit one) and the quarter-sample
   position. The position's taps (`scalar::taps`, now a `const fn`) are
   constants of each instance, so the choice of samples, the windows a
   position needs and the second tap's average fold away: a row is its
   arithmetic and one store. The 32 instances (two widths, sixteen
   positions) are reached through one jump table indexed by xFrac, yFrac
   and the width; together they are 12 KB of code, less than the kernel
   they replace.
2. **One check per call, then pointers.** The views hold exactly the
   window (`h + 5` rows of `w + 5` samples) and the block. `luma_mc_into`
   checks both extents once (`window_fits`, checked arithmetic) and then
   reads and writes each row through a pointer, as the deblocking
   filter's `gather` does for an edge. Every read stays inside its row:
   the horizontal filter reads `w` bytes from columns 0 to 5, a full
   sample from column 2 or 3. Pointers step with `wrapping_add`, so the
   step past the last row forms no pointer that is used. Where a check
   fails, which no view allows, the block goes to the reference.
3. **Windows in registers.** A vertical filter (h, and j's vertical step)
   keeps its six rows in registers and moves down a row per output row.
   The window holds rows `y - 1` to `y + 4` when row `y` starts and reads
   row `y + 5` first, which every row of the block has, so the loop has no
   test for its last row. For f and q (j averaged with b), b is j's middle
   row rounded, not filtered again.
4. **The 6-tap by shifts.** `(a + f) - 5 (b + e) + 20 (c + d)` is
   `(a + f) + 5 t` with `t = 4 (c + d) - (b + e)`: three adds, two
   shifts, a subtract and two adds, no multiply, all inside 16 bits for
   samples. j's vertical step stays in 32 bits (`madd` on interleaved
   pairs), which keeps it exact.
5. **Helpers inlined by force.** The helpers (`Row`'s functions, `tap6`,
   `horizontal`, `sample`, `interpolate`) are `#[inline(always)]`
   `unsafe fn`s without `#[target_feature]`, called only from
   `luma_mc_into`, which has it; once inlined there, the intrinsics inline
   too. The first version used closures for the windows and the taps;
   the compiler kept those out of line, without AVX2, and the intrinsics
   in them became calls (8,170 instructions for a 16x16 e, against 949
   now; `shapes-first-version.txt`).
6. **8-wide full-sample blocks go to the kernel on x86-64**
   (`LUMA_COPY8_VECTOR`): the reference copies them through row iterators
   at about 540 instructions an 8x8 block. On arm64 the measured rule
   stays.
7. **Candidate C: full-sample blocks without a call.** A full-sample
   block is a load and a store a row. `luma_full` does that in SSE2, the
   x86-64 baseline, so it is an ordinary function that inlines into
   `Auto::luma_mc` and `Auto::luma_mc_avg`, with the same one check, and
   the block never reaches the AVX2 call. An earlier note measured a copy
   at this level as worse; that copy went through the views' row
   iterators. Time decides, by the rule below. It did not clear that
   rule (Result), so it is not merged; A's kernel copies these blocks.

Rejected:
- the averaging form as a constant of each instance: it saves a test and
  a branch a row (3 to 7% of a 16x16 fractional block's instructions) and
  doubles the instances to 64, about 25 KB;
- 4-wide blocks in vectors: 0.4% of the calls and 0.9% of the
  instructions, and an 8-byte read from column 5 of a 9-sample row
  leaves the window, so the one check would not cover it;
- j's vertical step in 16 bits: its sum before the shift reaches about
  475,000, so 16-bit lanes need intermediate shifts that drop low bits
  Equation 8-247 keeps; 32 bits are exact by construction;
- the horizontal filter on bytes with `pmaddubsw`: it needs the pairs of
  neighbouring samples interleaved first, more shuffles than the six
  widening loads it would save;
- fractional positions in SSE2, inlined like chroma: the work of a
  fractional block (about 300 to 1,300 instructions now) dwarfs the call, and
  AVX2 halves it for 16-wide blocks.

Instructions (callgrind, `--discard`, one thread, whole decode, against
`main` at b66e452f; `instructions.txt`):

| Stream | Pictures | main | A | C |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 6da34958296c (1080p) | 60 | 5,274 M | 4,692 M (−11.0%) | 4,656 M (−11.7%) |
| 3b1b441e23ae (4k, weighted) | 30 | 2,084 M | 1,934 M (−7.2%) | 1,897 M (−9.0%) |
| 41e324ebb708 (sd) | 300 | 2,442 M | 2,347 M (−3.9%) | 2,323 M (−4.9%) |
| 9db41aa16b5a (720p) | 150 | 3,456 M | 3,442 M (−0.4%) | 3,421 M (−1.0%) |

The luma entry points of `6da34958296c` go from 823 to 205 million
instructions with C. The per-shape model above gives 100 G before, 33.0 G
with A and 28.9 G with C. `9db41aa16b5a` moves least: its B pictures use
explicit weights, which predict into scratch and combine afterwards, the
next round's subject.

Bit-exact by construction (the reference's integers) and by test: the
crate's x86 test compares every width (4, 8, 16), every height from 1 to
16 and every position, plain and averaged, at the tightest strides the
views allow, with a margin round the block; the `luma_mc` fuzz target compares `Simd` and `Auto` with the
reference, plain and averaged.

## Kernel round: weighted prediction inlined

Not merged: the candidate below missed its bars (Result). Its code is on
the branch `rejected/h264-weighted-sse2`; `main` keeps the AVX2 kernel.

### What the measurement says

Weighted prediction is the combining of clause 8.4.2.3 with explicit
weights, or with implicit ones other than 32 and 32: round 8 sends every
other bi-predicted block straight to the picture. Such a block is
predicted from each list into scratch and then combined, a call to
`combine` per plane. The stage-by-stage comparison
(`docs/measurements/h264-gap-2/`) put combining at +0.46 s on its eight
streams. After the luma round it is the largest single kernel cost on
the streams that use it:

- On `41e324ebb708` (sd, 300 pictures) the 322,137 calls take 517
  million of the decode's 2,323 million instructions (22%), about 1,600 a
  call; on `9db41aa16b5a` (720p, 150 pictures) 419,199 calls take 669 of
  3,421 million.
- A call costs that much around its arithmetic, not in it. The AVX2
  kernel walks the three views' row iterators, matches the mode per row,
  reads and writes each 8 samples through a helper that checks the
  slice's length, and calls `weighted_one` or `weighted_two` per row,
  which set their constants up again. It is also a call into a
  `#[target_feature]` function, three per block.
- Nine of the 32 training streams use it for at least 10% of their luma
  blocks (counting a combine call per plane, `luma-mc/calls.txt`):
  `9db41aa16b5a`, `41e324ebb708`, `b41f70a7fa60`, `65ec61f95a00`,
  `1d4b1775d78a`, `dcb262cf0138`, `8ae90cadb5bc`, `7650ae466748` and
  `278dbf5a63bb`. Three more use it for 1 to 3%, and twenty not at all.

### Design

1. **SSE2, inlined.** The weighting needs no instruction beyond SSE2,
   the x86-64 baseline, so `combine` is an ordinary function that inlines
   into `Auto::combine`, as the chroma interpolation does: no call into a
   `#[target_feature]` function. (`Auto` still takes it only where it
   holds a `Simd`, as for chroma.)
2. **One check per block, then pointers.** It accepts blocks 2, 4, 8 or
   16 samples wide and 1 to 16 rows high (every luma and chroma
   partition), checks the destination and each list's prediction it
   reads once (`window_fits`), and then reads and writes each row through
   a pointer: rows of 8 and 16 bytes as vectors, rows of 2 and 4 as
   integers. The width is a constant of each instance, and the mode is
   matched once per block, outside the row loop. Anything else, and
   copying and averaging, is declined and goes to the reference, and so
   is a block either of whose lists is smaller than it, as the reference
   leaves such a block alone, in the one-list form as well as the
   two-list one.
3. **Both lists: pairs multiplied and added.** The two samples of a
   position are interleaved, and `pmaddwd` multiplies the pair by
   (w0, w1) and adds in 32 bits. The offset joins the rounding term,
   `((x + 2^logWD) >> (logWD + 1)) + o = (x + 2^logWD + o 2^(logWD + 1))
   >> (logWD + 1)`, exact since the added term is a multiple of the
   divisor. The packs saturate to 16 bits, which every value fits, and
   then to 0 to 255, which is Clip1. A 16-wide row is 32 instructions.
4. **One list in 16 bits.** A sample times a weight is at most 32,640 in
   size, and adding the rounding term (at most 64) or, without a shift,
   the offset (-128 to 127) keeps the sum inside 16 bits, so Equations
   8-286 and 8-287 fit 16-bit lanes; `packuswb` is the clip.
5. **Weights up to 128.** An implicit weight reaches 128 (w1 = 128 where
   w0 = -64); the arithmetic above holds for weights of -128 to 128, so
   the kernel takes them, where the AVX2 one sent them to the reference.
   Offsets stop at 127 (clause 7.4.3.2): one more, with a weight of 128
   and no shift, is 32,768, which a 16-bit lane does not hold, and the
   kernel declines it (the fuzz target found that case when it allowed
   offsets of 128).

Rejected:
- an AVX2 form: twice the lanes, but behind a call, three per block,
  which is what the chroma round removed;
- weighting inside the interpolation, so that a list's prediction goes
  to the picture weighted instead of through scratch: it would remove a
  store and a load a row, the three combine calls' fixed cost (about 150
  instructions each) and the views built for them, together about 80
  million of `41e324ebb708`'s 1,945 million (4%), but it changes the
  decoder's prediction loop (`inter.rs`) and the kernel trait;
- tightening the entry further: the remaining fixed cost, about 150
  instructions a call, is the three extent checks and the call frame of
  `Auto::combine`.

Instructions (callgrind, whole decode, `--discard`, one thread, against
the luma round's candidate C, which that round's run later rejected;
`docs/measurements/h264-rounds/combine/instructions.txt`). This round
changes no luma kernel, so the weighted blocks' savings should carry
over to A; they were not counted again on A:

| Stream | Pictures | before | after |
|---|---|---|---|
| 41e324ebb708 (sd) | 300 | 2,323 M | 1,945 M (−16.3%) |
| 9db41aa16b5a (720p) | 150 | 3,421 M | 2,932 M (−14.3%) |
| b41f70a7fa60 (1080p) | 60 | 6,504 M | 6,151 M (−5.4%) |
| 65ec61f95a00 (720p) | 150 | 6,577 M | 6,363 M (−3.2%) |

`Auto::combine` goes from 517 to 139 million instructions on
`41e324ebb708`. Bit-exact by construction and by test: the x86 test
compares every width and height the kernel takes, every denominator,
weights and offsets at the ends of their range (weights of 128 included,
and the one-list sums at their limits), samples at 0 and 255, and blocks
whose last row ends at their slice's end, with the reference, and checks
that every other shape and mode is declined with nothing written; the
shared kernel test compares `Simd` with the reference, and the `combine`
fuzz target `Simd` and `Auto`, weights of 128 included.

candidate with the larger saving (about 4% more of `41e324ebb708`'s
instructions), and it needs the decoder's prediction loop to change.

## Kernel round: deblocking edges read into registers

### What the measurement says

A profile of `main` at 3d4c2e63 against FFmpeg 9.0.2, one session on
the 2.90 GHz class, the eight streams of `docs/measurements/h264-gap-2/`,
puts deblocking at +0.84 s (filters +0.64 s, the driver +0.20 s), the
largest gap after macroblock-level work. Per edge shape on
`6da34958296c` (perf samples, information): vertical luma edges 106
against FFmpeg's 26, horizontal luma edges 42 against 42, vertical
chroma edges 44 against 19, horizontal chroma edges 32 against 8.

The vertical luma edge is the outlier, and its instructions do not
explain it: a harness that calls `Auto::filter_edge` on one shape at a
time (`docs/measurements/h264-rounds/deblock-registers/`) counts about
550 instructions a call and times it at about 50 ns, while the decoder
spends about 260 ns a call. Its samples are spread over the function,
with stack stores and reloads among the hottest. The standard shapes
read their lines with `gather` into byte arrays, convert the arrays to
vectors, and on the way back convert vectors to byte arrays for
`scatter`: the lines go through the stack twice, and on a vertical edge
that is sixteen rows each way. (Chroma motion compensation, the other
large kernel gap, is not taken this round: half of its time is the
full-sample copy, whose cost sits on the reference load, and two earlier
copy changes moved instructions but not time; `h264-rejected.md`.)

### Design

1. **Rows straight into and out of registers.** For a standard edge
   (sixteen luma or eight chroma lines), `rows_at` makes the check of
   `gather` (`rows_fit`: the last row ends inside the slice, in checked
   arithmetic) and returns a pointer to the first row; each row is then
   one vector load or store through it: `movq` for the eight-byte rows
   of a vertical luma edge, `movq` and an unaligned 64-bit write of the
   high half for the two lines a transposed pair holds, `movq` for the rows of a horizontal chroma
   edge, a 32-bit load and a 16-bit store per line of a vertical chroma
   edge. No byte array is built. Where the check fails, which no view
   allows, `gather` and `scatter` keep the slice path.
2. **Horizontal luma edges keep `gather` and `scatter`.** Counted per
   call, the direct form is 14 instructions more there (385 against
   371); its rows are sixteen bytes, which the compiler already moves as
   vectors.

Rejected:
- one call for all the edges of a macroblock, or for Cb and Cr together:
  each needs the driver (`deblock.rs`) and the kernel trait to change, and
  this round shows the per-edge path still had a large cost of its own;
- a smaller transpose with AVX2 (two lines per 128-bit lane): the
  transposes are the standard unpack network already, and the stack
  traffic around them was the larger cost.

Instructions a call through `Auto::filter_edge` (harness, about 65 of
each count its own, bS 2 and 4):

| Edge | `main` | this round |
|---|---|---|
| luma, vertical | 616, 654 | 423, 463 |
| luma, horizontal | 371, 405 | 371, 405 |
| chroma, vertical | 341 | 252 |
| chroma, horizontal | 256 | 246 |

Instructions of the whole decode (callgrind, `--discard`, one thread,
`dist` with line tables, against `main`; `instructions.txt`):

| Stream | Pictures | `main` | this round |
|---|---|---|---|
| 6da34958296c (1080p) | 60 | 3,970 M | 3,841 M (−3.2%) |
| 9db41aa16b5a (720p) | 150 | 3,108 M | 2,924 M (−5.9%) |
| 41e324ebb708 (sd) | 300 | 2,045 M | 2,005 M (−2.0%) |
| e624cbe0d2be (4k) | 30 | 2,714 M | 2,674 M (−1.5%) |

Timed locally on the first version, before the horizontal luma edges
went back to `gather` and the high half to an unaligned write
(information, not a bar run: `dist` builds of one tree each, pinned,
five interleaved rounds, the 2.90 GHz class):
`9db41aa16b5a` 1,515 to 1,404 ms (0.927), `6da34958296c` 2,017 to
1,953 ms (0.968), medians.

Bit-exact by construction (the same arithmetic; only where the lines
are moved changes) and by test: the x86 test of the tightest edges
compares every standard shape with the reference in a plane that ends
where the edge's window does, so the last row read or written is the
slice's last byte; the `filter_edge` fuzz target compares `Simd` and
`Auto` with the reference from the narrowest steps a view takes and at
eight offsets of the first line. Alignment is what Miri checks: the
harness in `tools/miri` (run with `cargo +nightly miri run`, AVX2 and
SSE4.1 enabled) was run on each standard shape at the narrowest steps
and others, at several offsets from alignment, the plane ending at the
window's last byte, `Simd` and `Auto` against the reference (the rows
are byte addresses, so every
access through the pointer is unaligned: the high half of a transposed
pair is written as an unaligned 64-bit value, not with `movhps`'s typed
`_mm_storeh_pd`).

### Bars

Fixed before the A/B run, which is the luma round's: the branch tip
against its base on `main`, both built alike from one tree each, on a
host that reports the 2.90 GHz class, `scripts/h264_parity.py --pin 2
--rounds 5 --require-cpu "@ 2.90GHz"`, the training set, one call per
class with the class's frame count, FFmpeg 9.0.2 as the third command.
The change adds `unsafe` (pointer loads and stores after one check), so
the bar is the safe rounds':

| Bar | Quantity | Threshold |
|---|---|---|
| DR-1 | median per-stream ratio, branch over base, discard | at most **0.98**, upper end of the 95% interval below 1.00 |
| DR-2 | the same, write | at most **0.985** |
| DR-3 | the same per class (sd, 720p, 1080p, 4k), discard | at most **1.005** in each |
| DR-4 | output | the 32 training streams byte-identical to the base at 1 and 8 threads, against the base at 1; conformance 97 of 97 at 1, 2 and 8 threads and with scalar kernels, on the measured commit |

A miss on any of DR-1 to DR-3 rejects the change, and this section then
records the result. The ratio to FFmpeg 9.0.2 and the share of streams
faster than it, overall and per class, are reported as information.

The gain sits in sd (0.969, 8 of 8 faster) and 720p (0.955, 8 of 8),

## Kernel round: the transforms, a row to a vector

### What the measurement says

A profile of `main` at 3d4c2e63 against FFmpeg 9.0.2, the eight streams
of `docs/measurements/h264-gap-2/` on the 2.90 GHz class
(`docs/measurements/h264-rounds/idct-rows/profile/`), puts the inverse
transforms with their scaling and adding at 356 ms against FFmpeg's
138 ms (+0.22 s of a +4.58 s gap). Of ours, the four-block 4x4 kernel
(`idct4x4_add_quad`) takes 175 ms, the 8x8 kernel 48 ms, the reference
4x4 transform of the Intra_4x4 path 29 ms, and the decoder's own
scaling and DC work the rest.

Callgrind of `main` at 540c770c counts 504 instructions a call of the
four-block kernel on `6da34958296c` and 656 a call of the 8x8 kernel on
`9db41aa16b5a` (`instructions.txt` in the round's directory,
`docs/measurements/h264-rounds/idct-rows/`). The transform itself is
about 50 vector instructions a 4x4 block, inlined and kept in
registers. The rest is the adding:
- each row went through the view's row iterator and `add_row8`, whose
  load and store checked the row's slice;
- the residual waited on the stack (a 216-byte frame in the four-block
  kernel) between the transform and the adding;
- each half row was clipped with a minimum and a maximum before packing.

### Design

1. **One row of the 8x8 block, one vector.** Both kernels hold a row of
   the 8x8 block they add to in one 256-bit vector of eight 32-bit
   values. For the 8x8 transform that is the block's row. For the
   four-block kernel it is a horizontal pair of 4x4 blocks: the left
   block's row in the low 128-bit lane and the right block's in the high
   one. AVX2's unpacks work within a lane, so one 4x4 transpose
   transposes both blocks, and one pass transforms both. Before, each
   4x4 block went through its own 128-bit vectors and the 8x8 block
   through sixteen of them.
2. **One check, then pointers.** As for the deblocking filter's standard
   edges (`rows_at_mut`, the check of `gather`), the kernel checks once
   that eight rows of eight samples lie inside the view's slice. It then
   reads and writes each row through a pointer: a `movq` load and an
   unaligned 64-bit read inserted into the high half for two rows, a
   `movq` store and an unaligned 64-bit write of the high half (`pextrq`)
   to write them back, none a typed access that needs alignment. A view
   of an 8x8 block always passes the check; where it would fail, the
   block goes to the reference.
3. **Four rows added at a time, clipped by saturation.** The residual is
   rounded in 32 bits (`(r + 32) >> 6`), packed to 16 bits with signed
   saturation, added to the prediction with signed saturation, and
   packed to bytes with unsigned saturation. A residual the 16-bit pack
   changes is above 32,767 or below −32,768, and with any prediction
   from 0 to 255 its sum stays above 255 or below 0, as the clamped
   value's does; every other step clamps to a range that holds 0 to 255.
   So the result is `Clip1(p + r)` for every rounded 32-bit residual:
   the same as the reference, with no minimum or maximum. Packing two
   rows interleaves them by lane, so the prediction's two rows are
   shuffled into that order (`pshufb`) before widening, and the result is
   unpacked back into rows.
4. **A clear block in a pair is masked to zero.** A pair whose two bits
   of the mask are clear is skipped. Where one is set, the other block's
   coefficients are masked to zero (one `vpand` a row), and zero
   coefficients give a zero residual. This keeps the trait's rule that a
   block whose bit is clear is left unchanged.
5. **Helpers inlined by force, no closures.** As in the luma round, the
   helpers are `#[inline(always)] unsafe fn`s without
   `#[target_feature]`. They are called only from the two kernels, which
   have AVX2, and they define no closures (a closure there would not
   inherit AVX2). Both kernels compile to straight-line code with no
   stack frame.

Rejected:
- **The single 4x4 transform of Intra_4x4 blocks in vectors.** It is
  29 ms of the eight streams, about 0.3% of the decode, which a run
  cannot resolve as a part of its own. A vector 4x4 transform behind a
  call lost before (round 9). The block sits between two predictions in
  the decoder's Intra_4x4 loop, so it belongs to the intra prediction
  round: there a block's prediction and residual can be one call.
- **16-bit lanes**, as in round 9. The reference computes in 32 bits,
  and a coefficient near the edge of its range would differ without a
  range check per block.
- **Coefficients stored transposed**, to save the first transpose. That
  changes the decoder's coefficient layout and scan tables, to save
  eight unpacks a pair.

Bit-exact by construction (the reference's integers, and clamps that
compose to `Clip1`) and by test:
- the crate's tests compare both kernels with the reference over random
  coefficients, the ends of their range and every mask;
- a new x86 test does the same at the narrowest strides a view allows,
  in a plane that ends at the block's last sample and at offsets 0 to 7;
- the `transform` fuzz target compares `Simd` with the reference.

Alignment is what Miri checks. The harness in `tools/miri` of the
round's directory runs both kernels through `Simd` and `Auto` against
the reference, with AVX2 and SSE4.1 enabled (`cargo +nightly miri run`).
It covers strides 8, 9, 11 and 48, offsets 0 to 7 from a misaligned
base, and a plane that ends at the block's last sample: 160 cases, no
error.

Instructions (callgrind, `--discard`, one thread, against `main` at
540c770c; `instructions.txt`). Q is the four-block kernel alone, A both
kernels:

| Stream | Pictures | `main` | Q | A |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 6da34958296c (1080p) | 60 | 3,841 M | 3,748 M (−2.4%) | 3,748 M (−2.4%) |
| 41e324ebb708 (sd) | 300 | 2,005 M | 1,974 M (−1.6%) | 1,974 M (−1.6%) |
| 9db41aa16b5a (720p) | 150 | 2,924 M | 2,918 M (−0.2%) | 2,900 M (−0.8%) |
| e624cbe0d2be (4k) | 30 | 2,674 M | 2,624 M (−1.9%) | 2,624 M (−1.9%) |

A call of the four-block kernel goes from 504 to 165 instructions, of
the 8x8 kernel from 656 to 207. Timed locally on the eight profiled
streams (information, `local-timing.txt`): A over `main` 0.985 on
discard and 0.980 on write, medians, with single streams moving by 1 to
4% between pairings.

### Bars

Fixed before the A/B run, which is the luma round's: three decoders in
the same rounds, built alike from one tree each (`main` at 540c770c as

summary of the three builds is `analyze.py` in the round's directory.

The speed bar is lower than the 0.98 of the rounds before, because the

10.06 s, 2.2%. Removing all of their time would reach about 0.978, so
0.98 would ask the round to remove nearly all of it. (The profile is of

| Bar | Quantity | Threshold |

| TR-1 | median per-stream ratio, candidate over base, discard | at most **0.99**, upper end of the 95% interval below 1.00 |
| TR-2 | the same, write | at most **0.995** |

The ratio to FFmpeg 9.0.2 and the share of streams faster than it,

## Kernel round: intra prediction in the kernels crate

### What the measurement says

The profile of the transform round (`main` at 3d4c2e63 against FFmpeg
9.0.2, the eight streams of `docs/measurements/h264-gap-2/`, the 2.90 GHz
class; `docs/measurements/h264-rounds/idct-rows/profile/`) puts intra
prediction at 371 ms against FFmpeg's 67 ms, 5.5 times as long (+0.30 s of
a +4.58 s gap). A build of the base with the four prediction functions kept
out of line (`profile-intra.txt` in the round's directory,
`docs/measurements/h264-rounds/intra/`) splits it:

| Function | ms |
|---|---|
| `pred16x16` | 107 |
| `pred_chroma` | 98 |
| `reconstruct_intra`, the loops and the Intra_16x16 DC | 73 |
| `pred4x4` | 62 |
| `pred8x8` | 35 |
| `Scalar::idct4x4_add`, the Intra_4x4 residual | 23 |

Intra_16x16 and chroma prediction are a copy, a fill or a plane of 256 or
64 samples, and they took as long as the 4x4 blocks: each built its block
in a local buffer one sample at a time (the plane mode with a
multiplication and a clamp per sample) and copied it out row by row through
checked slices. The Intra_4x4 macroblock ran sixteen predictions, sixteen
view builds and up to sixteen calls of the reference transform, each block
waiting on the stack between its prediction and its residual.

### Design

1. **The predictions move into the kernels crate**, behind the trait like
   every other pixel kernel: `intra16x16`, `intra_chroma`, and one call
   for each Intra_4x4 and Intra_8x8 macroblock, `intra4x4_mb` and
   `intra8x8_mb`, which predict the blocks in decoding order and add each
   block's residual before the next block reads it. The reference is the
   decoder's prediction code as it was (`intra.rs` of the kernels crate);
   the decoder's `intra.rs` is gone, and `reconstruct_intra` builds one
   view and makes one call per macroblock and plane. The frozen oracle
   `intra_reference.rs` moved with the code, and its test with it.
2. **A view with its neighbours, `IntraMut`.** It holds an n by n block
   and the neighbours `IntraAvail` names: the column left, the row above
   (2n samples with `top_right`) and the sample above and left. Its
   constructor checks each named neighbour, and the view starts at the
   first of them, so a kernel never reaches before a neighbour the caller
   did not say exists. (The Intra_4x4 kernel reads a block's row above
   right with the row above, inside the view, and replaces it where the
   block has none.) The decoder keeps the rule for what
   exists (macroblocks A to D, constrained intra prediction); for the
   blocks inside an Intra_4x4 or Intra_8x8 macroblock, the kernel derives
   each block's neighbours from the macroblock's and the block's position
   (clause 6.4.11.4, the decoder's former `block_avail`). One check of the
   macroblock's view then covers every block, and no caller can name a
   block neighbour outside it.
3. **Intra_16x16 and chroma by rows.** After one check (`IntraRows::of`),
   a vertical prediction is one load and a store a row, horizontal a
   broadcast a row, DC a sum of absolute differences and a broadcast. The
   plane mode holds a row in one vector of 16-bit lanes and adds `c` a
   row: every value before its shift, `a + b(x - 7) + c(y - 7) + 16`, has
   a magnitude below 2^15 with samples of 0 to 255 (at most 16 · 510 +
   2 · 8 · 717 + 16 = 19,648 for 16x16, 16 · 510 + 2 · 4 · 1,355 + 16 =
   19,016 for chroma), so the lanes hold it exactly, and the unsigned
   saturating pack is `Clip1`.
4. **An Intra_4x4 block from one vector.** Each block's edge line (13
   samples, the ends repeated) is one vector, built from the row above
   (one 8-byte read, its last four repeated where there is no top right),
   the column left and the corner. The line's 2-tap averages are one
   `pavgb`. Its 3-tap filter, `(a + 2b + c + 2) >> 2`, is
   `pavgb(b, ((a + c) >> 1))`, the truncated average being
   `pavgb(a, c) − ((a ^ c) & 1)`. This is exact: with a + c = 2k + r,
   both sides are `(k + b + 1) >> 1`. The `const fn` tables of round 9
   (`intra::sources`) become three byte shuffles a mode, one for each of
   the line, the averages and the filter (each under 16 bytes for 4x4),
   or-ed together. Vertical and horizontal are shuffles of the line too;
   DC is a sum and a broadcast.
5. **The residual in registers.** Where a block has coefficients, its
   inverse transform (the four-block kernel's helpers, one block in the
   low lane) is added to the prediction while it is still in a register,
   with the saturating chain of the transform round (point 3 there), and
   the block's four rows are written once. The next block reads its
   neighbours from those rows.

Intra_8x8 keeps the reference prediction behind the new call, with the
vector 8x8 transform (`Simd::intra8x8_mb` runs the reference loop with its
own `idct8x8_add`), until "Kernel round: Intra_8x8 in vectors". It is 35 ms of the eight streams, below what a run
resolves as a part, and its filtered edge of 25 samples does not fit the
shuffles of point 4.

Rejected:
- **Neighbours passed per block** (`&[IntraAvail; 16]` from the decoder).
  The kernel would have to check every block's flags against the view,
  or trust them; deriving them from the macroblock's makes a wrong flag
  impossible.
- **The prediction kept in the decoder, written straight to the picture**
  without moving. The vector forms need `unsafe`, which the decoder crate
  does not allow outside its hot-path module, and the kernels
  crate is where the other pixel kernels and their checks live.
- **Keeping a macroblock's reconstructed blocks in registers** between
  Intra_4x4 blocks instead of reading back what the block before wrote.
  The next block's neighbours come from up to three earlier blocks in
  different positions; the read-back is a few loads a block.

Bit-exact by construction (the clauses' integers, and the identities of
points 3 to 5) and by test:
- the reference against the frozen oracle, every mode, every combination
  of neighbours, blocks across a plane, its edges included;
- each macroblock call against the decoder's former loop (the frozen
  prediction, the former availability and the reference transform), for
  every combination of the macroblock's neighbours, random modes,
  coefficients and masks;
- the availability rule against the decoder's former `block_avail` and
  against a derivation from first principles, for every block and every
  combination of macroblock neighbours, including the top right from C
  for luma4x4BlkIdx 5 and the never-available top right of 3, 7, 11, 13
  and 15;
- `Simd` against `Scalar` for the three vector kernels, every
  combination of neighbours, every mode and some out of range, strides
  from the narrowest a view allows and planes that end at the block's last
  sample (`intra_kernels_match_the_reference`), and the `intra` fuzz
  target;
- Miri, with AVX2 and SSE4.1 enabled, over the three kernels through
  `Simd` and `Auto` against the reference, in planes that start at the
  first neighbour the view names and end at the block's last sample, from

The profile of a build of this design (`profile-intra.txt`) puts the

over its base is 0.974 on discard and 0.978 on write, medians, with the

## Round 11: macroblock records in cache, and the common prediction block

Rejected by its bars (the result is at the end): neither part merged.
The code stays on `rejected/h264-mb-records` (part M) and
`rejected/h264-predict-glue` (part P), each on `main` at `555689b`, with
rows in `docs/measurements/h264-rejected.md`; what follows describes
those branches.

Chosen from a fresh profile of `main` at `555689b` after rounds 9 and 10
and the kernel rounds: callgrind with cache and branch simulation and
`perf` (cpu-clock) on the eight streams of the stage-by-stage gap
(`docs/measurements/h264-gap-2/README.md`), at its frame counts for
`perf` and a third of them for callgrind. Macroblock-level control is
still the largest stage, 25% of the sampled time, and two of its costs
are of two different kinds: the records macroblocks leave each other
(memory), and the glue of motion compensation (instructions). The round
takes one part for each. The profile's summaries are
`docs/measurements/h264-rounds/round11/profile-main.txt`, and the
annotations and counts behind the figures below are in `evidence.txt`
beside it.

### What the measurement says

Part M, the macroblock records:

- **Every macroblock's record was a cache miss.** `MbInfo` was 124 bytes,
  a picture's worth of them (1 MB at 1080p, 4 MB at 4k), allocated and
  filled for every picture. `PictureWork::decode_slice` spends 45% of its
  samples on one load, the check that the macroblock's own record is
  still undecoded, and 21% on writing the record back (`finish_mb`): about
  3% of the decode between them (`decode_slice` is 4.5%). The fill is
  all of `start_picture`'s time (0.9%), and at 4k the allocation adds
  page faults.
- **Neighbours read little of it.** A macroblock reads its own row and
  the row above; the deblocking filter, the row it filters and the row
  above. Of the per-block arrays only the right column and the bottom row
  are read from a neighbour: `mvd` (64 bytes) and `total_coeff` (24) are
  read from macroblocks A and B at those blocks alone.

Part P, motion compensation's glue:

- **`predict_list` is 7.4% of the time and up to 19% of the
  instructions** (`b71b6b31e54f`), with almost no cache misses: about 419
  instructions a call of its own, outside the kernels. They are the
  window test of each of the three planes, six checked block views,
  the reference's band lookup kept live for blocks that do not need it,
  and the spills of a function with three calls.
- **One test answers for three planes.** A luma window inside the
  picture puts both chroma windows inside theirs (below), and almost
  every block reads a reference that is one band of the picture's size
  (`SliceDecoder::whole`; with one thread, every reference).

### Design

Part M:

1. **A slice map** (`SliceDecoder::slices`): the slice of every
   macroblock, 4 bytes each, cleared once a picture. It answers
   availability (clause 6.4.9), "a macroblock decoded twice" and the
   deblocking filter's slice tests, which read `MbInfo::slice` before.
2. **Records in a ring of four macroblock rows** (`RING_ROWS`), reused
   from picture to picture through `Spare` and never cleared: a record is
   read only where the slice map says its macroblock was decoded in this
   picture, and the oldest row anything reads is two above the one being
   decoded (deblocking runs at most two rows behind, `enter_row`). 30 KB
   at 1080p, 61 KB at 4k, against a picture's worth.
3. **A record of one cache line**, aligned to it: the per-block state
   neighbours read is kept for the right column and the bottom row only
   (`MbInfo::edges`, 32 bytes): with CABAC the capped motion vector
   differences, with CAVLC TotalCoeff. A slice has one entropy coder and a
   neighbour in another slice is not available, so the two share the
   bytes. The current macroblock keeps every block's state in
   `SliceDecoder::own`, which `finish_mb` reduces to the edges.

Part P:

4. **A hot path for the common block** (`predict_list`): a reference that
   is one band of the picture's size, through a luma window inside the
   picture. One test covers all three windows: with px, w and the
   picture's width even and q = mv >> 2, a luma window's left end
   px + q - 2 >= 0 gives q >> 1 >= 1 - px / 2, so the chroma window
   (px / 2 + (mv >> 3), w / 2 + 1 wide) starts at 1 or more; its right end
   px + q + w + 3 <= width gives q >> 1 <= (width - px - w) / 2 - 2, so
   the chroma window ends at width / 2 - 1 or before; the same down the
   picture. The blocks are still built by the kernels' checked
   constructors. Every other block (a band of another picture, a window
   reaching outside) takes `predict_list_any`, the code as it was, out of
   line.

Bit-exact by construction: the same values are derived from the same
inputs, and only where they are kept changes.

Rejected:
- **The picture's records reused, with the slice map, but not a ring**
  (built first): the load miss of the undecoded check went, and the same
  miss moved to the store of the record; a record written a picture
  earlier is not in cache however it is reached.
- **Slice numbers in the ring's records, each row cleared as it is
  entered, rather than a slice map:** a row is entered again by every
  slice that starts inside it, so a clear would have to know whether this
  picture cleared the row already; and a row a damaged stream skips is
  never entered, though the deblocking filter still visits it and would
  read the slice numbers of the row four above. A map of 4 bytes a
  macroblock, cleared once a picture, answers both without bookkeeping.
- **A generation stamp in each record instead of a cleared map:** no
  clear at all, but a stamp that wraps can make a stale record look
  current on a damaged stream, and the map costs 32 KB a picture at
  1080p.
- **Block views specialised per partition shape** (const generics): the
  views' checks of width and height fold, the checks against the stride
  and the plane do not, and seven copies of the function cost
  instruction cache.
- **Both chroma planes in one kernel call:** fewer calls and views, but
  it is the kernels' interface, which the kernel rounds own.
- **Each plane placed at its own line of the cache's period** (a third
  part, built and measured with the others): part M changes where the
  allocator puts the picture's planes, as a side effect. `main` freed a
  1 MB array every picture, which raises glibc's mapping threshold, so the
  chroma planes came from the heap at no particular offset; without it
  they are mapped page-aligned, and `chroma_mc`'s simulated D1 read misses
  double on `6da34958296c`. Placing every plane deliberately took the
  simulated misses below `main`'s, and was slower: 1.044 over part M
  alone on the 2.50 GHz class (`docs/measurements/h264-rejected.md`,
  `docs/measurements/h264-rounds/round11/local/`). So part M is measured
  with the allocator placing the planes, as a user's build would.

## Kernel round: both chroma planes' edges in one call

### What the measurement says

A profile of `main` at e6d810cf against FFmpeg 9.0.2, the eight streams
of `docs/measurements/h264-gap-2/`
(`docs/measurements/h264-rounds/deblock-pair/profile/`, `report.txt`),
leaves these gaps in the kernels' stages. It ran on a VM that reported an
Intel Xeon @ 2.50GHz (family 6, model 85), not the 2.90 GHz class of the
bars: its milliseconds are that host's, and the ratios to FFmpeg are what
compare with the profiles before.

| Stage | ours, ms | FFmpeg, ms | gap, ms |
|---|---|---|---|
| chroma interpolation | 1,189 | 243 | +946 |
| luma interpolation | 1,033 | 529 | +504 |
| combining | 517 | 113 | +404 |
| deblocking filter | 932 | 600 | +332 |
| intra prediction | 243 | 62 | +181 |
| transforms | 242 | 143 | +99 |

The two interpolations spend most of their time where a row of the
reference is read: the hottest instruction of each is the one after the
load in the full-sample copy, which a kernel cannot make shorter, and
fetching references ahead is the prediction loop's business, not a
kernel's. Combining is weighted prediction, used by 9 of the 32 training
streams. Of the deblocking filter, luma edges take 575 ms against
FFmpeg's 472, and chroma edges 357 ms against 98, 3.6 times as long and
3.6% of the decode.

A chroma edge of a 4:2:0 picture is eight lines of two samples a side.
The kernel spends about 170 instructions a call on it (callgrind,
`instructions.txt`): the extent checks, the boundary strengths and
thresholds spread to lanes, the four rows or the transposed lines read,
and the filter in one 128-bit vector of 16-bit lanes, half of whose work
is the setup. The decoder calls it twice for each edge, once per plane,
building two views and two thresholds.

### Design

1. **One call for the same edge of both planes,**
   `Kernels::filter_chroma_pair(cb, cr, params)`. The two planes' edges
   share their position, direction and boundary strengths; their
   thresholds may differ, since each plane has its own chroma QP offset.
   A plane whose thresholds filter nothing takes an α of 0, which filters
   no line, as skipping it did. The reference is `filter_edge` on each
   plane, and so is every pair whose two edges differ in shape, and every
   pair on arm64, where `Auto` keeps `filter_edge`'s measured choice per
   edge.
2. **Both planes in one 256-bit vector.** Cb's eight lines fill the low
   128-bit half and Cr's the high one, in 16-bit lanes, so the filter of
   the single-plane kernel runs once, at full width, for both, with α, β
   and t'C0 set per half. A horizontal edge reads each plane's four rows
   of eight samples and joins them per row; a vertical one transposes
   each plane's eight rows of four as the single-plane kernel does.
3. **One check per plane, then pointers**, as for the standard edges of
   the single-plane kernel (`rows_at_mut`): the whole extent of p1 to q1
   is checked before anything is read, and p0 and q0 are written back
   inside it. Where either check fails, both edges go to `filter_edge`.
4. **The decoder** computes both planes' thresholds for an edge, builds
   both views and makes one call; the luma loop and the boundary
   strengths do not change.

Rejected:
- **All of a macroblock's chroma edges in one call.** A macroblock
  filters one or two chroma edges a direction on the profiled streams
  (about 136,000 pair calls for 3,600 macroblocks a picture over 30
  pictures of `9db41aa16b5a`), so a call per macroblock would save little
  over a call per edge, and vertical edges must all be filtered before
  horizontal ones. Counted over the class frame counts, a macroblock
  that filters chroma makes 1.93 to 3.79 calls, and a later round makes
  one ("Kernel round: a macroblock's chroma edges in one call").
- **The same for luma edges**, for the same reason: about 1.2 filtered
  luma edges a macroblock a direction, and the luma kernel's per-call
  cost is a smaller share of its work (16 lines of four samples a side).

Bit-exact by construction (the single-plane kernel's arithmetic in twice
the lanes) and by test: `the_chroma_pair_matches_the_reference_on_each_plane`
compares `Simd` with the reference on each plane over both directions,
every boundary strength, thresholds that differ between the planes (α 0
included), strides from the narrowest a view takes, planes of different
strides and planes that end at the edge's last sample; the
`filter_chroma_pair` fuzz target compares `Simd` and `Auto`; Miri, with
AVX2 and SSE4.1, runs both directions through `Simd` and `Auto` in planes
that start at the edge's first sample and end at its last, from
misaligned bases (`tools/miri`): 144 cases, no error.

Instructions (callgrind, whole decode, `--discard`, one thread, 30
pictures, against `main` at e6d810cf; `instructions.txt`):

| Stream | `main` | pair | chroma calls |
|---|---|---|---|
| 9db41aa16b5a (720p) | 582.8 M | 561.4 M (−3.7%) | 272,568 → 136,284 |
| 6da34958296c (1080p) | 1,926.2 M | 1,878.2 M (−2.5%) | 521,028 → 260,514 |

A chroma edge goes from about 168 instructions a plane to 110. Timed
locally on the eight profiled streams, on the same 2.50 GHz VM
(information, `local-timing.txt`):
0.987 on discard and 0.976 on write, medians, single streams moving by
up to 4% between pairings, the 32 training streams' output unchanged.

Fixed before the A/B run: two decoders in the same rounds, built alike

the branch tip), on a host that reports the 2.90 GHz class,
`scripts/h264_parity.py --pin 2 --rounds 5 --require-cpu "@ 2.90GHz"`,
the training set, one call per class with the class's frame count,
FFmpeg 9.0.2 as the reference command. The summary is `analyze.py` in the

The chroma filter is 3.6% of the profiled decode; the instructions

|---|---|---|
| DP-1 | median per-stream ratio, branch over base, discard | at most **0.99**, upper end of the 95% interval below 1.00 |
| DP-2 | the same, write | at most **0.995** |
| DP-3 | the same per class (sd, 720p, 1080p, 4k), discard and write | at most **1.005** in each |
| DP-4 | output | the 32 training streams byte-identical to the base at 1 and 8 threads, against the base at 1; conformance 97 of 97 at 1, 2 and 8 threads and with scalar kernels, on the measured commit |

## Round 12: motion compensation's lines requested ahead

### What the measurement says

- **Motion compensation waits for memory.** In `chroma_mc`'s full-sample
  copy, one 8-byte load of a reference row and one 8-byte store into the
  picture a row, the samples gather on the store: 28% of the function on
  `b71b6b31e54f`, 46% on `3b1b441e23ae`, where the function is 13% and
  18% of the decode (`docs/measurements/h264-rounds/round12/evidence.txt`;
  the 2.90 GHz class). The store waits on the load before it, or on the
  store queue, which fills when the picture's lines being written are not
  in cache.
- **Both sides are cold above about a megabyte.** A reference was decoded
  a picture or more ago, and the picture being decoded reuses a buffer
  last written several pictures ago ("Reusing a picture without clearing
  it"); at 1080p a picture is 3 MB, at 4k 12 MB, against 1 to 1.25 MB of
  second-level cache a core.
- **What was tried before** (`docs/measurements/h264-rejected.md`): the
  picture's lines read ahead with ordinary loads (`WARM_AHEAD`), which
  hold up retirement when they miss; the reference rows of every
  partition prefetched at the next macroblock's position (0.82 to 0.86 on
  static streams, 1.03 to 1.06 on others); prefetching after skipped
  macroblocks. A prefetch instruction needed `unsafe`, which the decoder
  crate forbids; the kernels crate now offers it behind a safe,
  slice-checked wrapper (`coreav_kernels_h264::prefetch`, one
  `prefetcht0` a row, `docs/unsafe-sites.md`).
- **Which side, measured** (`round12/local/README.txt`, information only:
  the 2.90 GHz class, three rounds, one binary with the hints switched at
  run time, on `main` at `e6d810c` with the size rule below): over the
  720p, 1080p and 4k classes, the destination's lines alone 0.986 on
  discard, the reference's alone 0.984, both 0.971 [0.916, 0.988], the 4k
  class 0.80; each on top of the other 0.978 and 0.982. The same on round
  11's tip gave 0.958 over all 32 streams, and 1.014 on the sd class,
  where the hints only cost.

### Design

1. **The picture's lines, a cache line ahead** (part D,
   `SliceDecoder::request_destination`): a 64-byte line holds four
   macroblocks of luma and eight of chroma, so the first macroblock of
   each four asks for the sixteen luma rows of the next four, and the first
   of each eight for the eight rows of each chroma plane of the next eight.
   Every macroblock writes its area, inter or intra, so these lines are
   always used. About six hints a macroblock.
2. **The reference's lines, a cache line ahead** (part R, in
   `predict_list`; measured and left out, "Result" below): the first block
   of each four macroblocks, at the left edge of its macroblock, asks for
   the rows its window would read one line to the right at its own vector
   (both ends of each of the window's rows, and the chroma rows of both
   planes): neighbouring blocks mostly move alike, and a wrong guess costs
   a hint, not a stall. Only for a reference that is one band of the
   picture (one thread; with more, the reference is looked up by band and
   not hinted).
3. **Only for pictures above 1 MiB of samples** (`mb::ahead`, 384 bytes a
   macroblock): the smallest second-level cache of the x86-64 cores the
   speed bars name (1 MiB on the 2.50 GHz class, 1.25 MiB on the bar
   machine). A picture that fits there stays in that cache from one
   macroblock row to the next with the part of its reference a row
   reads, and the hints would cost without saving a miss. The rule was
   chosen after the local runs above, where the sd class lost 1.014 with
   the hints on; it is a rule from the cache size, not a threshold fitted
   to the training streams, and the next held-out draw tests it.

Hints change no value: the output is the same by construction, and a
hint whose row lies past the plane is not issued. The hints are plain
reads (`prefetcht0`): a write hint needs a target feature the default
build does not enable.

Rejected:
- **Hints two lines ahead, or every macroblock:** not measured; one line
  is what the local runs measured, and a line holds four macroblocks of
  luma, so hinting every macroblock repeats three hints in four.
- **Ordinary loads ahead:** measured before (`WARM_AHEAD`); a load that
  misses holds up retirement, which a hint does not.
- **The reference hinted from the next macroblock's own motion:** it is
  known only after that macroblock is parsed; parsing a macroblock ahead
  of reconstruction was measured before and lost
  (`rejected/h264-prefetch-reorder`).

### Bars

Fixed before the A/B run: `scripts/h264_parity.py --pin 2 --rounds 5
--require-cpu "@ 2.90GHz"` on the training set, one call per class with
the class's frame count, FFmpeg 9.0.2 (BtbN `n9.0.2-17-g2a571b6068`) as
the last command, and four builds timed in the same rounds, all built
alike (`dist`, one toolchain): `main` at `686fb48` (`base`), part D alone
(`d`, branch `perf/h264-mc-dst`), part R alone (`r`, branch
`perf/h264-mc-ref`) and both (`dr`, the branch as it was run; it now carries `d`, "Result"). No arm allocates
differently from another, so the placement control of "Where the
allocator puts the planes" does not apply.

Each part has to earn its place where the size rule turns it on, the 24
streams of the 720p, 1080p and 4k classes (on the sd class both arms run
the same code):

| Bar | Quantity | Threshold |
|---|---|---|
| R12-5 | D on top of R (`dr` over `r`), and R on top of D (`dr` over `d`), discard and write, the 720p, 1080p and 4k classes | upper end of the 95% interval below 1.00 on both pairings |

The round keeps both parts where both pass R12-5, the one that passes
where one does, and where neither does, the part that is faster alone

| R12-3 | the same, discard, the 1080p and 4k classes together (16 streams) | at most **0.98**, upper end below 1.00 |
| R12-4 | the same per class (sd, 720p, 1080p, 4k), discard | at most **1.005** in each |

`docs/measurements/h264-rounds/round12/analyze.py` reads R12-1 to R12-5
