### Stalls at the macroblock record, moved not removed

Two local screenings after the profile above (three runs), each against bars written before its run
(`docs/measurements/h264-rounds/round26-screen/plan.txt`: queue for gating only if the 32 streams' median
is at most 0.997 and, for the last run, no class above 1.003). Both arms decode identically to `main`, one
and eight threads. Neither reached its bar; both diffs are kept on `rejected/` branches for a bundle round.

1. **`colocated`, the co-located picture's motion** (0.010 of FFmpeg's time; the MB layer's most L1
   misses). `rejected/h264-colocated` at `23d67c8` reads the four corners of the co-located macroblock
   once, through one view of its sixteen motion entries, and, when the co-located picture's motion is
   whole and the picture is large enough that lines are asked for ahead (`ahead`), hints the next
   macroblock's four corner lines. It needs a
   generic read hint in the kernels crate (`prefetch::item_for_read`). Five rounds, all 32 streams: with
   the hint 1.0004 of `main` (interval 0.9986 to 1.0034; sd 1.0029, 720p 1.0013, 1080p 0.9999, 4k
   0.9994); the corners alone 1.0034 (4k 1.0080; medians as `classes.txt` computes them).
2. **The macroblock record (`finish_mb`)**, the MB layer's largest item (0.027). Per source line (perf
   time per address folded to the innermost CoreAV inline frame, against callgrind's instructions and
   simulated misses of the same pictures; `lines-sd-6f7799768413.txt`), the largest excess of time over
   instructions on the sd stream is one line: `*slot = self.cur`, the copy of the 60-byte `MbInfo` into
   the picture's records (two 32-byte stores, at offsets 0 and 28), 2.69% of the stream's time for
   0.08% of its instructions, 56 simulated L1 write misses per 1000 instructions and no read misses
   (`record-misses.txt`). Two causes show in the code: a one-byte store to `self.cur`
   just before the copy reloads it 16 and 32 bytes at a time (a failed store-to-load forward), and a
   slot whose line was last written a picture ago.
   - Copying first and setting the slot's `uniform` after it (`rec-p1`) removes the forward: the
     line's time falls from 45.4 to 2.2 ms a run on the sd stream and from 12.8 to 1.7 ms on a 1080p
     CABAC stream, but the next stores take it up (`record-p1-shift.txt`): the motion field's rows
     (`put_row`, +9.0 ms), the next macroblock's `self.cur` (+4.7), the line before (+5.3). Two
     screenings: 0.9998 and 1.0000 of `main`.
   - Adding write hints for the next macroblock's four motion lines and its record slot, every picture
     size (`rec-p2`, `rejected/h264-mb-record` at `aa45cc8`): 1.0017 (interval 0.9997 to 1.0044); the
     hints alone 1.0010. Of these two, only the 4k class came under 0.997 (0.9969 and 0.9919); the
     fix alone ranged 0.9909 to 1.0056 by class over its two runs.

What it says (an inference from two streams' lines and three A/Bs that did not move): **the MB layer
is bound by its store traffic**, not by one slow line. Its writes go to the
motion field and the records, whose lines were last touched a picture ago; the stores wait for those lines,
and the wait shows at whichever store comes first. Per-line excess shows where the wait surfaces, not its
cause: removing it at one line moves it to the next store, and asking for the lines earlier did not
shorten it. Untested yet: a round that should move the MB layer's time likely has to store fewer bytes
per macroblock (a smaller record or motion entry, fewer copies), not reorder or hint the same ones.

### Where the stores go, and a probe that could not bound them

The test that note left open, in three steps (`docs/measurements/h264-rounds/round27-stores/`).

1. **The CABAC streams' lines** (`lines-*.txt`, `addr.py` as above). The decision chain
   (`cabac.rs` 194 to 215; `chain-*.txt`, summed in `chain-sum.txt`) is 26.8% of the time for 19.8% of the
   instructions on the 1080p-class CABAC stream (1560x720), 14.2/10.0 on the 720p one and 5.8/3.4 on the 4k one. Its excess sits at the state store with the next
   decision's start (line 204) and at the `LPS_NORM` load (197): no mispredictions (the chain is
   branchless) and 9 to 43.5 simulated L1 read misses per 1000 instructions at the table loads, whose
   tables (2 and 4 KB, one copy each in the binary) the rest of the decode evicts. The residual loops
   (600 to 799) show little excess. One cut aimed at those misses, the two tables read as one table of
   `[rangeLPS, renormalized rangeLPS]` pairs so that a decision touches one line
   (`rejected/h264-cabac-lps-pair`; same output, 32 of 32, one and eight threads), was slower: 1.0151 of
   `main` over the 32 streams (interval 1.0054 to 1.0218; 1080p 1.0251; `plan-lps.txt`, `ab-lps-pair.txt`,
   `classes-lps-pair.txt`), likely as its 8 KB table takes more of L1 than the 6 KB of two. Nothing there has a
   cause beyond the chain itself; next come the MB
   layer's store lines again (the record copy, `store_mb`'s row copy, the record fill: 3.1% excess on
   the 1080p stream, 7.3% on the 4k one).
2. **The store account** (`stores-*.txt`, `stores.py`: callgrind's data writes per instruction times
   the store's width read from the disassembly). A macroblock stores 385 to 908 times, 2.8 to 6.9 KB,
   mostly to lines already in L1 (the stack, the decoder's state). Its 11 to 12.3 simulated L1 write
   misses split into the picture (about 6, near the minimum for 384 bytes of rows), the motion field
   (2.9 to 3.0: its 192 bytes a macroblock, three lines; `store_mb`'s row copy alone 2.3 to 2.95) and
   the records (about 1.2: written twice, by the fill and the copy). One-partition macroblocks
   (`store_mb`) are 0.77 (720p) to 0.98 (4k) of all macroblocks. Of a one-motion macroblock's sixteen
   entries, readers use the edges: neighbours read A's right column, B's bottom row, C's block 12 and
   D's block 15; P_Skip blocks 3 and 12; deblocking the edges (and block 0 alone inside a uniform
   macroblock); a later B picture's colocated the corners (all sixteen without
   `direct_8x8_inference`). Rows 1 to 3 are read, by neighbours,
   P_Skip and deblocking.
3. **The change and its probe.** Storing one entry for a macroblock with one motion, with a
   per-macroblock byte that readers resolve, would cut about two of the motion field's three missed
   lines for those macroblocks. The profile bounds the gain by the excess time (time share less
   instruction share) of `store_mb`'s row copy (`inter.rs` 569) and the colocated read (905) in `lines-*.txt`:
   sd 0.72%, 720p 1.56%, 1080p 1.27%, 4k 3.86%, with perhaps half of it reachable.
   Before building it, a timing probe (`probe.diff`) wrote `store_mb`'s rows 1 to 3 to a scratch array
   instead of the picture, its output wrong by design. Bars set before the run (`plan.txt`): build
   only if the probe's median over the 32 streams is at most 0.990 or the 720p or 1080p class's at most
   0.985. Six rounds, all 32 (`ab-probe.txt`, `classes-probe.txt`): **1.0779** (bootstrap interval 1.0400
   to 1.1102; sd 1.1052, 720p 1.0363, 1080p 1.0417, 4k 1.0836; faster on 7 of 32). Not built.

The probe measured the wrong thing, which the result shows: rows 1 to 3 are read (step 2), so the
stale entries it left changed every later prediction from them, and with it how much the decoder does.
On the 720p stream's first 180 pictures it ran 2.79 G instructions against `main`'s 4.04 G
(`probe-instructions.txt`); on most streams it ran slower. A probe of the stores alone has to keep the
readers right, which is the change itself (one accessor every reader goes through); the profile's
bound (1.56% at most on the 720p stream, 1.27% on the 1080p-class one) is near the build bar even if all of it were
reached. The change stays unbuilt. A smaller store traffic would have to come from somewhere the
readers do not depend on, or from a cheaper picture-row store (the larger share of the misses).


## Kernel round: the three planes in one call

### What the measurement says

The profile of the AVX-512 round (`docs/measurements/h264-rounds/avx512-deblock/`,
`profile.txt`, `main` at b7cad07, the training set, one thread) puts
inter prediction's kernels and glue at these mean per-stream shares:
the luma interpolation 9.9%, `Auto::chroma_mc` 8.0% and
`chroma_mc_avg` 1.0%, `predict_list` 4.4% and `inter_pred` 4.5%. A
block predicted from a whole reference (every block, with one thread)
builds six views (a window and a block for each plane, each `Block::new`
or `BlockMut::new` a checked range) and makes three calls through `Auto`,
each of which tests its shape again. The two chroma planes share the
block's vector, fractions and shape, and the x86 chroma kernel is SSE2,
eight samples a vector, one plane at a time.

Instruction counts (callgrind, information; `predict/instructions.txt`)
on a 720p stream's first 60 frames: `predict_list` 354 instructions a
call before the kernels it calls; the chroma kernels and their dispatch
about 188 million of the decode's 1,840 million.

### The interface (agreed with the decoder's side)

- `Kernels::predict(&self, dst: PlanesMut, src: &Planes, px, py, w, h,
  mv: [i16; 2], ops: [PlaneOp; 3]) -> bool`. `PlaneOp` is `Put`, `Avg`
  or `Weigh(Weighting)`, one per plane (luma, Cb, Cr), the three
  operations of round 14's `Target::Weighted` (explicit weighting may
  leave luma at the default and weight chroma). Round 14 itself was
  rejected (section "Round 14"); its call site is carried over here, step
  0 below. `false` means the call
  declined the block and wrote nothing; the caller predicts it the old
  way (`predict_list_any`).
- `Planes` is a whole reference, three planes, the stride and the rows,
  checked once when it is made (each plane holds its rows); the decoder
  makes one per whole reference when a slice starts
  (`SliceDecoder::whole`). Banded references (more than one thread) keep
  `predict_list_any`.
- `PlanesMut` is the picture's three planes as the decoder holds them
  (`self.out`, taken per band row), the stride and the rows the planes
  start at, luma's and chroma's, each given: today chroma's is half of
  luma's, but a band's apron of another size would break that, and the
  kernel would then write chroma at the wrong rows without a sign. It is
  built per call and checks nothing; the kernel checks each block it
  writes.
- The kernel checks every window itself, chroma's included: that the
  luma window lies inside implies chroma's for 4:2:0 (the decoder's
  comment of round 13), but the kernel does not rely on it.
- The default is by parts: the six views and the three per-plane
  kernels, as the decoder called them. It is the reference for the tests
  and the fuzz target. The prefetch hints stay where they are.

### Design

0. **Round 14's call site, carried over** (build `w`). Round 14
   (`rejected/h264-weighted-call`, code d440615) predicts a weighted
   block straight into the picture: `combine_modes` and `fused_ops` map
   the block's weighting to one operation per plane, `Target::Weighted`
   carries them by reference, implicit weights are worked out once a
   slice (`implicit_w1`), and a weighting outside `Weighting::in_range`
   keeps scratch and `combine`. It is the call site this round's
   `predict` takes operations from, so it is ported in its code only,
   and measured as a part of its own: round 14 lost 1.7% on 4k in its
   second run without an explanation, which this round's bars guard
   against (P-3, P-4). Round 14 traced its first run's loss to a large
   `Target` taking the unweighted kernels' dispatch out of line; here
   `predict_whole` makes one kernel call, `Kernels::predict`, and
   callgrind on the 1080p stream shows `Auto::luma_mc` and
   `luma_mc_avg` not called from it, and `Auto::chroma_mc` called only
   from `predict_list_any`, as on `main`.
1. **One check, `predict::place`.** Sizes 4, 8 or 16 each way (the
   partitions), weightings in `Weighting::in_range`, the windows inside
   the reference (luma `(w + 5)` by `(h + 5)` from two samples before the
   block, chroma `(w / 2 + 1)` by `(h / 2 + 1)` at the block's chroma
   position plus the vector's whole chroma samples, Equations 8-229 and
   8-230), the blocks inside the picture's planes, and a position at most
   `MAX_SIZE` (2^15, four times the largest level's width). With the
   reference's stride and rows held to `MAX_SIZE` by `Planes::new`, every
   offset fits 64 bits with room, so the check is plain arithmetic, not
   checked arithmetic: the first form, with `checked_mul` and
   `try_from`, took about 140 instructions a call. It returns the six
   regions' offsets; every row of each lies inside its slice (a window's
   rows are rows of the reference, which `Planes::new` checked; a block's
   last row is checked against its plane's length).
2. **x86: luma on the checked offsets** (`simd/x86/predict.rs`). An 8- or
   16-wide block goes to `luma_mc_ptrs`, the body of `luma_mc_into` after
   its check, split out of it; a 4-wide block goes where `Auto` sends it
   today (the reference, `Simd::prefers_luma_mc`). The luma code (64
   forms by width, position and finish) is a function of its own,
   `luma_block`: inlined, it took the registers of the check, which then
   spilled to the stack.
3. **Both chroma planes in one AVX2 pass** (`chroma_block`): Cb in the
   low 128 bits of each vector and Cr in the high. `H` of Equation 8-266
   is `pmaddubsw` of each sample and its right neighbour, interleaved as
   byte pairs, against `(8 - xFracC, xFracC)`: `(8 - xFracC) A + xFracC B`
   is at most 2,040 and never saturates. The vertical step is the SSE2
   kernel's, `8 up + yFracC (down - up)`, in 16-bit lanes, rounded and
   shifted, packed to bytes. An 8-wide block takes one row a step and
   reuses the row below as the next step's row above; 4- and 2-wide
   blocks take two rows a step. Each plane is then finished as its
   operation says, written, averaged or weighted, by the SSE2 kernel's
   `Finish` (so the weighting is the one conformance covers), and stored
   a row at a time. A full-sample position copies the rows. Rows are read
   and written as `W`-byte arrays through pointers from `place`'s
   offsets, as `luma_mc_into` does after its check.
4. **The call site** (`SliceDecoder::predict_whole`, which round 13's
   `predict_list` calls in a slice with a reference in one band): a
   whole reference and a target that writes the picture (not round 14's
   `Target::Scratch`, a weighting out of range) call `predict` with the
   target's operations; a decline goes to `predict_list_any`, which still
   handles every block. Round 13's body of `predict_whole` (its own
   window test, six views, three calls) is gone.
5. **AVX-512 is not used here.** The AVX-512 round measured luma
   interpolation in that tier as no gain in the decoder (memory-bound),
   and the chroma pass above is a third of `predict`'s instructions;
   masked loads would save the second read of each row, a few
   instructions a row. Left for a later round, measured in the decoder.

Rejected:
- **Keeping the per-plane kernels behind `predict`, with only the check
  shared** (commit c6733f9 alone): 0.6% to 3.7% more instructions than
  `base` on the four streams above when it was measured on round 14's
  first form; not timed as a part, since the one check alone has no
  reason to be faster.
- **Checking the windows in the decoder and handing the kernel views**:
  the six views are the cost being removed, and the kernel would still
  have to trust the decoder's arithmetic for its pointers.
- **A `Planes` per call**: its check (three lengths against the stride
  times the rows) belongs once a slice, as `SliceDecoder::whole` did for
  the band lookup.
- **Chroma in 512-bit vectors, both planes and two rows**: a block's
  chroma is 2 to 8 rows of 8 samples or fewer; the wider vector would
  mostly be shuffled into and out of.

Bit-exact by construction (the equations' integer forms, the same
finishing code) and by test: `tests/equivalence.rs` runs `Auto`, `Simd`
and `Scalar`, with and without the AVX-512 tier, against the planes
written out by the per-plane reference kernels, over every block size,
every luma and chroma fraction, each operation in each plane, vectors
that reach every edge of the reference and past it, and blocks at every
edge of a band (10,800 blocks, of which 263 to 522 of each size's
1,200 are predicted and the rest declined), and checks that what is
declined writes nothing; a rounding constant changed by one
fails it. The fuzz target `predict` compares the same kernels with
planes no longer than they must be.

### Bars

Fixed before the A/B run: four decoders in the same rounds, built alike
from one tree each, on one host of either bar class (the 2.90 GHz class,
family 6 model 106, or the 2.50 GHz class, model 85; the run records
which): `base`, `main` at 678bd69, the commit the branch is based on
(named in the request to the A/B run and the PR), `w` (round 14's call
site, step 0), `k1` (+ `predict` by parts and the call site) and `k2`
(+ the x86 `predict`, steps 2 and 3, the branch's last code commit);
`scripts/h264_parity.py --pin 2 --rounds 5 --require-cpu` with the
host's class, the training set, one call per class with the class's
frame count, FFmpeg 9.0.2 as the reference command, each call between
two host gates (`HOST-GATE.md`; a failed gate after a call voids it and
it runs again)
(`docs/measurements/h264-rounds/predict/run-ab-helper.sh`; the summary
is `analyze.py`, which prints the bars). The change allocates nothing,
so the placement guard of "Speed (step 6)" does not apply. The
weighted streams are round 14's nine (`analyze.py`, `WEIGHTED`); the
other 23 have no weighted block to speak of.

On four training streams (one a class, the first frames), `k2`
executes 0.639 to 0.961 of `base`'s instructions (0.639 is the weighted
sd stream, most of it from `w`), `w` 0.715 to 1.003 and `k1` over `w`
1.018 to 1.084 (`predict/instructions.txt`). Instructions are
not time: memory, not instructions, bounded the AVX-512 luma

| Bar | Quantity | Threshold |
|---|---|---|
| P-1 | median per-stream ratio, `k2` over `base`, discard | at most **0.990**, upper end of the 95% interval below 1.00 |

| P-5 | output | the 32 training streams byte-identical to `base` with each build at 1 and 8 threads, against `base` at 1; conformance 97 of 97 at 1, 2 and 8 threads and with scalar kernels, on `k2` |

The branch ships if `k2` meets P-1 to P-5; otherwise this section

7 of 8 streams faster; `w` over `base` 1.004 and 1.006. The
ratio to FFmpeg 9.0.2 and the share of streams faster than it, overall
and per class, for each build, are reported as information.

## Kernel round: chroma interpolation in four weights

### What the measurement says

A profile of `main` at `3ebeda9` (the three-plane round merged), made as
"Profile: where the time goes against FFmpeg" made its own, one round
(`docs/measurements/h264-rounds/chroma-kernel/profile.txt`): the chroma
kernels take 0.067 of FFmpeg's time against FFmpeg's 0.033 (sd 0.055,
720p 0.050, 1080p 0.059, 4k 0.105 against 0.028 to 0.041), down from
0.132 at `82c7f7b`. Of that, `chroma_block` (the three-plane call's
two-plane pass) is 0.058 and the per-plane kernel of the edge path 0.009.

- **At 4k it waits on the reference.** Half of `chroma_block`'s samples
  at 4k (a fifth at 1080p) fall on the instruction after a reference
  row's load in the full-sample copy. Exploratory variants
  (`chroma-kernel/local/`, information): with no chroma prediction at all
  the decode takes 0.965 of `main`'s time (4k 0.917); copying every block
  as at a full-sample position 0.984 (4k 0.976); at 4k, the copy reading
  the reference and writing nothing 0.957, writing and reading nothing
  0.966. The arithmetic is worth about 1.6% of the time; the rest is the
  calls, the copies and the reference's latency.
- **Hints do not buy that latency back here.** A `prefetcht0` of both
  chroma windows' rows when the call starts, so that they arrive while
  luma is predicted, cost 1.4% on 1080p and 4k (8.7% on the static
  `3b1b441e23ae`). Round 12's part R moved into the kernel (the next
  line of the window's rows, at every fourth macroblock) measured 1.000
  [0.990, 1.010] over 720p, 1080p and 4k, streams from 0.85 to 1.08, as
  in its two runs before.
- **The kernel's instructions** (callgrind, `chroma-kernel/instructions.txt`):
  288 a call on a 720p stream. An interpolated 8-wide row takes about 28:
  the separable form's horizontal `pmaddubsw` and its vertical step of
  seven operations, and each plane's finishing operation tested on every
  row, with pointers reloaded from the stack around the tests. A copied
  row takes about 17. On the weighted sd stream the weighted copy is most
  of it, each plane weighted on its own, at about 36 instructions a row.

### Design

1. **Equation 8-266 in its own form.** `((8 - xFracC)(8 - yFracC) A +
   xFracC (8 - yFracC) B + (8 - xFracC) yFracC C + xFracC yFracC D + 32) >>
   6`: each row's samples and their right neighbours as byte pairs (Cb in
   the low 128 bits, Cr in the high, as the three-plane round has them),
   one `pmaddubsw` against `(A, B)` for the row and one against `(C, D)` for
   the row below, an add, and `(sum + 32) >> 6` as one `pmulhrsw` by 512
   (`(512 sum + 2^14) >> 15` is the same value). The weights add to 64, so
   each product pair and the sum are at most 64 * 255 and nothing
   saturates. With one row a step the row below's pairs are the next
   step's row, so each row is read once. The weights come from a table of
   the 64 positions. About 18 instructions an interpolated row, from 28.
2. **The finishing operation chosen once a block.** The kernel is a
   generic loop over a `Finishes` type, picked by the two planes'
   operations: both written, both averaged (the two most common: a list's
   prediction, and the second of two lists), both weighted with the same
   kind of weighting, or each as its own `Finish` says (the general form,
   as before). Nothing is tested per row, and a written block's rows are
   never read.
3. **Both weighted planes in one 256-bit pass.** `weigh8`, the weighting
   conformance covers, on Cb's samples in the low 128 bits and Cr's in the
   high: each half with its own plane's weights, rounding and offset, and
   `vpsravd` shifting each 32-bit lane by its own plane's count (H.264
   shares the chroma planes' log2 denominator, but the kernel does not rely
   on that). Uni-prediction (the block's prediction weighted) and
   bi-prediction (the block's samples as list 0) are separate forms; a
   block with one of each falls to the general form.

Instructions (`instructions.txt`): `chroma_block` 0.60 to 0.66 of
`main`'s, the whole decode 0.958 on the weighted sd stream, 0.986 on a
weighted 720p stream and 0.970 on the 1080p stream. The reads and
writes are those of the three-plane round's kernel: rows of `W` bytes
inside the windows and blocks `place` checked, nothing beyond them
(`docs/unsafe-sites.md`), so a window whose unused samples are not the
picture's would not change the output.

Rejected:
- **One-dimensional forms** where one fraction is 0 (one `pmaddubsw` a
  row, and for xFracC 0 half the reads): more instructions on two of the
  three streams counted (1.001 and 1.001 of the build without them, 0.9996
  on the third); the added forms cost more in the call than they save.
- **Hints of the chroma windows at the call's start, and the reference's
  next line from the kernel** (above): slower, and mixed.
- **512-bit vectors** (the three-plane round's reason: a block's chroma is
  at most eight rows of eight samples a plane).

Bit-exact by construction (the equation as written; the averaging and
weighting are the same integer formulas) and by test: the three-plane
round's equivalence test (every block size, fraction and operation in
each plane, `Auto` and `Simd` with and without the AVX-512 tier) and its
fuzz target `predict`, run for 1.1 million inputs on the branch. A
rounding constant of 513, Cr weighted with Cb's weights or shift, or list
0 read from Cb's block for both planes each fails the test
(`chroma-kernel/verification.txt`). A third of the test's blocks give
both chroma planes the same operation, so that each paired form is
reached on purpose.

### Bars

decoders in the same rounds, built alike from one tree each, on this host

The instruction counts above drop 1.4% to 4.2% of the decode; time

## Round 16: tight motion-compensation windows

The profile's edge fetch ("Profile: where the time goes against FFmpeg",
item 4): blocks whose interpolation reads no sample outside the
reference picture still took the edge path, because the window's fixed
size reached past the picture.

### What the measurement says

- **5.05% of the luma predictions from a whole reference were declined
  by `Kernels::predict`** (median per stream; 1.90% to 28.21%), and 86%
  of those read no sample outside the picture: their vector's fraction
  is zero in the direction that crosses the edge, so the interpolation
  does not use the window's margin there (`edge-counts.txt` of the
  profile).
- **A replicated border is not the answer here.** A prototype stored
  single-band pictures with a border of 32 luma and 16 chroma samples,
  filled from the edges when a picture is published, so that windows
  within it took the fast path (`exp/h264-ref-border`, `61cf164` and
  `e9bfa7c`; identical output, conformance 97 of 97). Locally it gained
  2% to 4% on sd and lost up to 10% on the cheapest 4k streams: median
  about 1.00 on 16 streams (`docs/measurements/h264-rounds/round16/local/`).
  Its instructions fell 1% to 4%, so the loss is memory: writing about
  0.6 MB of border a 4k reference picture costs what the edge path
  saves, and borders of 64 and 128 samples lose more. Rejected, with the
  averaging round's reason (the layout of every picture changes) now
  measured.
- **Without a border, the upper bound is there**: a build that clamps
  every window into the picture (not bit-exact) ran 0.91 to 0.97 on
  edge-heavy sd streams and 0.93 to 0.97 on two 4k streams
  (`local/ab-upper-bound.txt`).

### Design

1. **The kernels' contract states what a prediction reads.** A
   prediction depends only on the window samples its fraction uses
   (Equations 8-243 to 8-261 for luma, 8-266 for chroma, where a sample
   of weight 0 is unused); the window's other samples may hold anything.
   With xf 0 no luma column but the block's own is used, with yf 0 no
   row; the chroma window's extra column is unused with cxf 0 and its
   extra row with cyf 0. Property tests give every unused sample random
   values and require the same output from every kernel form (scalar,
   vector, with and without AVX-512), for the single-plane forms and for
   `predict`.
2. **`place()` takes a block whose used samples are inside the
   picture**: the luma margin counts only along a non-zero fraction, the
   chroma extra column or row only with a non-zero chroma fraction. The
   whole window must still lie in each plane's slice, which is what keeps
   the views in bounds; it may run into the neighbouring row or the slack
   below.
3. **Slack rows instead of a border.** A picture of one band (one thread,
   whose references `predict_whole` reads) stores 4 luma rows and 2
   chroma rows above and below each plane, never filled, so that a window
   at the top or bottom edge stays inside its slice. The stride is
   unchanged and nothing is written. `Planes::with_origin` and
   `PlanesMut::with_origin` carry each plane's origin (`Planes::new` is
   origin 0); `MAX_ORIGIN` keeps `place()`'s arithmetic within 2^32.
4. **Pictures of more than one band keep their layout.** With more than
   one thread, references are banded and motion compensation takes the
   banded path (`predict_list_any`) for every block, so slack rows there
   would serve no reader; giving banded references the fast path,
   windows inside a band and its aprons, is a separate round, which
   would then extend the slack to bands. The relaxed `place()` already
   accepts edge windows in middle rows of any reference whose whole
   window lies in the slice.

The memory estimate counts the slack rows (a test covers a one-thread
picture). Output identical to `main` (`3ebeda9`) on the 32 training
streams at one and eight threads; conformance 97 of 97 at 1, 2 and 8
threads and with scalar kernels; declines fall to 1.06% median per
stream, 1.21% of all predictions (`docs/measurements/h264-rounds/round16/`).
Locally (information only, noisy): median 0.979 on 14 streams weighted
to edge-heavy ones, sd 0.89 to 1.00 (`local/ab-tight.txt`).

## Kernel round: luma interpolation by byte pairs

### What the measurement says

The profile of `main` at `3ebeda9` (`docs/measurements/h264-rounds/chroma-kernel/profile.txt`)
puts the luma interpolation at 0.104 of FFmpeg's time against FFmpeg's 0.081 (sd 0.083 against
0.071, 720p 0.087 against 0.073, 1080p 0.104 against 0.092, 4k 0.140 against 0.086). The evidence
for this round is in `docs/measurements/h264-rounds/luma-kernel/`.

- **Most samples are copies.** Of the luma samples the three-plane call predicts in 8- and
  16-wide blocks, 0.64 are at the full-sample position, 0.10 at b, a or c, 0.08 at h, d or n,
  0.08 at e, g, p or r (b and h averaged), 0.07 at f, i, k or q (j with b or h) and 0.03 at j.
  0.95 are in 16-wide blocks. 0.05 are weighted, 0.04 of them at the full-sample position
  (`positions.txt`).
- **The arithmetic is worth a few percent at most.** Exploratory variants of the chroma branch
  (`local/`, information): with no luma prediction in those blocks the decode takes 0.937 of the
  base's time (4k 0.892), and with every such block copied as if at the full-sample position
  0.957 [0.946, 0.978] (sd 0.969, 720p 0.982, 1080p 0.957, 4k 0.941). The second bound takes in
  the interpolation's extra reads, the five rows and columns of the window, as well as its
  arithmetic.
- **The kernel's instructions** (callgrind, `instructions.txt`): `luma_block` is 4.1% of the
  instructions on a weighted 720p stream, at about 295 a call. Its largest loops are the 16-wide
  copy and the 16-wide weighted copy, which weighs in 32-bit lanes at 25 instructions a row and
  tests for each row whether list 0 is the block's samples. Then come the interpolated rows. The
  horizontal 6-tap widens six shifted loads of the row (six shuffles on port 5 for a 16-wide row),
  and the centre j's vertical 6-tap unpacks six rows of intermediates into 32-bit pairs, twelve
  more shuffles a row.

### Design

1. **The horizontal 6-tap as three `pmaddubsw` of byte pairs.** A row's `w + 5` samples are
   loaded as two vectors that end inside the row: for a 16-wide block samples 0 to 15 in the low
   128 bits and 5 to 20 in the high; for an 8-wide block 0 to 7 and 5 to 12 in one 128-bit vector.
   Three `pshufb` pair output column `i`'s samples `i` with `i + 1`, `i + 2` with `i + 3`, and
   `i + 5` with `i + 4`, and `pmaddubsw` takes them against (1, -5), (20, 20) and (1, -5). Each
   pair's sum is -1,275 to 10,200 and the total -2,550 to 10,710, b1's range, so nothing
   saturates, and the lanes come out in column order. A 16-wide row costs two loads, three
   shuffles, three `pmaddubsw` and two adds, where it cost six widening loads and eight adds and
   shifts.
2. **The centre j in 16-bit lanes.** With `x`, `y` and `z` the sums of the outer, second and
   inner pairs of the six rows of b1, Equation 8-247's `(x - 5 y + 20 z + 512) >> 10` equals
   `((c >> 2) + z + 32) >> 6` with `c = ((x - y) >> 2) - y + z`. The bits each `>> 2` drops lie
   below the units of the rest, an integer. Every step fits 16 bits except `c`, whose add
   saturates. Where `c` would pass 32,767, `z` is above 21,037 and both the true and the saturated
   results clip to 255; where it would pass -32,768, both are negative and clip to 0. The code
   comment "The centre j in 16 bits" gives the bounds. That is ten operations a row with no
   unpacking, in place of the 32-bit form's twelve unpacks, six `pmaddwd` and nine adds and shifts.
3. **The roundings as `pmulhrsw`.** `(v + 16) >> 5` is `pmulhrsw` by 1024 and `(d + 32) >> 6`
   by 512, one operation each.
4. **A weighted full-sample block weighed in 16-bit lanes** (`Words`). `pmaddubsw` of the
   (list 0, list 1) byte pairs against the weights as bytes gives `x w0 + y w1` exactly where the
   weights are -128 to 127, the positive ones add to at most 128 and the negative ones to at least
   -128 (then the sum is within 32,640). Equation 8-288's rounding and shift are a `pmulhrsw` by
   `2^(14 - logWD)`, and Equations 8-286 and 8-287's (logWD 1 or more) by `2^(15 - logWD)`, with
   the prediction as both samples and a second weight of 0. The offset is added and the pack
   clips. That is about ten instructions a 16-wide row in place of 25, and whether list 0 is the
   block's samples is a constant of the loop. Weightings outside those bounds (a weight of 128,
   one list with logWD 0) and interpolated weighted blocks keep the 32-bit form. The edge path's
   weighted kernel (`luma_mc_weighted`) is unchanged.

Instructions (`instructions.txt`): the decode takes 0.9824 of the base's on the weighted sd
stream, 0.9940 on the weighted 720p stream, 0.9998 on the 1080p stream (almost all copies)
and 0.9990 on a 4k stream. Over the 32 training streams in short segments the median is 0.9953
(sd 0.9956, 720p 0.9928, 1080p 0.9941, 4k 0.9996), the nine weighted streams 0.9909 and the 23
others 0.9990. Memory touched: the reads stay inside the window rows and the writes inside the
block rows that `place` and `window_fits` check (`docs/unsafe-sites.md`).

Rejected:
- **An AVX-512 luma tier** (`docs/measurements/h264-rounds/avx512-luma-mc/`): no gain in one
  binary, memory-bound.
- **The vertical 6-tap by byte pairs** (each new row interleaved with the one above, three
  `pmaddubsw` a row into three pending outputs): three shuffles a row for about one operation
  saved against the widened form.
- **The weighting in words at every position** (a finish of its own per kind of weighting, for
  all 32 positions and both widths): 64 more loop bodies in `luma_block`, for the 1% of samples
  that are weighted and interpolated.
- **The weighting in words through `luma_mc_ptrs`**, which would cover the edge path too:
  `luma_block`'s prologue grew, a net gain on the weighted streams but 0.07% more instructions on
  the 1080p stream. With `weigh_full` out of line, the prologue grew by about eight
  instructions a call.

Bit-exact by construction (each step is the equation's integer value, as argued above) and by
test. The luma kernels' tests against the reference cover every width, height, position and
operation, and the three-plane equivalence test and fuzz target `predict` cover them too. Two
tests are new. `the_centre_in_words_is_the_equation` checks the 16-bit steps against the equation
over b1's range, both saturating cases included. `the_centre_of_extreme_rows_matches_the_reference`
runs the j positions on windows whose rows give b1 its extremes in phase and checks that the
saturating add is reached. The equivalence test `full_sample_weighting_at_its_bounds_matches_the_reference`
covers weights at and just past the bounds of `Words`, every logWD, offsets at their ends and
samples mostly 0 and 255.

### Bars

Fixed before the A/B run, on the method of the chroma kernel round: two decoders in the same
rounds, built alike from one tree each, on this host (the 2.90 GHz class, family 6 model 106; the
run records it). `base` is `main` at `3443dfc`, the commit the branch is based on, and `k` is the
branch's code commit `d10c367`. The run is `scripts/h264_parity.py --pin 2 --rounds 5
--require-cpu` with the host's class, on the training set, one call per class with the class's
frame count, FFmpeg 9.0.2 as the reference command, each call between two host gates (a failed
gate after a call voids it and it runs again). The script is
`docs/measurements/h264-rounds/luma-kernel/run-ab-helper.sh`, and `analyze.py` beside it prints
the bars. The change allocates nothing, so the placement guard of "Speed (step 6)" does not
apply. The weighted streams are round 14's nine. No build of `k` was timed before these bars were
committed; the exploratory runs above timed throwaway variants.

The instruction counts drop 0.5% at the median, 0.9% on the weighted streams and almost nothing
at 4k, and time follows instructions less than one to one here. The expected gain is a few tenths
of a percent, smaller than the half-width of the interval over 32 streams (about 0.5% in the
chroma round), so the bar asks for the median to gain 0.3%, without an interval that excludes no
gain. The weighted streams must gain as much, and no class, nor the unweighted streams, may lose
more than half a percent:

| Bar | Quantity | Threshold |
|---|---|---|
| LK-1 | median per-stream ratio, `k` over `base`, discard | at most **0.997** |
| LK-2 | the same, write | at most **1.00** |
| LK-3 | the same per class (sd, 720p, 1080p, 4k), discard and write | at most **1.005** in each |
| LK-4 | the same over the nine weighted streams, discard; over the 23 others, discard and write | at most **0.997**; at most **1.005** |
| LK-5 | output | the 32 training streams byte-identical to `base` with `k` at 1 and 8 threads, against `base` at 1; conformance 97 of 97 at 1, 2 and 8 threads and with scalar kernels, on `k` |

The branch ships if `k` meets LK-1 to LK-5; otherwise this section records the result. The
ratio to FFmpeg 9.0.2 and the share of streams faster than it, overall and per class, for both
builds, are reported as information, each naming its build's commit.

### Result: passed

`docs/measurements/h264-rounds/luma-kernel/gating/` (`analysis.txt`, `identity.txt`,
`hostgate.log`, `provenance.txt`, `conformance.txt`): one run on the 2.90 GHz Intel class (family 6,
model 106), with `base` = `main` at `3443dfc` and `k` = `d10c367` in the same rounds. The host gate
passed before and after each of the four calls (FFmpeg at 0.965 to 0.998 of the class's
reference), and no call was void. Output was identical on 32 of 32 streams for `k` at 1 and 8

| Bar | Result | Threshold |
|---|---|---|
| LK-1, discard | **0.9896 [0.9859, 0.9931]**, 31/32 faster: met | at most 0.997 |
| LK-2, write | 0.9902 [0.9859, 0.9948], 28/32: met | at most 1.00 |
| LK-3, per class | discard sd 0.9888, 720p 0.9918, 1080p 0.9921, 4k 0.9715; write sd 0.9907, 720p 0.9922, 1080p 0.9916, 4k 0.9776: met | at most 1.005 in each |

**Some of the 4k gain is code placement.** `ed75c044e944` (4k) measured 0.845, yet 99.9% of its
luma samples are full-sample copies, whose loop this round leaves alone. A software-clock profile
puts its difference in `predict` itself, on the same instructions at other addresses. An
information check (`luma-kernel/aligned/`) rebuilt both arms with every function and loop aligned
to 64 bytes and timed them interleaved, three rounds, between host gates. Aligned `k` over aligned
`base` is 0.9930 [0.9892, 0.9956] over the 32 streams, 25 faster (sd 0.9935, 720p 0.9932, 1080p
0.9910, 4k 0.9963, the weighted nine 0.9920). Aligned `base` is 0.967 of the default `base` at
4k, and 0.793 on `ed75c044e944`. So the bars hold with placement fixed in both arms, and about
0.7% is the kernels'. The rest of the 4k figure, about 2.5 points, is where the default build
happens to put `base`'s code. That cost is a candidate for a round of its own: the build's
alignment, on all classes.

Against FFmpeg 9.0.2 (median per-stream ratio, one thread, the 2.90 GHz class, information;
`base` is `main` at `3443dfc`, `k` is `d10c367`, default builds as gated):

| | overall | sd | 720p | 1080p | 4k |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| discard, `base` / `k` | 1.287 / **1.274** | 1.211 / 1.186 | 1.324 / 1.313 | 1.332 / 1.313 | 1.291 / 1.259 |
| write, `base` / `k` | 1.262 / **1.238** | 1.185 / 1.162 | 1.272 / 1.258 | 1.315 / 1.304 | 1.233 / 1.194 |

With `k`, one stream of 32 is faster than FFmpeg on discard (the same sd stream as before) and
three are on write.

The branch was then rebased onto `814eb2a` (round 16's tight windows), which changes
`place()` but not these kernels; the kernel code is `d10c367`'s. On the rebased tree, output is
identical to `main` at `814eb2a` (32 of 32), and conformance is 97 of 97 again at 1, 2 and 8
threads and with scalar kernels (`gating/conformance.txt`).

Verification (`luma-kernel/verification.txt`): the fuzz targets `predict` (1.17 million inputs),
`luma_mc` and `weighted_mc` (3.7 and 3.8 million) ran under AddressSanitizer with no finding. Each
mutant of the new arithmetic fails a test: a non-saturating `c`, the third byte pair reversed, a
rounding multiplier off by one, a shift off by one, the positive weights' bound or Equation
8-288's multiplier changed, or weights cast without their range check. The negative weights'
bound is one no test can break: a sum that saturates there clips to 0 either way.

## Build round: code alignment

### What the measurement says

The luma kernel round's gating run showed 4k streams gaining more than the kernel's
instructions allow, and `docs/measurements/h264-rounds/luma-kernel/aligned/` traced it to where
the default build puts code. With every function and every loop head aligned to 64 bytes in
both arms (`-C llvm-args=-align-all-functions=6 -C llvm-args=-align-loops=64`), the aligned
base over the default base was 0.967 on the 4k streams (the median over those eight), and
0.793 on `ed75c044e944`, whose luma samples are 99.9% full-sample copies, a loop that did not
change. The same flags in both arms moved the kernel round's own result from 0.9896 to 0.9930.
So a build made without them loses a few percent to placement on some streams, and an A/B
between two commits picks up a change of placement as if it were a change of speed.

### Design

Built as the patch `docs/measurements/h264-rounds/build-alignment/k.patch` (code commit `433ca30`
and the wheel check); the round did not pass and the patch is not in the tree ("Result").

1. **The flags.** Both of `-C llvm-args=-align-all-functions=6` (every function starts on a
   64-byte line, the size of a cache line and of a ZMM load) and `-C llvm-args=-align-loops=64`
   (every loop head on one). They are LLVM options and stable `rustc` takes them. The cost is
   binary size: the `decode` example grows by 5% (1,074,696 to 1,132,072 bytes in the run below), and the padding is
   `nop`s between functions, executed only by fall-through into a loop head.
2. **Scope: x86-64 only.** Where it was measured. `.cargo/config.toml` set them for
   `cfg(target_arch = "x86_64")`, so the arm64, wasm32 and any other build was untouched; an
   arm64 build has not been measured with them and would get nothing until it is.
3. **What users get.**
   - *The CLI's release binaries* (`.github/workflows/npm.yml`, `packages/cli/scripts/platform.sh`).
     The script sets `RUSTFLAGS` for some targets, and cargo then ignores `.cargo/config.toml`
     entirely, so the patch has the script set the same two flags itself for every x86-64
     target (linux-x64 musl, darwin-x64, win32-x64) and, because a silent loss would be
     invisible, build with `cargo build -v` and fail unless the `coreav` binary's own `rustc` call (the one that
     generates the code under fat LTO) carries them.
   - *The wheels* (`.github/workflows/python.yml`, `maturin --profile dist`). maturin-action
     passes no `RUSTFLAGS`, and its manylinux container mounts the workspace at the same path
     and runs from it, so cargo reads `.cargo/config.toml`. Checked with a local
     `maturin build --profile dist -vv`: both flags on the `coreav_py` call, and 4,737 of the
     wheel's 4,854 text symbols on a 64-byte line (the rest are C and assembly from other
     crates). The patch adds a check of that share to the x86-64 wheel job
     (`scripts/check-code-alignment.sh`). These checks, and a local run of `platform.sh linux-x64
     x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` with its guard, were made by hand and are not logged in the
     evidence; the CI jobs were not run on the patch.
   - *The benchmark and gating builds* (`bench-guard.yml`, the A/B helpers) build in the
     repository's tree and would pick the file up. The first `bench-guard` run after a merge
     would compare a base tree without the file against a head with it, so it would show the
     gain once.
   - *A crates.io source build* (`cargo install coreav-cli`, or a crate that depends on ours)
     does not read our `.cargo/config.toml`: cargo reads the configuration of the directory it
     is run in and its parents, never a dependency's. It gets the compiler's default placement.
     A user who wants the flags sets `RUSTFLAGS="-C llvm-args=-align-all-functions=6 -C
     llvm-args=-align-loops=64"`.
4. **No `build.rs` or crate attribute can do it**: alignment is a code-generation option of the
   crate being compiled, and the stable attributes (`#[repr(align)]`) apply to data. Rejected.
   `-Zmin-function-alignment` is nightly. A `[profile.dist] rustflags` is the unstable
   `profile-rustflags`. The file and the script are the stable ways.

Rejected without timing: a variant with only function alignment, or loops at 32. The
probe in `luma-kernel/aligned/` measured the pair, and the round decides on it.

### Bars

Fixed before the A/B run, on the method of the luma kernel round: two decoders in the same
rounds, built alike (`cargo build --locked --profile dist --example decode -p coreav-h264`, one
toolchain, `RUSTFLAGS` unset) from one tree each, on this host (the 2.90 GHz class, family 6
model 106; the run records it). `base` is `main` at `32bbbff`, without the file, as users have
had it; `k` is the branch's code commit `433ca30`, `main`'s tree plus `.cargo/config.toml` and
`platform.sh`. The run is `scripts/h264_parity.py` on the training set, FFmpeg 9.0.2 as the
reference command, five rounds, each call between two host gates (a failed gate after a call
voids it and it runs again), the class frame counts (sd 1800, 720p 900, 1080p 300, 4k 150): per
class, one call at one thread pinned to core 2 (`--pin 2`) and one at eight threads, unpinned
(`--threads 8`). The script is `docs/measurements/h264-rounds/build-alignment/run-ab-helper.sh`,
and `analyze.py` beside it prints the bars. The change allocates nothing and the arms differ
in no code, so the placement guard of "Speed (step 6)" about allocations does not apply. No
build of `k` was timed before these bars were committed beyond the luma round's probe above.

| Bar | Quantity | Threshold |
|---|---|---|
| AL-1 | median per-stream ratio, `k` over `base`, one thread, discard (the primary) | at most **1.000**, and the upper end of its 95% interval below **1.000** |
| AL-2 | the same, write | at most **1.000** |
| AL-3 | the same per class (sd, 720p, 1080p, 4k), discard and write | at most **1.005** in each |
| AL-4 | the median over the 32 streams at eight threads, discard and write | at most **1.005** (per class, information) |
| AL-5 | output | the 32 training streams byte-identical to `base` with `k` at 1 and 8 threads; conformance 97 of 97 at 1, 2 and 8 threads and with scalar kernels, on `k` |

The branch ships if `k` meets AL-1 to AL-5; otherwise this section records the result and the

### Result: rejected, by AL-4

`docs/measurements/h264-rounds/build-alignment/gating/` (`analysis.txt`, `summary.json`,
`identity.txt`, `hostgate.log`, `provenance.txt`): one run on the 2.90 GHz Intel class (family 6,

passed before and after each of the eight calls (FFmpeg within 5% of the class's reference,
at 0.958 to 1.004 of it), none void. The decode examples' text symbols on a 64-byte line: `base` 206 of 824,
`k` 818 of 824; sizes 1,074,696 and 1,132,072 bytes (+5.3%, `gating/sizes.txt`). Output identical on 32 of 32
streams for `k` at 1 and 8 threads against `base` at 1.

| Bar | Result | Threshold |
|---|---|---|
| AL-1, 1 thread, discard | **0.9965 [0.9932, 0.9987]**, 24/32 faster: met | at most 1.000, upper end below 1.000 |
| AL-2, 1 thread, write | 0.9994 [0.9933, 1.0010], 18/32: met | at most 1.000 |
| AL-3, per class | discard sd 0.9966, 720p 0.9954, 1080p 0.9948, 4k 0.9984; write sd 1.0003, 720p 0.9913, 1080p 0.9988, 4k 1.0015: met | at most 1.005 in each |
| AL-4, 8 threads | discard 0.9983 [0.9883, 1.0025]; write **1.00503** [0.9980, 1.0147]: **not met** | at most 1.005 |
| AL-5, output | identity as above; conformance not run, the round having failed | |

AL-4's write median is above its bar by 0.003%, inside an interval from 0.998 to 1.015; the eight-thread per-stream ratios range from 0.865 to 1.184, against 0.965 to 1.023
at one thread. The bars stand as set, so the flags are not merged. Against FFmpeg 9.0.2
(median per-stream ratio, information; `base` is `main` at `32bbbff`, `k` is `433ca30`),
one thread: discard `base` 1.278, `k` 1.266; write 1.244 and 1.247; eight threads: discard
1.121 and 1.132, write 1.119 and 1.123.

What the run says about placement. On `main` at `32bbbff` the default build's placement costs
the median stream 0.35% at one thread on discard and 0.06% on write (the 4k discard median is
0.2%, and `ed75c044e944` 0.2%, not the 3% and 21% that the luma kernel round's probe found on
its two arms), with single streams from 0.965 to 1.023. The probe and this run differ in the
commit, so the cost is likely to move when code anywhere in the binary does, which this run
does not show on its own. That is the layout noise an A/B picks up between two commits, a few
tenths of a percent at the median and a few percent on a stream, as in the allocator-placement
note of "Speed (step 6)".
The method of that section is unchanged by this round; a round whose bar is within half a
percent may add an information row timing both arms aligned (`RUSTFLAGS` set to the two flags
for both), as `luma-kernel/aligned/` did.

### Second run

The first run's AL-4 was not met by 0.003% on a write median whose interval spans 0.998 to 1.015,
and the per-stream eight-thread ratios ranged from 0.865 to 1.184: the unpinned eight-thread
calls at five rounds are noisier than the guard's width of 0.5%, so the guard could not tell a
loss of that size from none. The round is therefore run again, once, with the same arms (the
first run's two binaries, checked by hash, not rebuilt), the same bars (AL-1 to AL-5 exactly as
above, AL-4 at 1.005), and the eight-thread calls at ten rounds in place of five; the one-thread
calls are the same as before (five rounds, pinned to core 2). All of AL-1 to AL-5 are measured
again, and the second run's results are the round's: the first run's stand in the record above
and do not combine with it. One attempt: if any bar fails in this run the round is rejected for
this patch, and a failed host gate voids a call and re-runs only that call, as before. The script
is `docs/measurements/h264-rounds/build-alignment/run2/run-ab-helper.sh`, committed before the run
with this section.

## Snapshot outliers: `6f7799768413` and `b41f70a7fa60`

The official snapshot (`main` at `06141b3`, Intel 2.90 GHz) had two per-stream outliers that repeated at one
and eight threads: `6f7799768413` (sd) at 1.62 on discard, and `b41f70a7fa60` (1080p) at 2.33 on write with
a discard ratio of 1.36. Evidence and tools: `docs/measurements/h264-rounds/snapshot-outliers/`; this
session's timings are on `main` at `a9017ba`, one thread, pinned, FFmpeg 9.0.2, the same host class. FFmpeg is
used as a black box (its output, `trace_headers`, a symbol table of a build of the 9.0.2 release); none of its
source was read.

### `b41f70a7fa60`: not the decoder, the harness

- **Features** (`features.tsv`): High profile, CABAC, 8x8 transform, one slice per picture, implicit
  bi-prediction (`weighted_bipred_idc` 2), I, P and B pictures, progressive 4:2:0, cropped from 1088 to 1080 rows.
  Nothing in the set is unique to it: other 1080p and 4k streams share each of those fields, and its discard
  ratio (1.34 to 1.36) is the 1080p class's.
- **The cause**: its timestamps are not a steady rate (25 fps average, 26 fps stream rate). FFmpeg's default
  frame-rate conversion for `-f rawvideo` therefore duplicates frames: with `-frames:v 300` it reports `dup=150`,
  so it decodes 150 pictures and writes each twice, while ours decodes 300 (`vsync.txt`). The bytes are the same,
  the work is not. `-f null` does not convert, so the discard pairing is unaffected.
- **Corrected** with `-fps_mode passthrough` (now in `scripts/h264_parity.py` and `scripts/h264_speed.py`):
  FFmpeg's `-f rawvideo` takes 1.78 s where the snapshot has 1.00 s, and the write ratio is **1.30** (5 rounds,
  `corrected.1080p.json`) against the snapshot's 2.33.
- **Three more streams have the opposite fault.** `3b1b441e23ae`, `6da34958296c` and `8ae90cadb5bc` have
  timestamps that FFmpeg's conversion takes for frames to drop, so its `-f rawvideo` writes 6, 3 and 3
  pictures of the 150, 300 and 1800 (`drop=145`, `298`, `1798`) while it decodes all of them, and ours writes all.
  Their write ratios were overstated: snapshot 1.35, 1.41 and 1.31 against 1.08, 1.27 and 1.20 on the corrected
  harness (`corrected.*.json`; the snapshot's code is older by a few percent of the 1.3).
- **What it does to the medians**: replacing the four streams' snapshot write ratios with the corrected ones moves
  the overall write median from 1.258 to 1.249, the 1080p class's from 1.313 to 1.271 and the 4k class's from
  1.205 to 1.157, sd and 720p unchanged (`corrected-medians.txt`; the corrected runs are on newer code, which
  accounts for about 1% of that). The discard medians, and every A/B between two builds of ours, do not carry
  the fault.

### `6f7799768413`: CAVLC at 48 kbit a picture

- **Features** (`features.tsv`): Constrained Baseline, **CAVLC**, 640x480 with no cropping, `pic_order_cnt_type` 2,
  three reference frames, P pictures only (293 P, 7 I), one slice per picture, no weighting, no B pictures,
  no 8x8 transform, progressive, 4:2:0 8-bit. It is one of six CAVLC streams in the set, and the one with the most
  bits for its size: 48 kbit a picture, 40 bits a macroblock (the training set's `es.json`), where the other
  CAVLC streams of 1,000 macroblocks or more have 16 (`9db41aa16b5a`, 720p) and 12 (`b71b6b31e54f`, 1080p). Their
  discard ratios against their classes' medians are 1.62 against 1.20 (sd), 1.36 against 1.32 and 1.49 against 1.32;
  the CABAC streams of 1 to 2.3 Mbit a picture (`175433794e02`, `f8d92a911e72`) are at their classes' medians.
  Three points, so the suggestion is that the CAVLC residual path costs more per bit than CABAC's does, not that
  it is shown. The three small CAVLC streams (112 to 396 macroblocks) have too little work in a picture to say.
- **Where the time goes** (`stages.txt`, cpu-clock, two rounds): CoreAV 1.80 s against FFmpeg's 1.13 s (1.60).
  The excess over 1.10 is 0.50 of FFmpeg's time: entropy 0.24 (49%; 0.60 against 0.33), the macroblock layer 0.16
  (31%; 0.25 against 0.09, where the two decoders divide the syntax parsing differently, so read the two together:
  80% of the excess), deblocking 0.08 (17%), the rest small. On the CABAC 1080p stream the same table has the
  entropy stage at 1.19 times FFmpeg's.
- **Instructions do not explain the time**: callgrind counts CoreAV at 1.29 times FFmpeg's instructions on the
  first 200 pictures, but its time is 1.60 times, so part of the gap is stalls rather than work (this VM has no
  cache counters, so which stalls is inferred). One is visible: in `cavlc::Code::read`, 48.6% of the function's
  samples sit on the instruction after the table load (about 0.085 s, 4.7% of the run). The coeff_token table of the
  first class is a flat lookup of 16 bits, 64 K three-byte entries (192 KB, beyond L1), indexed by the next 16 bits
  of the stream, which is the case two-level tables exist for. The prototype below recovers about a third of that
  estimate, 1.5% of the run, so the table is part of the stall, not all of it. The rest is the shape of the path:
  `residual_block` decodes into a 16-entry array, then `levels`, `place` and a copy loop in `block` scan it again to
  write the scaled coefficients, each reading the bit position through a bounds-checked `peek32`.

### Proposals

1. **Two-level code tables** (prototype `cavlc-two-level.patch`, tested against a scan of every 16-bit window of
   every table, which is exhaustive for the lookup; the rest of the decode is unchanged): `Code::read` falls from
   0.17 to 0.12 s on the stream (cpu-clock) and an ungated interleaved A/B gives **0.9845** on it (the seven others
   timed, five CAVLC and two CABAC, ran 0.9932 to 1.0082, three of them (`9db41aa16b5a`, `ec473c99c538`, `8ae90cadb5bc`) 0.1% to 0.8% slower; the eight's median is 0.9968
   [0.9932, 1.0011]). Six of the 32 streams are CAVLC and the gain is under 2% on the largest, so the 32-stream median
   does not move and the mean moves by about 0.1% (1.5% on one stream in six, over 32). Decision: **not a round on
   its own**, since no overall bar could show it; the change is kept as the first step of the fused CAVLC residual (item 2).
2. **A fused CAVLC residual** (to hand to the roadmap): one function per block that reads coeff_token, the
   levels (leading-zero count for the prefix, a 64-bit bit cache instead of a bounds-checked `peek32` for each
   read), total_zeros and run_before from the two-level tables, and writes each coefficient to its scanned,
   scaled position directly, with no intermediate arrays or second scan, and with nC taken from a per-macroblock
   record of the neighbours' TotalCoeff in place of `neighbour_4x4` calls. Expected gain, an estimate and not a
   measurement: the entropy stage's 0.24 of excess falls by half (0.12 of FFmpeg's time), so the stream goes from
   1.60 to about 1.48; the other CAVLC streams, with less of their time in the residual, by less than half of that,
   about 3%; over the 32 streams, 0.12 on one, about 0.03 on five others, 0 on twenty-six: the median does not
   move, the mean moves by about 0.7%, and the sd class's median (four of its eight streams are CAVLC) might
   move by 1%. The benefit is for CAVLC content, not the headline ratio, so it is for the maintainer to place on the
   roadmap. Taken up as round 19 ("Round 19: the CAVLC residual in one pass").
3. **The harness**, done here: `-fps_mode passthrough` for FFmpeg in `h264_parity.py` and `h264_speed.py`, so that
   both decoders decode the same pictures. The write medians of earlier snapshots and reports are overstated by
   the four streams above (the 4k class's by about 4%, which a speed bar on write at 4k would feel). The next
   snapshot should be taken with the corrected harness. The bars of the earlier rounds are between two builds of
   ours and are unaffected; ratios to FFmpeg on the write pairing are read on the corrected harness from here on.

## FFmpeg write timing without `-fps_mode passthrough`: the audit

"Snapshot outliers" found that FFmpeg's default frame-rate conversion duplicates or drops frames of a
stream with irregular timestamps in the `-f rawvideo` pairing. This is the audit of everywhere FFmpeg is
timed or its raw output is read, and of which committed ratios to FFmpeg carry the fault. Evidence:
`docs/measurements/h264-rounds/ffmpeg-write-audit/`.

### Where FFmpeg's raw output is produced

- **Fixed**: `scripts/h264_parity.py` and `scripts/h264_speed.py` (the harnesses of every ratio below; fixed with
  the outliers note), `scripts/h264_counts.py` (its usage line, for instruction counts of FFmpeg's command) and
  `scripts/thumbnail_oracle.py` (`rgb()`, a PSNR oracle on one still image, where no conversion applies; changed for
  consistency).
- **Already `passthrough`**: the Stage 0 baseline harness (since removed), the native FFmpeg backend and the tests that
  compare against FFmpeg (`coreav-backend-ffmpeg`, `-dav1d`, `-h264`, `coreav-worker`), the spikes' measurement and
  oracle scripts (`spike-a`, `nvdec-direct`, N2's `corpus.py`, `speed.py` and `investigate.py`, which the arm64 speed
  workflow runs), so N2's P1 and P2 results, which timed `framemd5`, are not affected. `coreav-cli`'s thumbnail
  test decodes one still image and is left as it is.
- **No FFmpeg timing at all**: the CI guards (`bench-guard`) time CoreAV against its own base, and
  install FFmpeg only as an oracle for correctness and as the fallback backend. There is no CI speed guard against
  FFmpeg yet.
- **The `-f null` pairing** (discard) never converts: the same command with and without `passthrough` takes the same
  time (1.671 s both ways on `b41f70a7fa60`, `ffmpeg-write-audit/null-check.txt`).
- **Historical measurement scripts** in `docs/measurements/` (the gating containers, the profile and host-gate
  tools, the held-out tools) are evidence of what ran and are not edited; those that time `-f rawvideo` ran the
  harnesses above.

### Which streams, and which committed ratios

`vsync.txt` (training, 32 streams) and `vsync-heldout.txt` (the 64 held-out streams, extracted for this check
only) list the streams whose `-f rawvideo` differs: six in all.

| Stream | Set | Default conversion | Factor (passthrough time over default) |
|---|---|---|---|
| `b41f70a7fa60` | training, 1080p | duplicates (`dup=150`): decodes half | 1.78 to 1.80 |
| `3b1b441e23ae` | training, 4k | drops all but 6 pictures | 1.23 to 1.24 |
| `6da34958296c` | training, 1080p | drops all but 3 | 1.10 to 1.11 |
| `8ae90cadb5bc` | training, sd | drops all but 3 | 1.09 |
| `48640c5a3dd7` | held-out, 1080p | drops all but 3 | 1.20 to 1.21 |
| `9d99b565f2ec` | held-out, sd | drops all but 3 | 1.16 to 1.17 |

The factors are FFmpeg alone, one thread, pinned, five rounds, FFmpeg 9.0.2 and 7.0.2 (`factors.json`). A committed
`:write` or `:mixed` ratio of one of these streams is too high by its factor, so `correct_reports.py` divides each by
it, in every committed `h264_parity.py` report that holds one of the six, the `--threads 1,8` reports' `:write@N`
keys included (`corrected-reports.txt`, 445 rows where a median moves by 0.003 or more). This is an estimate and not a re-run: the factor is measured on this VM at one thread
and applied to reports from other hosts and code states, so the eight-thread rows in particular are rougher.

- **The held-out P1 (FFmpeg 7.0.2, write)**: the two held-out streams are in sd and 1080p. The overall median stays
  3.095, the sd median goes from 3.262 to 3.247 and the 1080p median does not move (`heldout-medians.txt`; FFmpeg
  9.0.2: no median moves). The bar was missed by more than a factor of two (3.1 against 1.15), and the verdict stands.
- **The training-set reports** (`h264-training/reports`, `h264-kernels-training/reports`): the four training
  streams move class medians of their write ratios by up to 4.5% in the kernels reports and 8% in the one calibration
  report, always downward (one sd, two 1080p and one 4k stream of the training set's eight a class; the kernels reports'
  sd class moves 4.5% and their 1080p 1.8%, the calibration report's 1080p 8%). The snapshot of `06141b3` is handled in "Snapshot outliers".
- **The rounds' information rows**: each round's ratio to FFmpeg on write over the training set carries the same
  shift: 420 rows, a median of 3.0% lower, by round a median of 1.4% to 5.3%, up to 13% on a 1080p or 4k row of round 6
  and `motion-12b` (`corrected-reports.txt` has each row). The discard ratios, and the rounds' gating of CoreAV against CoreAV, are
  not affected.
- **Bars**: no bar of a CoreAV-against-CoreAV round depends on FFmpeg's time, so none is affected: both arms share
  FFmpeg's, or have none. Of the bars against FFmpeg, N2's P1 and P2 timed `framemd5` with `passthrough` and are
  unaffected; step 6's P1 (this harness, both pairings) was measured on the held-out draw above, where the write
  cells move as shown and the verdict does not; and the threaded bars (P3, P4, G3), which use the same harness,
  read their discard pairing unchanged and their write pairing with the six streams' factors (the `:write@8`
  rows). From the next snapshot, ratios on the write pairing come from the corrected harness.

## Round 17: banded references on the fast path

With more than one thread every reference is stored in bands
("Threading (step 7): our design"), and round 16 left every block of
such a decode on the banded path (`predict_list_any`): a band lookup
and a window for each plane, and three kernel calls, where a block from
a whole reference takes one call of `Kernels::predict`. Against FFmpeg
9.0.2 at eight threads `main` was 1.137 (discard, a cloud container on Zen 5, base
`3ebeda9`, round 16's run) and 1.146 (`06141b3`, the 2.90 GHz class,
the A/B helper's snapshot `measured/h264-snapshot-06141b3`), against
1.164 and 1.279 at one thread.

### What the measurement says

On the development VM (Intel Xeon @ 2.90GHz, family 6 model 106, 4 cores
and 8 logical CPUs; information, not the bar host;
`docs/measurements/h264-rounds/round17/local/`):

- **The banded path costs about a tenth of the time.** A one-thread
  build of `06141b3` that sends every block to `predict_list_any`,
  though its references are whole, took 1.08 to 1.22 of `main`'s CPU
  time, median 1.12 on 16 streams (`ab-banded-path-1t.txt`). That is
  what the path costs over the fast one on the same blocks, without
  the waits and the band lookups, which remain either way.
- **At eight threads motion compensation grows more than the rest.**
  By time-based samples (`profile-8t.txt`), its CPU time at eight
  threads is 1.2 to 2.4 times its time at one, the rest's 1.1 to 2.0
  times; the part beyond the rest's growth is 7.4% of the eight-thread
  CPU time, median per stream (sd 7.1%, 720p 8.5%, 1080p 6.0%, 4k 8.2%).

### Design

1. **A band of a reference as `Planes` (kernels crate).** `Planes::band`
   takes the rows one band stores: the luma rows from a first row on and
   the chroma rows from theirs, each slice from its origin and as many
   rows as it holds, of a picture of `rows` rows. `Planes` keeps where
   sample (0, 0) would sit in each slice, the origin less the rows before
   the first, as a signed offset computed once; `place()` reads it where
   it read the origin, so a call costs the same for a whole reference.
   The test of the samples a prediction uses stays against the whole
   picture, and a window that reaches rows the band does not hold fails
   the same slice checks as one past a slice's end: above the first row
   it starts before the slice. So a plane that does not start at row 0
   has origin 0; one that does may keep slack before it. Which of a
   band's rows are final is the caller's to know.
2. **One fast path for whole and banded references (decoder).**
   `predict_fast` (round 16's `predict_whole`) takes the whole
   reference from the slice's table and otherwise
   `reference_band`: the band the luma window's last row is read from,
   clamped into the picture, as `predict_list_any` reads it (rule 2 of
   the threading design, as the band-lag round edited it), waited for
   until it is published, as `Planes::band`. Both kinds of reference go
   through one call site of `Kernels::predict`: round 14 showed a
   second call site can move the dispatch out of line. A declined
   block, a weighted one that needs the scratch buffers, an index past
   its list and a reference of another size go to `predict_list_any` as
   before, which reports the errors. The slice's `any_whole` flag,
   which sent every block of a banded decode straight to the banded
   path, is gone: every block into the picture tries the fast path.
3. **The chroma windows come from the luma window's band.**
   `predict_list_any` looks the chroma band up by the chroma window's
   own last row; the fast path reads all three planes from one band.
   That band holds the chroma rows final: a chroma window ends at chroma
   row `(yi + h) / 2` at most (`yi` the block's integer row in the
   reference, since `2 * (mv >> 3) <= mv >> 2`), and the luma window's
   last row, `yi + h + 2`, is at most the band's end less four unless
   the band is the picture's last (the band owns the row three below
   it), so the chroma window ends at least two rows above the band's
   last chroma row, the one row the next band's filter changes. A chroma window above the band's apron
   lies outside the band, which `place()` declines. Both paths now take
   the band from one function, `Geometry::band_reading_luma_window`;
   `a_block_s_windows_are_final_in_the_band_of_its_luma_window` checks
   it, for luma and chroma, for every block height and row and vertical
   vectors up to 150 rows each way (a longer one puts both windows
   outside the picture) at band heights 1 to 8.

No new buffers: a band's `Planes` is a value on the stack, so the
memory estimate is unchanged. Tests:
`three_plane_prediction_from_a_band_matches_the_whole_reference` (every
kernel form takes from a band exactly the blocks the whole reference
takes whose windows lie in the band's slices, alike, and writes nothing
for the others, with bands' first luma and chroma rows cut as the
aprons cut them and otherwise),
`a_band_from_row_0_is_the_reference_with_its_origin` (a picture of one
band that is not yet whole when a slice starts takes this path),
`a_band_of_a_reference_checks_its_rows`,
and the `predict` fuzz target, which cuts its reference to a band and
holds every form to the whole reference's answer.

Measured locally (information only; `local/`): instructions at one
thread 0.991 to 0.995 of `main`'s on four streams, `predict_fast`
113 instructions a call where `predict_whole` took 123, the dispatch's
test and a copy gone (`instructions.txt`); at eight threads 0.908 on a
1080p stream, 2.9% of the fast path's blocks declined there, and
`reference_band` 161 instructions a call. Wall time at eight threads,
median over the 32 streams: 0.961 and 0.962 in two runs (sd 0.93 to
0.96, 720p 0.95 to 0.96, 1080p 0.97, 4k 0.93 to 0.97; `ab-8t-*.txt`);
CPU time at one thread 1.002 on 16 streams, within this VM's noise
(`ab-1t.txt`). Output identical to `main` (`06141b3`) on the 32 training
streams at one and eight threads; conformance 97 of 97 at 1, 2 and 8
threads and with scalar kernels (`identity.txt`, `conformance.txt`).

Rejected:
- **Shifting the band's coordinates in the decoder** so that the
  existing `Planes::with_origin` reads a band (sample (0, 0) placed at a
  row the band holds, and the block's row and the picture's first rows
  shifted to match): no kernel change, but the window test then puts
  the picture's top at that row, which declines windows in the top five
  rows of each apron, and every call shifts three more values.
- **Slack rows for bands**, as round 16 keeps for a picture of one band:
  a banded reference's windows at the picture's top and bottom edges
  stay on the banded path, among the 2.9% of blocks declined on the one
  stream counted; slack would add rows to every band of every reference
  for them.

Not tried here: resolving each reference's bands once per slice, as the
whole ones are. Bands are published while a slice is decoded, so such a
table would be refreshed as they appear; whether it pays is for a later
round, if `reference_band`'s 161 instructions a call show in the
eight-thread profile.

### Bars

Fixed before the A/B run: `scripts/h264_parity.py` on a host of one of
the classes of "Round A/B runs on more than one class" with at least 16
CPUs (named by `--require-cpu`, or recorded for a container), with the
host-health gate before and after each call, on the training set, one
call per class with the class's frame count. FFmpeg 9.0.2 (BtbN
`n9.0.2-17-g2a571b6068`) runs as the last command. Two builds are timed
in the same rounds and built alike (`dist`, one toolchain): `main` at
`06141b3` (`before`), or the `main` this branch is rebased onto, named
in the result, and this branch (`after`). The round depends on no ISA
tier. Two calls per class: `t8`, `--threads 8`, unpinned, five rounds,

## Deblocking round: thresholds from shifted tables

The profile's deblocking stage ("Profile: where the time goes against
FFmpeg") taken apart: which of its excess is the filter kernels and which
the glue around them, on `main` at `814eb2a1`.

### What the measurement says

The profile's method (`docs/measurements/h264-rounds/profile/`: software
`cpu-clock` samples at 4 kHz, one thread, pinned, `--discard` against
`ffmpeg -threads 1 -f null -`, FFmpeg 9.0.2's stages from its symbol table
and debug information alone, the 32 training streams with the class frame
counts, two rounds) on `main` at `814eb2a1`, the 2.90 GHz class. CoreAV
over FFmpeg: mean 1.273, median 1.267; deblocking is 0.216 against 0.170
of FFmpeg's time, 17% of the excess over 1.10 (`table.txt`). Its parts
(`deblock_split.py`, `split.txt`; time over FFmpeg's, mean per stream,
CoreAV / FFmpeg):

| Class | luma kernels | chroma kernels | strengths | thresholds | edge loop | edge views | border copy |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| sd | 0.066 / 0.064 | 0.047 / 0.021 | 0.066 / 0.063 | 0.030 / – | 0.032 / 0.046 | 0.008 / – | – / 0.007 |
| 720p | 0.105 / 0.112 | 0.071 / 0.035 | 0.048 / 0.056 | 0.045 / – | 0.035 / 0.044 | 0.011 / – | – / 0.007 |
| 1080p | 0.039 / 0.039 | 0.031 / 0.015 | 0.034 / 0.037 | 0.023 / – | 0.020 / 0.024 | 0.005 / – | – / 0.004 |
| 4k | 0.016 / 0.018 | 0.012 / 0.007 | 0.067 / 0.031 | 0.015 / – | 0.035 / 0.032 | 0.002 / – | – / 0.015 |
| all | 0.056 / 0.058 | 0.040 / 0.019 | 0.054 / 0.047 | 0.028 / – | 0.030 / 0.037 | 0.007 / – | – / 0.008 |

FFmpeg looks its thresholds up inside its edge functions, so they are in
its edge loop; CoreAV's thresholds are `Thresholds::new`, `params` and
`chroma_qp`, its edge views `EdgeMut::new` and the kernels' dispatch.

1. **The glue is the larger part**: 0.119 against 0.092, excess 0.027;
   the kernels 0.097 against 0.078, excess 0.019. The luma kernels are
   level with FFmpeg's; the kernels' whole gap is chroma (0.040 against
   0.019).
2. **Within the glue, the thresholds and the edge loop** together are
   0.058 against FFmpeg's 0.037, in every class; the strengths are level
   but at 4k (0.067 against 0.031), where most macroblocks have no edge to
   filter and the time is in reading their records (`lines.txt`).
3. **The thresholds' cost is per edge**: Equations 8-461 and 8-462 clip
   the average QP plus each offset, three tables are read with a bounds
   check each, and the kernel's t'C0 per segment is a variable shift of a
   word by bS (`deblock.rs` line 321 at `814eb2a1`, the single hottest
   line of the glue). Counted by callgrind on `9db41aa16b5a` (720p), with
   the tables of point 1 of the design below already in, that shift alone
   is 3.0% of the decode's instructions (`instructions.txt`).

So this round takes the glue, and in it the thresholds; the strengths at
4k and the chroma kernels are left for later rounds.

### Design

1. **Tables that hold the clip.** α' with t'C0 for bS 1 to 3 (one word),
   β', and QPC are tables of 256 entries built at compile time, entry `i`
   holding the row of `i − 51` clipped to 0 to 51. A slice's FilterOffsetA
   and FilterOffsetB, and the PPS's chroma QP offsets, are clamped to −51
   to 51 and shifted by 51 once (`shifted`); an edge's thresholds are then
   two loads indexed by the average QP plus the shifted offset, masked to
   a byte, with no clip and no bounds check left. Exact: every QP the
   filter reads is 0 to 51, and with such a QP an offset at or below −51
   clips to row 0 and one at or above 51 to row 51, as the clip of the sum
   does; a unit test compares every QP pair and offsets from −70 to 70
   (past the −12 to 12 the slice header and the PPS accept, so that the
   tables do not depend on that check) with the clauses' derivation.
2. **t'C0 by bS from eight bytes.** The per-segment t'C0 is a byte load
   indexed by bS masked to three bits, rather than a variable shift of a
   word.
3. **α = 0 for an edge that filters nothing**, in place of an `Option`:
   where α' or β' is 0 no sample passes filterSamplesFlag
   (Equation 8-468), and α = 0 alone says so to every kernel, as the chroma
   pair already relied on for a plane that filters nothing. The edge loop
   still skips such an edge before building its view.
4. **The internal chroma edges' thresholds once a macroblock**, per plane,
   rather than once per direction.

The tables are 1.5 KB of read-only data; nothing is allocated, so the
memory estimate does not change.

Rejected:
- a per-slice table of thresholds by average QP, built when a slice
  starts: it would need the slice state (`work.rs`, `mb.rs`) to carry it
  and to be counted in the memory estimate, for the same two loads;
- passing bS and t'C0 to the kernels as words, and spreading t'C0 there
  by a byte shuffle: it changes the kernel interface (`EdgeParams`) and
  every tier for what the byte loads already take;
- the strengths at 4k: a round of their own ("Deblocking round: the
  strengths of quiet macroblocks").

Output identical to `main` (`814eb2a1`) on the 32 training streams at one
and eight threads (`identity.txt`). Instructions of the whole decode fall
0.25% to 2.37% (callgrind, AVX2 tier, five streams;
`docs/measurements/h264-rounds/deblock-glue/instructions.txt`).

### Bars

Fixed before any timing of the branch: `scripts/h264_parity.py --pin 2
--rounds 5` on a host of one of the classes of "Round A/B runs on more
than one class" (named by `--require-cpu`, or recorded for a container;
the round depends on no ISA tier), with the host-health gate before and
after each call, on the training set, one call per class with the class's

| D-2 | the same, write | at most **1.000** |
