## Round 18: macroblock records kept from picture to picture

Rejected by its bars G-1 to G-4 (the result is at the end): not merged.
The code stays on `rejected/h264-records-kept` (at `fd069a8`: the code
measured, `4b3fed7`, and changes made after the run), on `main` at `051e169`,
with a row in `docs/measurements/h264-rejected.md`; what follows
describes that branch.

The MB layer is the decoding stage furthest from FFmpeg's time (1.65
times FFmpeg 9.0.2's at one thread in a profile of round 17's code,
`docs/measurements/h264-rounds/round18/local/profile.txt`). Its time is
spread over many items, and round 11's part M, round 15 and the motion
round, which cut its instructions or its records' size, were rejected.
This round takes one cost that is time, not instructions.

### What the measurement says

On the development VM (2.90 GHz class, 4 cores and 8 logical CPUs;
information, not the bar host; `docs/measurements/h264-rounds/round18/local/`):

- **Every picture allocated and filled its macroblock records.**
  `PictureWork::new` made `vec![MbInfo::NONE; n]`, 124 bytes a
  macroblock (1 MB at 1080p, 4 MB at 4k), only so that each macroblock
  would read as not decoded (`MbInfo::slice` 0) until a slice decoded
  it. The fill alone is 0.6% of the one-thread samples (4k 1.05%,
  `profile.txt`), and it writes a picture's worth of records that the
  decoding then reads back and writes again.
- **Keeping the records costs more instructions and less time.** A build
  that keeps them (below) runs 0.4% to 1.3% more instructions on four
  streams (`instructions.txt`), and took 0.982 and 0.991 of `main`'s CPU
  time at one thread, median of 16 streams in two runs (`ab-1t-*.txt`),
  0.994 of its wall time at eight threads (4k 0.974; `ab-8t.txt`).
- **Probes not taken** (`probes.txt`): a write hint for the next four
  macroblocks' motion and records, 1.006 and 1.002; `MbData::reset`
  clearing whole coefficient arrays, 0.997, 0.993 and 0.998; a 14-byte
  motion record, 0.997, and exact only while picture identities fit 16
  bits, which no bound on a stream guarantees.

### Design

1. **Each thread keeps its records** (`mb::Records`, in `work::Spare`
   beside the macroblock and scratch buffers it already keeps) and gives
   them to the next picture it decodes, if that picture is the same size;
   otherwise it makes new ones.
2. **A picture stamps the records it decodes.** `Records` counts its
   generation, one more for each picture that takes it; a macroblock's
   `MbInfo::slice` holds the generation in its high 14 bits and 1 + the
   slice's index in the low 18 (`SLICE_BITS`: a picture has at most
   139,264 macroblocks, Table A-1, so at most that many slices decode).
   `MbInfo::decoded` tests the generation and a non-zero slice; the
   check that a macroblock is decoded once, the availability of
   neighbours (a stamp equal to the slice's), and the deblocking filter's
   undecoded and slice tests read the stamps. The slice's filter
   parameters are found by the low bits.
3. **The output does not depend on which records a picture gets.** A
   generation belongs to one picture of those records until the count
   reaches 2^14, which clears them (`MbInfo::NONE`) and starts again at
   1, so a record of another generation is always one this picture has
   not decoded, whatever was left in it. That is what lets each worker
   thread keep its own.
4. A slice whose index does not fit 18 bits is refused. Within the
   default `Limits` (139,264 slices a picture) none is; a caller whose
   own limits allow pictures larger than the specification's, or that
   many slices, can reach it.

Memory: each thread held a picture's records before as well, one
picture at a time; the estimate's per-thread records
(`THREAD_BYTES_PER_MB`) are unchanged. Records of another size are freed
before new ones are made, and the workers past a lowered thread count,
which are not given pictures again, are stopped once none holds a
picture (`Workers::trim`), so that their kept records go with them. Tests:
`records_kept_for_the_next_picture_read_as_not_decoded`,
`records_are_cleared_when_their_generation_wraps`, and
`a_picture_missing_its_first_slice_gives_the_same_pictures_with_threads`,
where stale records lie next to a picture's first decoded slice (an
availability test of the slice bits alone fails it). Output identical to `main`
(`051e169`) on the 32 training streams at one and eight threads;
conformance 97 of 97 at 1, 2 and 8 threads and with scalar kernels
(`identity.txt`, `conformance.txt`).

Rejected:
- **Clearing the records in place** (keeping the vector, filling it with
  `MbInfo::NONE` each picture): no allocation, but the same writes.
- **A ring of two macroblock rows** for the records, as round 11's part
  M did: the deblocking filter and the threads' bands read records
  further back, and the part was rejected by its bars.
- **One generation counter for the decoder**, handed out in decoding
  order: the records a worker keeps would then hold stamps of other
  pictures' generations, and a wrap would need every thread's records
  cleared at once.

### Bars

Fixed before the A/B run: `scripts/h264_parity.py` on a host of one of
the classes of "Round A/B runs on more than one class", with the
host-health gate before and after each call, on the training set, one
call per class with the class's frame count. FFmpeg 9.0.2 (BtbN
`n9.0.2-17-g2a571b6068`) runs as the last command. Two builds timed in
the same rounds and built alike (`dist`, one toolchain): `main` at
`051e169` (`before`), or the `main` this branch is rebased onto, named
in the result, and this branch (`after`). The round depends on no ISA
tier. Three calls per class: `g`, `--pin 2 --rounds 5`; `gm`, the same
with `MALLOC_MMAP_THRESHOLD_=131072` in both decoders' environment, so
that every picture-sized allocation is mapped (the round changes
allocation); and `t8`, `--threads 8`, unpinned, ten rounds ("Rounds at
eight threads").

| Bar | Quantity | Threshold |
|---|---|---|
| G-1 | one thread (`g`), median per-stream ratio `after` over `before`, discard, all 32 streams | at most **0.995**, upper end of the 95% interval below 1.000 |
| G-2 | the same, write | at most **1.000** |
| G-3 | the same per class, discard | at most **1.005** in each |
| G-4 | eight threads (`t8`), discard, all 32 streams; and each class | at most **1.005**; at most **1.010** in each class |
| G-5 | mapped allocator (`gm`), discard, all 32 streams | at most **1.005** |
| G-6 | output | the 32 training streams byte-identical to `before` at 1 and 8 threads; conformance 97 of 97 at 1, 2 and 8 threads and with scalar kernels |

G-1 asks for about half of the local gain. G-4's class bound is 1.010
rather than 1.005 because a class is eight streams: at eight threads and
ten rounds, per-stream ratios between two builds of `main` spread 0.985
to 1.025 ("Rounds at eight threads"), so an eight-stream median moves by
about a percent with no change; the 32-stream bar stays at 1.005.
`docs/measurements/h264-rounds/round18/analyze.py` reads G-1 to G-5
(`python3 -I analyze.py DIR g gm t8`) and lists every stream's ratios;
the ratios to FFmpeg 9.0.2 are reported beside them, naming the base.

### Result: rejected, by G-1 to G-4

`docs/measurements/h264-rounds/round18/gating/` (`analysis.txt`, the
reports, `identity.txt`; branch `measured/h264-round18` `71bf8069`):
cloud container, AMD EPYC family 25 model 17 (Zen 4), 16 CPUs; `before`
`051e169`, `after` `4b3fed7`; 24 gate checks passed, none voided;
output identical, 32 of 32 at one and eight threads.

| Bar | Result | Threshold |
|---|---|---|
| G-1, one thread, discard, all 32 | 1.0061 [1.0040, 1.0122], 8 of 32 faster: missed | at most 0.995, upper end below 1.000 |
| G-2, write | 1.0070: missed | at most 1.000 |
| G-3, discard per class | sd 0.9989, 720p 1.0049, 1080p 1.0070, **4k 1.0351**: missed (4k) | at most 1.005 in each |
| G-4, eight threads (ten rounds) | 1.0028 [0.9983, 1.0102]; sd 0.9991, **720p 1.0154**, 1080p 1.0045, 4k 0.9832: missed (720p) | at most 1.005; 1.010 a class |
| G-5, mapped allocator, discard | 0.8630 [0.8074, 0.9305]: met | at most 1.005 |
| G-6 | identical; conformance 97 of 97 | met |

The direction the development VM showed did not hold on the bar host's
class: there the records kept cost time, most at 4k (every 4k stream
slower, 1.01 to 1.09), where they are 4 MB. Likely, not measured: the
fill brought a picture's records into the last-level cache (Zen 4's is
32 MB per core complex) just before decoding read and wrote them, where
kept records, last touched a picture earlier, come from memory. The
VM's result is not explained: its cache sizes were not recorded with
the runs. With every picture-sized allocation mapped (`gm`, the
variable applied to FFmpeg as well), the branch, which allocates no
records, took 0.73 of the base's time at 4k; likely the base's mapping
and page faults for each picture's records, as `before`'s ratio to
FFmpeg there (1.428, against 1.186 in `g`) suggests. glibc's default
threshold rises past those sizes after the first such free, so that is
not the default's steady state.

Against FFmpeg 9.0.2 on that host (one thread, discard):
1.186 for `051e169`, 1.198 for the branch.

Keeping a picture's records in cache within a picture is what round
11's part M tried, with a ring of two macroblock rows. The changes made
after the run (`fd069a8`: idle workers stopped past a lowered thread
count, records freed before new ones are made, a test of a picture
missing its first slice) are on the branch and were not timed.

## Kernel round: a reference's interior, found once

### What the measurement says

The profile of "Profile: where the time goes against FFmpeg", taken again on `main` at `084ee40` (after
the chroma and luma kernel rounds, round 16's tight windows and the corrected harness), with the same
method and scripts: `perf record -e cpu-clock` at 4 kHz, one thread pinned, `--discard` against
`ffmpeg -threads 1 -fps_mode passthrough -f null -` (FFmpeg 9.0.2, BtbN build for time, the unstripped
release build for attribution by its symbol table and debug information), the 32 training streams with
the class frame counts, two rounds, the 2.90 GHz class. Evidence and scripts:
`docs/measurements/h264-rounds/place-interior/profile/`. The host gate passed before the recording and
read 0.949 of the reference on its 1080p stream after it, 0.1% outside the gate on the fast side; the
profile is information, not a bar.

Time over FFmpeg's, all 32 streams (mean CoreAV/FFmpeg 1.256, median 1.265; at `82c7f7b` 1.382 and
1.284); "excess" is CoreAV less 1.10 times FFmpeg:

| Stage | CoreAV | FFmpeg | ratio | excess | share of excess | at `82c7f7b` |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| MB layer | 0.207 | 0.107 | 1.94 | 0.090 | 58% | 0.204, 30% |
| inter prediction and reference fetch | 0.244 | 0.182 | 1.34 | 0.043 | 28% | 0.411, 62% |
| deblocking | 0.219 | 0.173 | 1.26 | 0.028 | 18% | 0.212, 12% |
| entropy | 0.431 | 0.375 | 1.15 | 0.019 | 12% | 0.395, 5% |
| reconstruction | 0.096 | 0.078 | 1.23 | 0.010 | 7% | 0.091, 4% |
| other | 0.058 | 0.085 | 0.69 | -0.035 | -22% | 0.069, -13% |

Per class (median ratio; the largest shares of the class's excess): sd 1.176 (MB layer 140%, entropy
116%, deblocking 35%, against "other" at -234%), 720p 1.312 (MB layer 45%, deblocking 19%,
reconstruction 17%, inter 15%), 1080p 1.312 (MB layer 37%, inter 18%, reconstruction 16%, entropy
13%), 4k 1.246 (MB layer 67%, inter 57%, deblocking 21%; entropy and reconstruction below FFmpeg's).

Inter prediction by part, CoreAV / FFmpeg (`inter_split.txt`): luma kernels 0.089 / 0.073, chroma
kernels 0.042 / 0.031, edge fetch 0.004 / 0.003, prefetch 0.009 / 0.019, and the glue 0.099 / 0.046;
at 4k the luma kernels 0.125 / 0.079 and the glue 0.151 / 0.080. The kernel rounds closed most of the
kernels' gap; what is left of inter prediction is mostly the code around them. The largest single
item of that glue is in the kernels crate: `Kernels::predict`'s check of the block's regions,
`predict::place`, holds 0.047 of FFmpeg's time over the 32 streams (sd 0.038, 720p 0.033, 1080p
0.037, 4k 0.079; `predict_items.txt`), about 3.7% of CoreAV's time and 6% at 4k, with the rest of the
call's own code another 0.016. By instructions (`instructions.txt`, callgrind, a 1080p stream, 30
pictures): `place` and the call around it are 39.3 million of 380.7 million, 10.3%, about 225 a call
over 174,811 calls. It computes and tests, for every block, each window's samples used against the
picture (eight comparisons and the selects that pick each fraction's margins) and each window's extent
against its slice (four more, with their products), every time, although the reference and its size do
not change within a slice and almost every block lies well inside it.

The other parts a kernel round could address, and why not this round:

- **Entropy** (`cabac_split.txt`): CABAC as a whole is 1.15 to 1.17 times FFmpeg's at 720p and 1080p
  and 0.99 at 4k. Its residual loops had the register round and the four hot-path sites, which
  measured under 1% each; where the remaining time sits against FFmpeg's cannot be split by this
  method, since FFmpeg's out-of-line decisions are not attributed to their callers without call
  graphs. A fused CAVLC residual helps the six CAVLC streams, not the median ("Snapshot outliers").
- **Intra prediction** (`recon_split.txt`): 0.028 against 0.016 overall, 0.049 against 0.025 at
  720p: a smaller excess (0.010 overall) than `place`'s.
- **The transforms** are at FFmpeg's cost (0.032 against 0.043), and the scaling of levels as they
  are stored (`CoeffScale::apply`, 0.024) is inside FFmpeg's residual decoding, so it cannot be
  compared on its own.
- **The MB layer** is the largest excess, but it is the decoder's control code, spread over a dozen
  items of 0.005 to 0.024 each (`items.txt`), not a kernel.
- **Deblocking** and the **banded references** have rounds open by others.

### Design

`Planes` (a reference's three planes) gains an `Interior`, computed once when it is built: the
integer luma positions (xIntL and yIntL of the block's first sample, Equations 8-228 and 8-229
before their clip) at which every window `place` can take lies inside the picture and inside its
slices, whatever the block's size and fraction. `place` computes the block's integer position, as it
did, and where it lies in the interior, skips the window-by-window test; elsewhere the test runs as
before, moved into a cold out-of-line function (`Windows::fit`) so that it does not hold registers
in every call. The placement it returns, and which blocks it declines, are the same as before: the
interior is a sufficient condition for the test to pass, and the offsets are computed by the same
expressions either way.

The interior of a reference built by `Planes::with_origin` is x from 2 to `stride - 19` and y from
2 to `rows - 19`, because:

- a luma window starts at most two samples before the block and ends at most `16 + 3` after its
  first column and row, so its samples used lie in the picture, and its extent in the slice, which
  holds the picture's rows from the origin (`with_origin` checked the slice's length);
- the chroma position (xIntC, yIntC) of a 4:2:0 frame is the block's chroma position plus the
  vector's whole chroma samples, and twice it lies between the luma position less 2 and the luma
  position (for an even block position it is the luma position or one less), so a chroma window of
  at most `8 + 1` samples each way lies inside a chroma plane of half the stride and half the rows,
  and inside its slice for the same reason;
- `stride - 19 >= 2` needs a stride of 21 or more, so a plane narrower than a window row (`w + 5`)
  has an empty interior and every block goes through the full test, as before.

A band's `Planes` (`Planes::band`) holds only some rows of a picture, so `Interior::of(stride,
rows)`, a whole picture's interior, must not be given to it: its blocks would skip the test of
windows that reach rows the band's slices do not hold, and the vector kernels would read past them.
`Planes::band` computes its own (`Interior::band`), for which `Interior` gains a first row (2 for a
whole picture):

- across it is a whole picture's, x from 2 to `stride - 19`, where every window's columns lie in
  one row of its plane (the chroma window's through `x - 2 <= 2 * xIntC <= x`), so a window lies in
  its slice where each of its rows does;
- a slice holds plane row `r` whole where `first <= r < first + n`, with
  `n = (len - origin) / stride` (for chroma the shorter chroma slice and half the stride); the part
  of a row after them is left out, which only narrows the interior;
- down, the luma window's rows `y - 2` to `y + 18` give `first[0] + 2 <= y <= first[0] + n[0] - 19`;
  the chroma window's rows `yIntC` to `yIntC + 8`, with `y - 2 <= 2 * yIntC <= y` and `2 * yIntC`
  even, give `2 * first[1] + 1 <= y <= 2 * (first[1] + n[1]) - 17`; and the picture's
  `y <= rows - 19` stays (its `2 <= y` follows from the luma bound).

Where the slices hold whole rows each bound is the last position at which every window fits, which
the tests check one past each edge. The decoder builds a band's `Planes` for each block it predicts
from a banded reference, so the interior costs two divisions a block there. Rejected: an empty
interior for bands, which keeps every banded block (all of them at more than one thread) on the full
test; and the rows held derived from `at` alone, which needs two more divisions for lower bounds the
first rows give directly.

Blocks outside the interior, the picture's border rows and columns of up to 18 samples and those
whose vector reaches past it, are 5.6% of the calls on the 1080p stream above. Measured by
instructions (callgrind, the same stream; no timing before the bars below): `place` and the call
around it fall from 39.3 to 26.8 million (plus 1.0 million in `Windows::fit`), about 72 fewer a
call, and the whole decode from 380.7 to 368.3 million (0.967). If time follows those instructions
in `place`, the call gains about 0.015 of FFmpeg's time, about 1.2% of CoreAV's overall and 2% at
4k; that is an estimate, not a bar.

What the round does not do:

- **The picture side stays per call.** The block written (`PlanesMut`) is built by the decoder for
  every call, since it borrows the picture mutably; its bounds stay tested per call.
- **No change to the `unsafe` code.** The vector kernels' pointers rest on `place`'s result as
  before; `docs/unsafe-sites.md`'s row for `simd/x86/predict.rs` now names the interior as one of
  the two ways that result is checked.

Prior art: none. The interior is a rectangle derived from the specification's window sizes above.

decoders in the same rounds, built alike (`cargo build --locked --profile dist --example decode -p
coreav-h264`, one toolchain, `RUSTFLAGS` unset) from one tree each, on this host (the 2.90 GHz class,
family 6 model 106; the run records it). `base` is `main` at `084ee40`; `k` is the branch's code

## Kernel round: a macroblock's chroma edges in one call

The chroma kernels of the deblocking profile ("Deblocking round:
thresholds from shifted tables"): 0.040 of FFmpeg's time against its
0.019, at `814eb2a1`, the largest gap left in the deblocking filter's
kernels; the luma kernels are level.

### What the measurement says

- **A call's cost is mostly its overhead.** A harness that calls the
  paired kernel an edge at a time, its two views included
  (`tools/pairbench`, `harness.txt`), runs 279 instructions a macroblock
  for horizontal edge 0 alone and 1,022 for all four edges (callgrind,
  AVX2 tier, the harness's own loop of about 35 included). By the kernel's
  code, the filter's arithmetic and the rows it moves are about 100 of an
  edge's; the rest is the dispatch, the views, the kernel's checks of each
  plane's rows and the parameters turned into lanes.
- **A macroblock that filters chroma makes two to four calls.** Over the
  class frame counts, a macroblock that filters any chroma edge filters
  1.93 to 3.79 of its four on six training streams (`calls.txt`; on
  `9db41aa16b5a`, 912,295 of the 1,011,503 that filter any filter all
  four). The paired round rejected one call a macroblock from about 1.26
  calls over every macroblock of 30 pictures of that stream; counted that
  way over its class frame count it is 2.09, and from 0.10 (4k, where few
  macroblocks filter) to 2.09 on the six.
- **The edges of one direction do not touch.** Vertical edge 0 of a
  macroblock reads columns −2 to 1 of the block and edge 4 columns 2 to 5;
  horizontal edges 0 and 4 read rows −2 to 1 and 2 to 5. So the two edges
  of a direction may be filtered at once, from the same rows, and give
  what filtering one then the other gives; only the order of the
  directions matters (clause 8.7: every vertical edge of a macroblock
  before its horizontal ones).

### Design

1. **`Kernels::filter_chroma_mb(cb, cr, params)`**: the four chroma
   edges of a macroblock, both planes, `params` per edge and plane in the
   order vertical 0, vertical 4, horizontal 0, horizontal 4; an edge
   whose segments all have bS 0 in both planes is not filtered. Its
   default is the reference: `Kernels::filter_chroma_pair` an edge at a
   time, in that order (`chroma_mb_by_edges`), which the scalar kernels,
   arm64 and any other implementation use.
2. **A view of the macroblock's window, `ChromaMbMut`**: the block's 8x8
   samples with the two columns to its left and the two rows above it,
   ten rows of ten samples, checked once in checked arithmetic, with a
   stride of at least ten so that its rows do not overlap.
   `ChromaMbMut::edge` gives each edge's `EdgeMut` inside it.
3. **The AVX2 kernel (`simd/x86/chroma_mb.rs`)** checks each plane's
   window once (`rows_at_mut`, ten rows of ten bytes) and then:
   - for the vertical edges, reads the block's eight rows of columns −2
     to 5 of both planes (Cb in the low half of each vector, Cr in the
     high), transposes each half's 8x8 bytes into its eight columns,
     filters edge 0 on columns −2 to 1 and edge 4 on columns 2 to 5 with
     the paired kernel's filter (`filter_chroma16`, sixteen lines a
     vector), transposes back and writes the eight rows whole: the columns
     no edge changed are written as read;
   - for the horizontal edges, reads rows −2 to 5 of columns 0 to 7, one
     row of both planes a vector, filters edge 0 on rows −2 to 1 and edge
     4 on rows 2 to 5, and writes back the rows an edge changed.
   An edge with no bS is skipped. Where a check fails, or the planes'
   strides differ, the edges go to the paired kernel one at a time.
4. **The decoder** derives the four edges' parameters as before, makes
   one call a macroblock, and takes the per-edge path where a window does
   not fit inside a plane: the first macroblock of a picture of one band
   (whose two slack rows above are there, but not the two samples before
   the plane's first), the whole
   first macroblock row of the first band of a picture of several bands
   (no rows above it), and every macroblock of a picture one macroblock
   wide (a chroma stride of 8). Bands after the first hold rows above in
   their top apron.

Kept: the paired kernel, which the fallback and other implementations
call. Rejected:
- one call for the luma edges of a macroblock: its four edges a
  direction overlap (each reads three samples a side, four apart), so
  they cannot be filtered at once;
- forwarding the vertical pass's rows to the horizontal pass in
  registers rather than through memory: the horizontal pass's loads
  (columns 0 to 7) overlap the vertical pass's stores (columns −2 to 5)
  without matching them, so they wait for the stores; the paired kernel's
  path waits the same way, and the harness shows the two directions
  together at 40.3 ns against 44.3 (`harness.txt`), so it is left for
  later.

Bit-exact by construction (the paired kernel's arithmetic on disjoint
samples) and by test: `the_chroma_macroblock_matches_the_reference`
compares `Simd` and `Auto` with the scalar kernels an edge at a time over
every subset of the edges, strengths 0 to 4, thresholds that differ
between the planes (α 0 included), strides from ten, planes of different
strides and windows at the start and the end of their planes; the
`filter_chroma_mb` fuzz target does the same from fuzzed bytes (120 s
locally, 4.8 million runs, clean, `fuzz.txt`); Miri, with AVX2 and SSE4.1, runs every
edge, all four, and each direction's two, through `Simd` and `Auto`, in
planes that end at the window's last byte, from misaligned bases
(`tools/miri`: 168 cases, no error). The new pointer accesses are listed
in `docs/unsafe-sites.md`. Output identical to `main`
(`051e1692`) on the 32 training streams at one and eight threads
(`identity.txt`). Nothing is allocated.

Instructions of the whole decode fall 1.07% to 3.54% on five streams
(callgrind, AVX2 tier, `instructions.txt`). The harness (information,
`harness.txt`), ns a macroblock, the paired path against this one: all
four edges 81.3 against 61.5, both vertical edges 49.8 against 34.4,
both horizontal 34.1 against 33.5, vertical and horizontal edge 0 44.3
against 40.3, vertical edge 0 alone 27.6 against 25.9, horizontal edge 0
alone 19.0 against 20.6. Horizontal edge 0 alone is the one case slower:
the window's two views and checks cost more than the pair's, and that
edge is filtered alone mostly in macroblocks with no left neighbour and
in pictures with few edges, which is where the 4k class sits (0.10 calls
a macroblock). Timed locally (information, `local-timing.txt`): 0.963 to
1.005 on eight streams, the 720p ones lowest and one 4k stream
(`e624cbe0d2be`) at 1.005.

## Deblocking round: the strengths of quiet macroblocks

The strengths at 4k, which the deblocking profile left ("Deblocking
round: thresholds from shifted tables", item 2): 0.067 of FFmpeg's time
against its 0.031, at `814eb2a1`.

### What the measurement says

- **Waiting on records explains part of it, and fetching them ahead does
  not help.** The hottest instructions of the deblocking glue at 4k
  follow loads: the slice filter's lookup waits on the load of the
  macroblock's own record (`q.slice`), the motion comparison on the
  motion (`lines.txt` of that round's profile). In Valgrind's cache model
  (`cache.txt`, 4k, `main` at `051e1692`) the glue misses the first-level
  cache about three times a macroblock: the macroblock's record, its
  upper neighbour's, and the motion they compare, written a macroblock
  row earlier. Hints that fetch those records four macroblocks ahead
  (`prefetcht0`, one for the first line of each record, or one for every
  line) were level or slower on five 4k streams, timed locally
  (`local-prefetch.txt`, information; the one 1080p stream timed was
  faster with both, 0.994 and 0.981). Likely, not measured (Valgrind's
  model has no second-level cache): on the 2.90 GHz class the records are
  still in the second-level cache, whose latency the core hides.
- **The internal edges of a quiet macroblock are built anyway.** Every
  macroblock spreads its masks into the words of its three internal edges
  per direction (`column`, `row`, `spread`): their lines take about 48
  instructions a macroblock at 4k, edge 0's share included (callgrind,
  `cache.txt`), although a macroblock with no coefficient and one motion,
  as a skipped one, has no internal boundary with a coefficient or with
  differing motion, and every word comes out 0.

### Design

**The internal edges of a macroblock are 0 when their masks are.** Once
the coefficient mask and the motion mask of the internal boundaries are
known, a macroblock where both are 0 returns its internal strengths as 0
before building the words. This is round 15's part Z, timed alone here;
round 15 timed it only together with its parts N and T
(`docs/measurements/h264-rejected.md`).

Bit-exact by construction (the words built from two zero masks are 0) and
by the test of the masks against the derivation a segment at a time.
Output identical to `main` (`051e1692`) on the 32 training streams at one
and eight threads (`identity.txt`). Instructions of the whole decode
fall 0.71% to 2.76% on five streams (callgrind, AVX2 tier; 4k 1.66% and
2.76%, sd 1.63%; `instructions.txt`), and 0.02% on `a6af290d9053`, whose
macroblocks mostly hold coefficients (round 15 counted 0.09% more there
for part Z). Nothing is allocated.

Rejected: the prefetch hints above (no gain locally at 4k, and 0.88%
more instructions there, `instructions.txt`); deriving the strengths when
a macroblock is decoded, while its records are in the first-level cache,
and storing them for the filter: it moves work into the macroblock layer
and adds a buffer per macroblock, for misses that are likely served by the
second-level cache on this host (not measured, above).

## Round 19: the CAVLC residual in one pass

The second candidate of "Snapshot outliers" (the fused CAVLC residual). Six of the
32 training streams are CAVLC, and on the one with the most bits a
macroblock, `6f7799768413` (sd), CoreAV took 1.60 times FFmpeg 9.0.2's
time, half of the excess in the entropy stage. The round is for CAVLC
content: no bar of the 32 streams' median could show it, so its primary
bars are on the six CAVLC streams, and the 32 streams and every class are
guarded.

### What the measurement says

On the development VM (Intel Xeon, 2.50 GHz class, 8 logical CPUs;
information, not the bar host; `docs/measurements/h264-rounds/round19/local/`):

- **The residual path is a third of the stream's time** (`profile.txt`,
  `main` at `27b504a`, one thread): `parse_residual` for CAVLC 12.4% of
  the samples, `cavlc::residual_block` 12.2%, `Code::read` 8.4% and nC
  (`block_context`) 2.5%. Within `parse_residual`, 4% is the copy in
  `CavlcSyntax::block`: a 64-entry array zeroed for each block, then
  scanned in full, with a branch on each entry, to scale and place the
  levels that `residual_block` had already placed once.
- **It is time, not instructions.** A build that does the same work in
  one pass (below) runs 0.44% fewer instructions on the stream
  (`instructions.txt`) and takes 0.832 and 0.878 of `main`'s CPU time in
  two runs (`ab-1t-1.txt`, `ab-1t-2.txt`); over the six CAVLC streams the
  median is 0.940 and 0.947, every stream faster. What it removes is
  stalls: the 192 KB table of coeff_token's first class, whose lookup
  missed L1 ("Snapshot outliers"), and the mispredicted branches of the
  copy's scan.

### Design

`cavlc::block` is residual_block_cavlc() (clause 7.3.5.3.2) for a block
of maxNumCoeff up to 16, writing each scaled level to its raster
position, as `Syntax::block` asks; `CavlcSyntax::block` calls it with no
array of its own.

1. **Each code is one table indexed by its leading zeros.** Every code
   word of clause 9.2 is a run of zeros, a one and at most five more
   bits, or a run of zeros alone. A `Code` row is the count of leading
   zeros (`u64::leading_zeros`, capped at the row of the all-zeros code
   word or of no code word), and the entry within the row is the next
   `suffix` bits after the one. coeff_token's longest class is 16 rows
   of 8 entries (384 bytes) where a table indexed by the next 16 bits is
   64 K entries; every table is at most 224 entries, and each read is
   one load.
2. **A 64-bit window of the stream.** A block's reads take bits from a
   window loaded with one 8-byte read, refilled only when an element
   might not fit in what is left (an element is at most 32 bits, and a
   load gives at least 57), where the bit reader's `peek32` bounds-checks
   and loads for each element. Past the end of the RBSP the window reads
   zeros, and the position is checked against the end once, when the
   block is done: a block that ran past the end is `Truncated`, as
   before, though the error no longer names the element.
3. **Levels are placed as their positions are read.** The levels are
   decoded into a 16-entry array (the bitstream gives them all before
   total_zeros), then total_zeros gives the highest position, and each
   run_before the next one down; each level is scaled and written to
   `out[scan[k]]` when its position `k` is known. No array is zeroed or
   scanned, and the run_before values are not stored.

The arithmetic of each element (the level code of Equations 9-5 to 9-9,
suffixLength, the checks of levels, total_zeros and run_before) is the
same as before.

Rejected:
- **Two-level tables** (8 bits, then the rest; the prototype of
  "Snapshot outliers"): for the long code words of high-rate content a
  second dependent load and a branch on which level, where a count of
  leading zeros is one instruction.
- **nC from a per-macroblock record of the neighbours' TotalCoeff**, as
  the candidate had it (the edge blocks of macroblocks A and B taken once
  when the residual starts, like CABAC's `cbf_nb`): 0.08% more
  instructions than without it and no difference in time on the VM
  (0.944 against 0.947 over the six streams, `ab-1t-2.txt`), so the
  neighbour lookups stay.
- **Keeping the clause's steps as functions** with the copy removed:
  the steps exchange the levels and runs through arrays, which is the
  cost being removed.

Tests: `every_code_table_finds_what_a_flat_table_finds` reads every
16-bit window of every table, followed by zeros and by ones, against a
search of the code words; `the_fused_block_decodes_what_the_clause_decodes`
decodes 200,000 random blocks (every nC class, maxNumCoeff 4, 15 and 16)
with the decoder this round replaced, kept in the tests as the
reference: the same coefficients, TotalCoeff and bit position, or the
same kind of error. `an_8x8_block_takes_its_interleaved_positions_and_scale`
does the same for the four interleaved lists of an 8x8 block, with a
scaling that rounds and shifts.

## CABAC under BMI2: a pre-check, no round

Information, not a round: no bars, and nothing merges from it
(`docs/measurements/h264-rounds/cabac-precheck/`, `analysis.txt` from its
`analyze.py`). The pre-check's base is `main` at `27b504a`; the local split
below uses `main` at `c17ae06`, whose CABAC code is the same.

### What the measurement says

On the eight CABAC streams of the pre-check (one thread, discard; 2.90 GHz
class) the decoder takes a median of 1.272 times FFmpeg 9.0.2's time
(`175433794e02` 5.15 s against 4.08 s). The functions whose
name contains "cabac" (`decode_cabac` included) take 73% of the samples on
`175433794e02` and 33% on `1d4b1775d78a` (`local/functions.txt`, the run of
`c17ae06` without `+bmi2`). `decision` is inlined
at every call site. In the generated code a decision shifts by a register
twice: the more probable sub-range scaled by the bits loaded
(`mps_range << bits`), and its renormalization (`mps_range << mps_shift`).
On the x86-64 baseline such a shift takes its count in CL and writes the
flags; BMI2's `shlx` takes any register and writes none. Hence the
question: what is BMI2 worth to CABAC, and can a site hold it?

### Options weighed

1. **A hot-path site: the CABAC residual under
   `#[target_feature(enable = "bmi2")]`, chosen at run time.** The
   significance map and the levels, the same safe body in `cabac.rs`
   instantiated twice, once with the attribute; the one `unsafe`, in
   `fast/`, is the call into that instantiation, sound because a token only
   detection constructs is held. The residual's parsing stays safe Rust,
   as the hot-path exception asks: the site adds no pointer, no unchecked index
   and no memory access, only an instruction set. Its twin is the same body
   without the attribute. It still costs the hot-path machinery (a row, a
   twin and a fuzz target), so it has the bar the earlier sites had ("Result:
   no site merged"): 0.98 against its twin with the interval below 1.00,
   on the bar machine and the training set. Point 3 of "The kernel
   boundary" rejects BMI2 for the whole control code at build time, as not
   comparable with FFmpeg's baseline C. A path chosen at run time, where
   the CPU has the instruction set, is how the kernels already use AVX2
   (`Auto::detect()`); that a named hot path of the control code may be
   chosen the same way is a judgment this note makes, not a rule it
   inherits.
2. **Safe Rust that avoids the shifts.** The renormalization's doubling can
   be an addition (`e1`), which removes one shift of the two. The other
   stays: with codIOffset at a fixed bit position instead of one that moves
   with the data loaded, the shift moves to `value << n` after the
   decision, on the same chain (the rejected `map_4x4` and `map_8x8` did
   that in assembly). Safe Rust removes one of the two, not both.
3. **Rejected: the residual behind the kernel crate's dispatch.** Either
   parsing of stream bytes moves into `coreav-kernels-h264`, which the
   `unsafe` policy excludes, or the kernel crate offers a
   "run this closure under BMI2" call whose effect depends on the compiler
   inlining a closure from another crate into a `#[target_feature]`
   function, which nothing checks.
4. **Rejected: building the decoder for BMI2** (`x86-64-v3`, or `+bmi2`).
   Point 3 of "The kernel boundary" rejects it: the control code would get
   BMI2 too, which is not comparable with FFmpeg's baseline C. Besides,
   every binary would then require the instruction set, and a build from
   source with the default target would not get it.

How the options would be judged: option 1 only if `b1` (option 1, built
for measurement) could meet the 0.98 bar against `e1`, that is, gained 2%
or more on the CABAC streams; option 2 as a round only if `e1` took a
clear part of the whole-program gain, a judgment rather than a bar.

### The pre-check

The A/B helper timed four builds in the same rounds on the 2.90 GHz
class: `base` (`main` at `27b504a`), `bmi2all` (the same with
`-C target-feature=+bmi2`), `e1` (`exp/h264-cabac-levels` `6e8f7a70`) and
`b1` (`exp/h264-cabac-bmi2` `23f6877d`, `e1` with the residual under BMI2
behind detection); eight CABAC streams, two a class, one thread pinned,
five rounds, no intervals; output identical to `base` on the 32 training
streams. Median ratio over the eight streams, discard (write):

| Build | Against | Median | sd, 720p, 1080p, 4k (discard) |
|---|---|---|---|
| `bmi2all` | `base` | 0.9769 (0.9803), 7 of 8 faster | 0.9839, 0.9748, 0.9725, 0.9899 |
| `e1` | `base` | 0.9978 (1.0003) | 1.0010, 0.9904, 0.9954, 1.0098 |
| `b1` | `base` | 0.9975 (0.9972) | 1.0046, 0.9893, 0.9911, 1.0019 |
| `b1` | `e1` | 0.9994 (0.9982) | |

`b1`'s residual functions are compiled with BMI2: in the local build of
the same commit they have `shlx` and no shift by CL, where the twins have
four to six shifts by CL each (`local/b1-shifts.txt`). Within what this
pre-check resolves, the residual under BMI2 gains nothing on its own, and
neither does `e1`.

Where the whole-program gain sits (`local/functions.txt`: a development VM
with the bar class's CPU, Intel Xeon @ 2.90 GHz, family 6, model 106, not
a bar run; `perf` samples per function, five interleaved rounds; `main` at
`c17ae06` with and without `+bmi2`; shares of the base run's samples): on
`175433794e02` (2.6% in total) the residual functions 1.5%, `Cabac::mvd`
0.7% (its own samples 0.894), `decode_cabac` 0.4%, the rest a wash; on
`1d4b1775d78a` (1.5%) `mvd` 0.7% (0.837), the residual 0.5%,
`decode_cabac` 0.2%, the rest 0.1%. And `b1` against `e1` locally on
`175433794e02`: the residual functions 0.979, but `decode_cabac`, which
calls them, 1.049, 1.003 in total (the pre-check: 0.9994 for that stream).

### Result: no round

Neither condition holds: `b1` is level with `e1` (0.9994), and `e1` with
`base`. What BMI2 is worth sits in the CABAC parse of a macroblock as a
whole (the residual, `mvd` and `decode_cabac` around them), and the
residual alone loses its part to its caller. The widest site, all of
`decode_cabac` under BMI2, would compile the macroblock layer's whole
CABAC parse twice and could reach about what the whole-program build did,
0.977 on eight CABAC streams: the 0.98 bar with no margin and no interval.
So no hot-path site is built, and the CABAC engine stays safe Rust. The
arms are kept on `rejected/h264-cabac-mps-add` (`e1`) and
`rejected/h264-cabac-bmi2` (`b1`). Two leads remain, neither of them a
shift: `Cabac::mvd`, whose own time falls by a tenth or more under BMI2 (likely in its bypass suffix and
sign, not measured), and the cost of `decode_cabac` around the residual
calls, which `b1` moved by 5% without changing it.

### After the wider dispatch: still no site

Re-evaluated after "Kernel round: the hot paths compiled twice, wider",
which runs `decode_cabac` with everything inlined into it (the CABAC
syntax elements, the residual's parse and `decision` at every call site)
and `Cabac::mvd` in an x86-64-v3 instance, BMI2 included, on a CPU that
has it. The widest BMI2 site this section weighed is then the default
build's path: `after` over `v3` measured 1.0011 at one thread over the 32
streams, so what building for x86-64-v3 (BMI2 among it) is worth is
taken, CABAC's share with it by inference (the run has no CABAC-only
split). What is left for a
hot-path engine site is what bounds checks and branches cost against the
same chain compiled for v3, and the sites built for that ("Result: no
site merged") measured 0.990 to 0.9995 locally (2.50 GHz class, not bar
runs) against twins compiled for the baseline, short of the 0.98 bar; a
twin compiled for v3 would likely leave them less. The
entropy stage as a whole, NAL to macroblock syntax, was 1.16 times
FFmpeg 9.0.2's at `40f29a6` (4k 1.06; `profile-40f29a6/stages.txt`), a
difference of about 4.5% of the decoder's time before the wider dispatch
took part of it, of which the engine is a part. So no engine site is
built, and the CABAC engine stays safe Rust.

(time over FFmpeg 9.0.2's total, CoreAV / FFmpeg):

| chroma (`x86::intra_chroma`) | 0.0055 / 0.0026 | 0.0112 / 0.0045 | | |
| Intra_16x16 | 0.0023 / 0.0014 | | | |

Intra_8x8 is the one intra kind still on the reference: `Simd::intra8x8_mb` ran the reference loop
("Kernel round: intra prediction in the kernels crate", which left it there at 35 ms of eight streams), so
each block filtered its 25 neighbours one at a time, built a buffer of 74 samples (the line, its averages
and its filter) one at a time, and gathered its 64 samples through a table, before the vector transform
read the block back to add the residual. At FFmpeg's cost it would give about 0.005 of FFmpeg's time, 0.3
to 0.4% of CoreAV's overall and about 0.6% at 720p; none at sd, whose streams do not use the 8x8
transform. Chroma intra, the second largest gap, is already a vector kernel; it is left for a round of
its own.

### Design

`x86::intra8x8_mb` follows the Intra_4x4 kernel (point 4 of the intra round): one check of the
macroblock's view (`IntraRows::of`), then per block, in decoding order, its neighbours read through
pointers, the prediction made in registers, the residual added in registers, and the eight rows written
once; the next block reads what this one wrote.

1. **The edge line in one vector.** p[-1, 7] .. p[-1, 0], p[-1, -1], p[0, -1] .. p[15, -1] are bytes 0
   to 24 of a 256-bit vector, built from one 16-byte read of the row above (its last eight repeated by a
   shuffle where the block has no top right), the eight samples of the column left and the corner, each
   zero where the block has no such neighbour, as in the reference.
2. **The filter of clause 8.3.2.2.1 as one 3-tap filter.** Every filtered sample is `(a + 2b + c + 2) >> 2`
   of a sample and its two neighbours on the line, where at five places the clause uses the sample itself
   as one neighbour: the line's two ends, p[-1, 0] and p[0, -1] without `top_left`, and p[-1, -1] on the
   side without `left` or `top`. So the line moved one byte each way (a lane permute and an `alignr`
   each), with the sample itself blended in at those places, gives the two neighbour vectors; the masks
   come from the availability bits and three constant selections (`LINE_BEFORE`, `LINE_AFTER`) in one
   `and` and one compare each. The filter is the byte identity of the Intra_4x4 kernel,
   `pavgb(b, pavgb(a, c) - ((a ^ c) & 1))`. The result is masked to zero where the reference's filtered
   neighbours are zero (`LINE_FILTERED`).
3. **Averages and filter of the filtered line, then shuffles.** The directional modes (3 to 8) take each
   sample from the filtered line's 2-tap averages or its 3-tap filter (`intra::sources`, round 9), and
   horizontal-up's copies take p'[-1, 7], the line's first sample. The averages are one `pavgb` of the
   line and the line moved up a byte, with the first byte its own neighbour, so byte 0 is p'[-1, 7]
   itself and byte `k + 1` the average between positions `k` and `k + 1`; the filter is item 2's identity
   with both ends repeated. Each is under 32 bytes, so the block is two halves of four rows, each the
   `or` of four in-lane shuffles (`pshufb`), one per 16 bytes of the averages and of the filter, each
   broadcast to both lanes; a table built at compile time from `intra::sources` (`SHUFFLES_8X8`, 2,304
   bytes) holds the shuffles of each mode, with 0x80 where a byte comes from another source. Vertical and
   horizontal are shuffles of the filtered line itself through the same table; DC is a sum of absolute
   differences of the filtered line with the corner masked out, and a broadcast.
4. **The residual in registers.** The 8x8 transform's rows (`idct8x8`, the vector kernel's, factored out)
   are added to the two halves with the saturating chain of the transform round (`add_residual8`, factored
   out of `add_four_rows`, which now loads its prediction and calls it), and the rows are stored once
   (`store_four_rows`).

The kernel reads the row above as 16 bytes also where the block has no top right, as the Intra_4x4 kernel
reads 8: the row is the macroblock's row above or its eighth row, and its 24th sample ends before the
macroblock's last row does, since the stride is at least 16 (`docs/unsafe-sites.md`, the row for
`simd/x86.rs`, updated). The AVX-512 tier has no kernel of its own and runs this
one; arm64 keeps the reference loop.

Rejected:

- **AVX-512 VBMI byte permutes** (`vpermt2b` over the averages and filter as one 64-byte table, a half of
  four rows in one instruction, and `vpermb` for the one-byte moves). About 20 fewer instructions a block
  out of about 110 for the prediction, on the tier's CPUs only; the AVX2 kernel is needed anyway, and a
  second kernel is a second set of `unsafe` sites to list and fuzz. A later round can add it with its own bars if
  this one passes.
- **Windows of a buffer on the stack**, a 16-byte load per row at a mode- and row-dependent offset (every
  row draws on at most 11 consecutive positions). The loads cross the stores that wrote the buffer, which
  forwarding does not cover, and the table of offsets is per row; four shuffles of registers per half are
  fewer instructions and touch no memory.
- **Monomorphising each mode** with constant `alignr` shifts. Eight copies of the kernel for what one
  table of shuffles does.
- **Filtering in 16-bit lanes.** The 25 samples need two vectors; the byte identity is exact and keeps one.

Prior art: none. The method is the Intra_4x4 kernel's (the intra round's point 4), extended to the 8x8
filter from clause 8.3.2.2.1.

Bit-exact by construction and by test: `intra_kernels_match_the_reference` now also runs
`intra8x8_mb` through `Simd` against `Scalar` (every combination of neighbours, random modes 0 to 8 and
out of range, coefficients over their whole range, every mask, strides from 16, planes that end at the
block's last sample); five mutations of the kernel (the two neighbour selections, the DC rounding, the
top-right repeat, the DC mask) each fail it. The `intra` fuzz target gains the 8x8 macroblock (7.0 million runs, 300 s, no
failure). The Miri harness `docs/measurements/h264-rounds/intra8x8/tools/miri` runs the call through
`Simd` and `Auto` against the reference in planes that start at the first neighbour the view names and
end at the macroblock's last sample, from a misaligned base.

Instructions (callgrind, one thread, `--discard`, the first pictures of one stream per class; information,
not a bar, and biased to intra pictures): the whole decode falls by 0.0% on `41e324ebb708.0.sd` (120
pictures), 2.6% on `278dbf5a63bb.0.720p` (40), 3.9% on `1d4b1775d78a.0.720p` (60), 1.3% on
`175433794e02.0.1080p` (20) and 5.1% on `3b1b441e23ae.0.4k` (6). On `1d4b1775d78a`, Intra_8x8 with its
residual falls from about 84 to 30 million instructions (25,796 macroblocks: about 290 a block, the
transform included).

## Motion round: a block's motion in 12 bytes, on the current decoder

This round replicates "Motion round: a block's motion in 12 bytes"
(`docs/measurements/h264-rounds/motion-12b/`, rejected) on `main` at
`72b173b5`. The code is new, written from that section's design and not
from its branch. The run is fresh, and the bars below were fixed before
it.

That round's record, on the 2.90 GHz class, is the strongest timing
evidence for any change to the macroblock layer so far:
- discard over all 32 streams: 0.992 [0.979, 0.998] with the default
  allocator, 0.990 [0.981, 0.998] with every picture-sized allocation
  mapped;
- write: 0.993;
- every class at most 1.005 in both runs.

It was rejected only by M12-3, which asked for 0.985 on the 17 streams
with B slices and got 0.992 [0.981, 1.001].

M12-3 is not carried over. It tested a mechanism, not the effect: that
the gain would come from direct prediction's co-located reads, which
only B slices make. The run showed the gain comes from elsewhere. The
streams without B slices gained as much as those with them (0.991
against 0.992 on discard), and the counts put the removed misses in the
motion stores, the deblocking strengths and the neighbours' reads as
well. A bar on the B subset measures where the gain sits, not whether
there is one. The bars here ask for the effect: overall, in every class,
with the mapped allocator and at eight threads.

### What the measurement says

- **The macroblock layer is the stage furthest from FFmpeg.**
  - In a profile of `main` at `d7bb7aeb` it takes 0.213 of FFmpeg 9.0.2's
    time, against FFmpeg's 0.093: 2.2 to 2.5 times FFmpeg's in every
    class. The profile is one thread, discard, cpu-clock samples on the
    development VM of the 2.90 GHz class
    (`docs/measurements/h264-rounds/motion-12b-r2/local/profile-stages.txt`).
  - Among its largest items are the record and motion stores: `finish_mb`,
    `store_mb` and its row copies, and the co-located read
    (`profile-mb-items.txt`).
- **A block's motion is 20 bytes.** It holds two vectors, two reference
  indices and two four-byte picture identities, so a macroblock's sixteen
  blocks are 320 bytes, five cache lines.
  - Every inter macroblock writes them.
  - The deblocking filter reads them, as do the next macroblock row's
    neighbours and later pictures' direct prediction.
- **Simulated (callgrind with its cache model, whole decode, `--discard`,
  five streams, one per class plus a second B-heavy 1080p stream;
  `local/instructions.txt`):**
  - instructions within 0.6% of `main`'s;
  - first-level misses 8% to 12% fewer: read misses 3% to 8% fewer and
    write misses 14% to 17% fewer, on every stream.
- **Timed locally (information, `local/local-timing.txt`; this VM moves a
  stream by several percent between runs):** 0.932 to 0.998 on eight
  streams. The 4k streams show the most, 0.932 and 0.949, and the 1080p
  streams 0.970 and 0.980.
- **A probe in this round found no time in the record copy.**
  `finish_mb`'s copy of the macroblock's record is its hottest line,
  even at sd, where every record fits the second-level cache. Copying
  the record field by field, so that each load matches the store that
  wrote it, removed the hot line, but local time was level (0.992 to
  1.007) and the stage's share of the samples unchanged. The cost the
  line showed is waiting that surfaces there, not the copy. So this
  round takes the motion's memory, where the ledger has a measured gain.

### Design

1. **A block's motion in 12 bytes** (`picture::Motion`):
   - the two vectors, 8 bytes, unchanged;
   - the two reference indices, one `i8` each, unchanged;
   - the two pictures the block refers to, one byte each: the picture's
     slot (`ref_slot`), with `NO_SLOT` (255) for a list the block does not
     use.

   A macroblock's sixteen blocks are 192 bytes, three cache lines, and a
   compile-time assertion keeps the size.
2. **A picture's slot** (`Picture::slot`, 0 to 254). `Decoder::picture_slot`
   hands one out to each picture as it starts: the first slot, counting
   on from the last one handed out, that no picture of the decoded
   picture buffer holds. This covers the frames a `frame_num` gap
   invents, the stand-in shared by those that the sliding window drops at
   once included. That stand-in takes a slot of its own; on `main` it
   carried identity 0, which the first picture decoded carries as well.
3. Nothing else changes. Every reader reads the same values and compares
   slots where it compared identities.

**Exact for every conforming stream this decoder accepts, by these
bounds** (a damaged stream's concealment may differ, below):
- **Reference indices.** They are 0 to 31, or -1, in an `i8`.
  - A frame's lists hold at most 16 entries (`num_ref_idx_active`,
    checked in `slice.rs`); a field's could hold 32, but the decoder
    refuses field pictures and MBAFF (`Error::Unsupported`), and the
    syntax refuses an index of 32 or more (`syntax.rs`).
  - `every_reference_index_of_full_lists_keeps_its_picture` takes lists
    of 32 entries, a long-term one among them, through `InterTables` and
    the 12-byte record.
- **Slots: the buffer holds at most 18 pictures.**
  - `dpb_size` is at most 16 frames (MaxDpbFrames, Table A-1;
    `max_num_ref_frames` at most 16), plus those `Dpb::store` keeps past
    it where no picture can be bumped: one, or two when 16 long-term
    frames fill the buffer.
  - Every picture a picture's blocks refer to is in its reference lists,
    so it is in the buffer when that picture starts, with a slot no other
    picture there holds.
  - So two blocks of one picture name the same slot exactly when they name
    the same picture, which is what the deblocking filter compares
    (clause 8.7.2.1).
  - A long-term reference keeps its slot for as long as it stays, however
    many pictures pass, because the search skips the slots the buffer
    holds. The low byte of a picture counter, rejected in the first
    round, fails exactly there.
  - `slots_stay_distinct_in_a_full_buffer_with_long_term_frames` runs
    5,000 pictures through a buffer of 17 that keeps six long-term frames
    throughout. It drives the allocator with entries of its own; the
    buffer's own paths (`Dpb::store`, the frames of a `frame_num` gap) are
    covered by the identity and conformance runs. `free_slots_skip_the_held_ones_wrap_and_run_out` checks
    the search: the start, the wrap, a single free slot found from every
    start, `NO_SLOT` never handed out, and none when all 255 are held.
- **Temporal direct prediction.**
  - It looks up refPicCol, the picture a co-located block refers to, by
    slot in the current RefPicList0 (clause 8.4.1.2.3).
  - refPicCol was in the buffer when the co-located picture started. A
    conforming stream keeps it in RefPicList0, where it still holds its
    slot, so the lookup is exact.
  - Where a damaged stream lost it, `main` conceals with index 0. So does
    this branch, unless that slot has been handed out again since to a
    picture now in list 0. That takes at least about 237 slots handed out
    between the two (255 less those the buffer holds), and the output of
    such a stream may then differ from `main`'s, as any concealment
    choice would.
- **No slot free** returns `Error::Unsupported`. It cannot happen within
  the bounds above, at most 18 held against 255.
- **Fields, were they decoded.** A frame's two fields are two reference
  pictures to the deblocking filter, so a field's slot would need a
  parity bit. The 32 fields of 16 frames still fit a byte.

**Memory.** `MOTION_BYTES_PER_MB` is 192 against 320.
- A 4k picture keeps 6.2 MB of motion instead of 10.4 MB, a 1080p one
  1.57 MB instead of 2.61 MB.
- The decoder's memory estimate and `Geometry::stored_bytes` read the
  constant, and their test checks them against it.

Rejected:
- **The low byte of the decoder's picture counter, or a 16-bit
  identity:** exact only while every picture a picture refers to lies
  within 256 (or 65,536) pictures of it. A long-term reference need not.
- **16 bytes, keeping the four-byte identity and dropping the reference
  index,** as the first round found: motion vector prediction and
  colZeroFlag read the reference index of another picture's block.
- **Reference indices and slots per 8x8 quadrant, vectors per 4x4
  block, in arrays of their own:** smaller still, but every reader would
  index two arrays. It is a larger change, left until this one is
  measured.

### Bars

Fixed before the A/B run:
- **Host.** The A/B helper's VM of the 2.90 GHz class (Intel Xeon,
  family 6, model 106), every call with `--require-cpu "Intel(R) Xeon(R)
  Processor @ 2.90GHz"`, with the host-health gate before and after each
  call.
- **Streams and reference.** The training set, one call per class with
  the class's frame count, FFmpeg 9.0.2 (BtbN `n9.0.2-17-g2a571b6068`)
  as the last command.
- **Builds.** Two, timed in the same rounds and built alike (`dist`, one
  toolchain): `main` at `72b173b5` (`before`) and this branch (`after`).
- **Calls.** Three per class:
  - `g`: `--pin 2 --rounds 5`;
  - `gm`: the same with `MALLOC_MMAP_THRESHOLD_=131072` in the
    environment of every command. The arms allocate motion arrays of
    different sizes, so this is the placement guard ("Where the allocator
    puts the planes");
  - `t8`: `--threads 8`, unpinned, ten rounds ("Rounds at eight
    threads").

| Bar | Quantity | Threshold |
|---|---|---|
| MR-1 | one thread (`g`), median per-stream ratio `after` over `before`, discard, all 32 streams | at most **0.995**, upper end of the 95% interval below **1.000** |
| MR-2 | the same, write | at most **0.995** |
| MR-3 | the same per class, discard | at most **1.005** in each |
| MR-4 | mapped allocator (`gm`), discard, all 32 streams | at most **0.995**, upper end of the 95% interval below **1.000** |
| MR-5 | eight threads (`t8`), discard, all 32 streams; and each class | at most **1.005**; at most **1.010** in each class |
| MR-6 | output | the 32 training streams byte-identical to `before` at 1 and 8 threads; conformance 97 of 97 at 1, 2 and 8 threads and with scalar kernels |

- **Why these thresholds.** MR-1, MR-2 and MR-4 ask for the size of gain
  the first round measured, and MR-3 that no class pays for it.
- **MR-5's class bound** is 1.010 for round 18's reason: a class is eight
  streams, and at eight threads an eight-stream median moves by about a
  percent between identical builds.
- **Reading the bars.** `docs/measurements/h264-rounds/motion-12b-r2/analyze.py`
  reads MR-1 to MR-5 (`python3 -I analyze.py DIR g gm t8`) and lists
  every stream's ratios. The ratio to FFmpeg 9.0.2, and the share of
  streams faster than it, are reported beside them, naming the base.
- **One attempt.** A miss on any bar rejects the round, which is then
  recorded in `docs/measurements/h264-rejected.md`. A call is re-run only
  for a host fault the gate records.

## Round 20: an x86-64-v3 build tier

"CABAC under BMI2" found a whole-program `+bmi2` build 2.3% faster on eight
CABAC streams and no single site that holds it. This round asks how much a
build for a newer x86-64 level is worth to the whole decoder, and the
cheapest exact way to offer it.

### What the measurement says

Local, as information (`docs/measurements/h264-rounds/round20/local/`; a
development VM with the bar class's CPU, Intel Xeon @ 2.90 GHz, family 6,
model 106, not a bar run; CPU time at one thread, pinned, three rounds, all
32 training streams; `main` at `c17ae06` against `a7d8e4b`, which has the
same decoder code, built three ways). Median per-stream ratio to the
baseline build (`ab-whole.txt`):

| Build (`RUSTFLAGS`) | Median | Faster | Highest stream |
|---|---|---|---|
| `-C target-feature=+bmi2` | 0.992 | 26 of 32 | 1.023 |
| `-C target-feature=+bmi2,+lzcnt` | 0.982 | 30 of 32 | 1.022 |
| `-C target-cpu=x86-64-v3` | **0.958** | 32 of 32 | 0.994 |

The output of the v3 build is identical to the baseline's on 32 of 32
streams at one and eight threads (`identity-v3.txt`); its `decode` example
is 1.2% larger (`sizes.txt`). Most of v3's gain is beyond BMI2. Where it
goes, on `6da34958296c` (1080p, CABAC; `functions-v3.txt`, `perf` samples
per function, three rounds; 0.971 of the baseline's samples): the kernel
crate's dispatch, `predict::predict` (1,047 samples, 5.3% of the baseline
run), is inlined into the decoder's `predict_fast` once the caller has
AVX2 too, which grows by 515, a net 532 of the run's 584; the `Auto`
wrappers of `filter_chroma_mb` and `idct4x4_add_quad` are inlined the same
way, about even. In the control code the CABAC parse's functions fall by
321 samples (`decode_cabac`, `Cabac::mvd`, `parse_mvd`, `ref_idx`, the
levels of chroma DC) while others rise by about as much (`start_mb`,
`luma_block`, `deblock_rows`, `reconstruct_intra`), which three rounds do
not separate from noise. So on that stream the largest single part is the
call from the decoder into motion compensation's dispatch.

### Options weighed

What users get matters here: no default build contains the decoder
("Packaging: opt-in, separately packaged, with a disclaimer"). It reaches
users as a source build with a non-default feature (`cargo install
coreav-cli --features native-h264`, or the crate as a dependency), and a
package of it is the maintainer's to publish.

1. **A runtime-selected clone of the decode loop** (one hot-path site: a
   `#[target_feature]` instance of the slice decoder, chosen once by
   detection). It reaches every build, a source build included, without
   flags. But a `#[target_feature]` function passes its features only to
   what the compiler inlines into it, and the gain above sits in a dozen
   functions that are not inlined, in two crates. Keeping it exactly means
   a second, attributed instance of each of them; functions with the same
   features call each other safely, so the `unsafe` stays one call, but
   the twins run through `mb.rs`, `cabac.rs`, `syntax.rs` and the kernel
   crate's dispatch, and "CABAC under BMI2" saw a partial clone (`b1`)
   lose its gain to its caller. A clone of the slice loop alone keeps
   close to none of it; the CABAC parse cloned keeps at most the 1.6% its
   functions fell by on that stream; the dispatch part needs the kernel
   crate. Not now.
2. **A build tier**: the same source built for `x86-64-v3`, chosen at
   install or load time. It keeps all of the gain wherever it is used, adds
   no `unsafe` and no code, and is removed by deleting a build. It costs one
   more build of each decoder artifact and of its CI conformance run, and
   reaches a source build only when the user sets `RUSTFLAGS`.
3. **Rejected: `x86-64-v3` for the whole workspace** (`.cargo/config.toml`,
   as the alignment round did for its flags). Every default artifact (the
   CLI's binaries, the wheels) would then require the level, without the
   decoder in it to gain anything.
4. **Rejected for now: `x86-64-v4`** (AVX-512 everywhere). It narrows the
   hardware much further, and the kernels already choose their AVX-512 tier
   at run time. Not measured.

### Design

Option 2.

1. **Two tiers on x86-64**: the baseline (`x86-64`, what a build without
   flags gives) and v3 (`RUSTFLAGS="-C target-cpu=x86-64-v3"`: AVX, AVX2,
   BMI1, BMI2, F16C, FMA, LZCNT, MOVBE and the v2 set). The decoder's code
   does not change and does not know its tier; the kernels' run-time
   detection works as before in both (a v3 build can still take the
   AVX-512 tier where the CPU has it).
2. **Comparisons with FFmpeg name the tier.** Point 3 of "The kernel
   boundary" stays the rule for the baseline tier, the like-for-like
   comparison with FFmpeg's baseline build; the v3 tier is reported beside
   it, named, never in its place. The rounds keep gating on two arms of one
   tier, the baseline unless a round says otherwise.
3. **What ships is chosen at run time.** Distribution uses run-time
   selection: one binary, whose hot paths are chosen by
   coarse dispatch on the CPU's features. The v3 tier is therefore not a
   distribution build: it stays an opt-in build for source builds, and
   the ceiling against which that dispatch is measured. Not adopted, for
   that reason: a second conformance job in CI for the tier, and decoder
   packages that ship both tiers.
4. **Source builds**: the crate README's build section names the
   `RUSTFLAGS` of the v3 tier, with its measured gain.

### Bars

Fixed before the A/B run: `scripts/h264_parity.py` on the 2.90 GHz class
(Intel Xeon, family 6, model 106; `--require-cpu 'Intel(R) Xeon(R)
Processor @ 2.90GHz'`), with the host-health gate before and after each
call, on the training set, one call per class with the class's frame
count. If no VM of that class passes the gate before the run starts, the
run is made on a cloud container of that CPU instead, under the same bars,
and the result records it. FFmpeg 9.0.2 (BtbN `n9.0.2-17-g2a571b6068`)
runs as the last command. Two builds of one commit, this section's
(`before`: `cargo build --locked --profile dist --example decode -p

## Kernel round: a macroblock's chroma in one call

### What the measurement says

The profile of `main` at `084ee40` ("Kernel round: a reference's interior, found once"; one thread, the 32
training streams, `docs/measurements/h264-rounds/place-interior/profile/`) puts chroma intra prediction
(`x86::intra_chroma`) at 0.0055 of FFmpeg 9.0.2's time against FFmpeg's 0.0026 (0.0112 against 0.0045 at
720p), the largest intra gap left after the Intra_8x8 round, and the chroma residual's glue
(`reconstruct_chroma` 0.0076 and `chroma_qp` 0.0016, the transforms not included) at about half of the
reconstruction glue. At `93f7d87` (callgrind, one thread, `--discard`, the first six pictures of
`175433794e02.0.1080p`), the chroma of a macroblock is 24.5 million of 917 million instructions: the glue
11.1 million, the chroma calls of `idct4x4_add_quad` 8.9 million and `intra_chroma` 4.5 million. Each
component costs its own call, its own view and its own extent check, twice for an intra macroblock (the
prediction, then the residual), and the prediction goes through memory between the two.

Most of the transforms have nothing to transform. Counting the chroma residual a horizontal pair of 4x4 blocks
at a time over 300 pictures of `175433794e02` (a counting build, not kept): of about 4.1 million pairs of inter
macroblocks with a residual, about 3.4 million have a DC and no other coefficient in either block, and so do
about 0.8 million of 1.2 million pairs of intra macroblocks; on `a6af290d9053.0.1080p`, 1.3 million of 1.9
million inter pairs. The 2x2 DC transform gives every block of a component with a coded DC block a DC, so the
kernel transformed all four blocks, AC levels or not.

### Design

1. **Two calls per macroblock, both components each.** `Kernels::chroma_residual_mb(cb, cr, dc, ac,
   ac_nz)` adds an inter macroblock's residual to both 8x8 blocks, and `Kernels::intra_chroma_mb(cb, cr,
   mode, dc, ac, ac_nz)` predicts both blocks and adds theirs. The decoder makes one call where it made up to
   four (`reconstruct_chroma`), and none for an inter macroblock without a chroma residual.
2. **The DC apart from the AC.** Each block's DC value (the 2x2 transform's output, scaled) comes in `dc`,
   and replaces the block's first coefficient; `ac_nz` says which blocks have other coefficients, and a
   block whose bit is clear has them taken as zero. The decoder no longer writes the DC into the coefficient
   blocks, so `chroma_ac_nz` records only the blocks the entropy decoder wrote and `MbData::reset` clears
   only those.
3. **A pair with a DC alone needs no transform.** A 4x4 block whose only coefficient is its DC `d`
   transforms to `d` in every sample before rounding: in each pass a row (then a column) holding `d` and
   three zeros gives `d` four times (Equations 8-338 to 8-345 with every other input zero). So a pair
   without other coefficients is its DC vector repeated, the left block's DC in the low lane and the right
   one's in the high lane, rounded and added as a transformed pair is (`add_residual8`); a pair with
   neither is skipped. A pair where either block has other coefficients is transformed as before, its
   coefficients masked to zero for a block without them and the DCs blended into the first row.
4. **Both components' prediction in one set of vectors.** The two components share their neighbours'
   availability and mode, so one 256-bit vector holds both components' edges, p[0..7, -1] and p[-1, 0..7]
   of Cb in the low lane and of Cr in the high one (zero where absent, as in the reference). Vertical and
   horizontal are byte shuffles of it; plane is the 16-bit rows of the earlier kernel with each component's
   a, b and c in its lane. DC (clause 8.3.4.1 to 8.3.4.3) is the eight sums of four samples (two multiply-adds
   by one) and, per quarter, `(A + B + 4) >> 3` of two of them picked by a permute from a table by
   availability: the diagonal quarters average the top and left sums with both sides present, and a
   quarter that takes one side's sum `X` alone picks it twice, since `(2X + 4) >> 3 = (X + 2) >> 2`.
   Without either side the prediction is 128. Each component's rows then go to its residual in registers
   (item 3), and its eight rows are written once.
5. **The DC transform and scaling in the decoder, leaner.** The 2x2 transform as two butterflies, and the
   scaling as one product with `LevelScale4x4(qP % 6, 0, 0) << (qP / 6)`: the levels are clipped to 16
   bits and a scale is below 2^13, so the product is exact in 64 bits and equal to the clause's
   `(f * LevelScale) << (qP / 6)`.

The x86 kernels check each view once: `IntraRows::of` for each of the two intra views (the vector kernel
takes them together only where their availability is the same, which is always the decoder's case;
otherwise the reference), and `rows_at_mut` for each block of the inter call; the rows are read and
written through those pointers (`docs/unsafe-sites.md`, the row for `simd/x86.rs`, updated). The AVX-512 tier runs these kernels; arm64 and the portable build run the reference, the scalar
prediction and their `idct4x4_add_quad` a component at a time. `intra_chroma` stays in the trait as the
reference's piece.

A lesson of the first draft, kept here because it is not visible in the result: a closure or an array
`map` that holds intrinsics compiles to a function without the caller's target features, and LLVM will not
inline an AVX2 intrinsic into it, so each became a call (`_mm256_shuffle_epi8` and `_mm256_set_m128i`
out of line, and the rows spilled around `try_map`). The kernels write such steps as `#[inline(always)]`
functions or straight code.

Rejected:

- **One call for both kinds over intra views**, `mode` an `Option`: the first form. Its inter macroblocks paid
  for two intra views and two `IntraRows` checks, about 30 instructions a macroblock more than the calls a
  component at a time, and before item 3 the whole decode took more instructions than `main`.
- **Finding the DC-only blocks in `idct4x4_add_quad`** by testing the coefficients: it would serve luma
  too, but costs a test on every pair, while the decoder knows which blocks have AC levels. Luma is left to
  the transform round.
- **The DC transform in the kernel, in vectors**: about 20 instructions a component; its scaling needs the
  64-bit product or a proof of range, and it is the decoder's arithmetic (clause 8.5.11.2).
- **The left column by byte unpacks** of eight 8-byte loads (about 15 instructions a component against about
  25): left for later; about 0.05% of the instructions at most.

Prior art: none. The DC identity of item 3 is the transform's equations; the rest is the earlier kernels'.

Bit-exact by construction and by test: `chroma_mb_matches_the_reference` runs both calls through `Simd`
against `Scalar`, and against the residual built block by block from the trait's description (every
combination of neighbours and components that differ in them, modes 0 to 3 and out of range, DC and AC
over their range, blocks with a DC alone, with AC alone and with neither, every mask, strides from 8 and
differing between the components, planes that end at the block's last sample); seven mutations of the
kernel (a DC pick, the sides of the pick table, the zero-DC test, the DC blend mask, masking the DC with
the AC, a horizontal shuffle, the DC-only value) each fail it. A new fuzz target, `chroma_mb`, compares
`Simd` and `Auto` with `Scalar` for both calls. The Miri harness
`docs/measurements/h264-rounds/chroma-recon/tools/miri` runs both calls through `Simd` and `Auto` against
the reference in planes that start at the first neighbour the view names (the block's first sample for the
residual) and end at the block's last sample, from misaligned bases, with the components at different
strides.

Instructions (callgrind, one thread, `--discard`, the first pictures of each of the 32 training streams;
information, not a bar; `chroma-recon/instructions.txt`): `k` over `base` 0.9940 at the median, from
0.9866 to 0.9996, every stream fewer. On the first six pictures of `175433794e02.0.1080p` (builds with line
tables), the chroma falls from 24.5 to about 20.5 million instructions.

### Bars

Fixed before any timing of `k`, on the method of the Intra_8x8 round: two decoders in the same rounds, built
alike (`cargo build --locked --profile dist --example decode -p coreav-h264`, one toolchain, `RUSTFLAGS`

## Round 21: two entropy loops

Rejected by its bars E-2 and E-4 (the result is at the end): not merged.
The code stays on `rejected/h264-entropy-small` (at `0b73828`: the code
measured, `1395e3b`, and tests added later), on `main` at
`40f29a6`, with a row in `docs/measurements/h264-rejected.md`; what
follows describes that branch.

Two small changes in entropy decoding, one round: the level loop of a CAVLC
block, and mvd_lX in CABAC. Each was measured alone first; neither is
large, and both are kept in safe Rust.

### What the measurement says

- **CAVLC levels.** After round 19 the fused block decoder is still the
  largest single function on the CAVLC streams (20% of the samples on
  `6f7799768413`, `main` at `c17ae06`, local). Per level, the loop read
  level_prefix, skipped it, chose level_suffix's size among three cases,
  read the suffix, and turned levelCode into a level with two branches.
  Below a prefix of 14, which is nearly every level, the suffix's size is
  suffixLength and levelCode has no other term.
- **mvd_lX.** `Cabac::mvd` is up to 7% of the samples on the CABAC streams
  with the most motion (`175433794e02`), where half of all values have a
  prefix of nine regular bins and a suffix. Its loop went through
  `Cabac::decision`, storing the engine's three values and the context
  state back to memory at every bin; bins 4 to 8 share one context, so each
  reloaded the state the bin before had just stored.
- Local, as information (`round21/local/ab.txt`; a development VM with the bar
  class's CPU, CPU time at one thread, five rounds): the levels change
  0.987 to 0.991 on the six CAVLC streams in three runs (base `main` at
  `93f7d87`), every stream faster; the mvd change 0.997 on six CABAC streams
  (base `c17ae06`), from 0.990 to 1.008.

### Design

1. **The levels.** Below a prefix of 14, level_prefix, its terminating one
   and the suffixLength bits of level_suffix are read as one field, and one
   skip consumes them. levelCode becomes a level without a branch: the
   magnitude is levelCode / 2 + 1 for either parity (clause 9.2.2.1),
   negated where levelCode is odd. suffixLength's step up is a table by
   suffixLength. A prefix of 14 or more goes to an out-of-line function
   that keeps the clause's three cases and its checks, unchanged.
   Tried and dropped (`local/ab.txt`): every code table at 256 entries so
   that a masked index needs no bounds check, and the window's position
   derived from its end rather than updated at every read; both within the
   noise.
2. **mvd_lX.** The engine is copied into registers for the whole value and
   written back once; bins 1 to 3 use their fixed context increments; the
   run of bins 4 to 8 holds context 6's state in a register and stores it
   once. The suffix and the sign are as before.

Output is unchanged: identical to `main` at `40f29a6` on the 32 training
streams at one and eight threads (`round21/identity.txt`); the unit tests
include 200,000 random CAVLC blocks against the clause-by-clause decoder.

### Bars

Fixed before the A/B run, on the method of round 19: `scripts/h264_parity.py`
on the 2.90 GHz class (`--require-cpu 'Intel(R) Xeon(R) Processor @
2.90GHz'`), the host gate before and after each call, the training set at
the class frame counts, FFmpeg 9.0.2 last; a cloud container of that CPU
only if no VM passes the gate before the start, recorded. Two builds alike
(`dist`, one toolchain, `RUSTFLAGS` unset): `main` at `40f29a6` (`before`)
or the `main` this branch is rebased onto, named in the result, and this
branch (`after`). No allocation changes, so no mapped-allocator call. Two
calls per class: `g`, `--pin 2 --rounds 5`; `t8`, `--threads 8`, unpinned,
ten rounds.

The CABAC subset is fixed by a property of the streams, not by timing:
the thirteen of the 26 CABAC streams with the most context-coded mvd bins
per second of the baseline's decoding (`round21/mvd_subset.py`, from
`mvd-histograms.txt` and round 20's local baseline times; the list in

| Bar | Quantity | Threshold |
|---|---|---|
| E-1 | one thread (`g`), median per-stream ratio `after` over `before`, discard, the six CAVLC streams | at most **0.993**, upper end of the 95% interval below 1.000 |
| E-2 | the same, the thirteen mvd-heavy CABAC streams | at most **0.998**, and below the control's median |
| E-3 | one thread, discard and write, all 32 streams; and each class | at most **1.000**; at most **1.005** in each |
| E-4 | eight threads (`t8`), discard, all 32; and each class | at most **1.003**; at most **1.005** in each |
| E-5 | output | the 32 training streams byte-identical to `before` at 1 and 8 threads; conformance 97 of 97 at 1, 2 and 8 threads and with scalar kernels |

E-1 asks for about half the local gain. E-2 is weak evidence on its own:

and re-run; the round passes or fails as one.
`docs/measurements/h264-rounds/round21/analyze.py` reads E-1 to E-4
(`python3 -I analyze.py DIR g t8`).
